title: Technology at Service of Ecosystem Restoration: How AI can Support Restoring and Protecting Natural Ecosystems Around the Globe
organizers: Microsoft (Ms Weronika Kuna ) UNEP-GRID Warsaw (Ms Maria Andrzejewska )
key_issues: Discussion on how cloud computing and AI can contribute to ecosystem restoration, with a focus on the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration (2021-2030). Topics included the role of technology in achieving Sustainable Development Goals, particularly those related to poverty eradication, climate action, and biodiversity conservation.
policy_recommendations: Encouragement for collaboration between scientists, tech industry, environmental activists, and governmental bodies to integrate advanced technologies in ecosystem restoration plans for the UN decade.
description: The United Nations have proclaimed the years 2021-2030 to be the Decade on Ecosystem Restoration. As declared by the UN agencies in charge of this initiative, namely: UN Environment Programme (UNEP) and Food and Agricultural Organization (FAO), the better the condition of the Earth’s ecosystems, the healthier the whole planet and its human inhabitants. Improvement of the state of the ecosystems is central to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals, particularly those pertaining to ending poverty, combatting the climate crisis, or halting the still continuing massive loss of biodiversity. Modern advanced technologies are today an important part of the solution and should be integrated in plans for the upcoming UN decade. We would like to invite scientist, tech industry, environment activists and governmental bodies to discuss how cloud computing and AI bring value to the matter.
preparatory_focus: To prepare for discussions on the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration (2021-2030) by exploring the role of AI and cloud computing in ecosystem restoration and sustainable development.

title: Digital Brain
session_type: Hybrid interactive discussion panel and presentation with short films from the exhibition
organizers: Copernicus Science Center
key_issues: Discussion on the role of AI in decision-making, trust in AI systems, privacy, security, and intimacy in the context of AI technologies.
format: Hybrid interactive discussion panel and presentation with short films from the exhibition
description: What kind of decision would you let an AI system make for you? Would you trust it to manage your daily tasks, public image, or romantic relations? History of science teaches us that major scientific revolutions every time initiated new age that changed human mankind in the fundamental way. The Copernican, Darwinian and Quantum Revolution turned upside down our claim about role and place of man in the world. Development of Artificial Intelligence Systems seems to lead to the new turning point in our history. The idea for some is delightful, and for others fearful. Such concern appears in the media more and more often and as it is an important issue the Copernicus Science Center decided to tackle it by making new exhibition "The future is today Digital brain". "The future is today Digital brain" consists of the cutting-edge technology samples that unavoidably trigger the questions of the trust, privacy, security, and intimacy definitions. During the panel we would like to collect your answers on the most burning questions (From both online and on-site participants) to stay together and push our discussion further!
preparatory_focus: To prepare for discussions on AI's role in society, trust, privacy, security, and intimacy, and to gather perspectives from participants for further dialogue.

title: Cross-sectoral cooperation for digital inclusion
organizers: Kyndryl Poland Polish Economic Institute
speakers: President Orange Foundation Open Future Foundation Co-Founder - Dr. Aleksander Tarkowski
IBM - Director for Government Affairs Jolanta Jaworska
Maria Thun-Janowska, Corporate Affairs Director for CEE & EM, Board Member, Kyndryl Poland
key_issues: Digital exclusion in Poland, the impact of the pandemic, infrastructural, skill, and financial barriers, social exclusion, and the need for collaboration between Government, business, and NGO to reduce the digital divide.
policy_recommendations: Collaboration between Government, business, and NGO to decrease the digital divide.
description: Cross-sectoral cooperation for digital inclusion (06.12.2021, 09:30 - 10:10 CET). Our discussion is to bring closer actions taken to combat the digital divide by the institutions and sectors represented by the speakers. The cross sectoral cooperation and coordination of projectstowards one common goal also refers to the implementation of the UN's Sustainable Development Goal 17 "Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development". The starting point of the discussion is the increased awareness of the persistent problem of digital exclusion in Poland, which, together with the pandemic, has increasingly become a major problem in many regions of our country. Exclusion suddenly manifested itself in many layers - infrastructural, lack of digital skills and financial, and it is also intertwined with social exclusion. This is shown, amongst others, in the recent report of the Orange Foundation ( https://fundacja.orange.pl/strefa-wiedzy/post/wykluczenie-spoleczno-cyf…) and in the Polish Economic Institute report published recently (https: // pie.net.pl/nierownomierna-jakosc-dostepu-do-internetu-w-polsce-w-dobie-pandemii-covid-19/). Moreover, the persistent digital exclusion, with the ever-increasing digitization of life, will deepen the divisions in our society. How can we (Govermnet, business and NGO) work together to have impact in decreasing the digital divide?
onsite_moderator: Ignacy Święcicki - Digital Economy Team Leader, Polish Economic Institute
sdgs: SDG 17: Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
preparatory_focus: To prepare for discussions on digital inclusion and cross-sectoral cooperation in the main IGF event by highlighting the issue of digital exclusion in Poland and the need for collaboration between Government, business, and NGO.

title: Closing the gap between the theory of digital security and the practice of insecurity
organizers: Dynamic Coalition on Internet Standards, safety and security (DC-ISSS)
key_issues: The gap between theoretical digital security and practical insecurity by design; the need for secure by design principles in ICT development; challenges in implementing global security standards and best practices.
policy_recommendations: Promote secure by design principles in ICT development; enhance collaboration across stakeholder groups to adopt global security standards; improve end-user protection against online threats.
format: Breakout sessions and plenary reporting including final comments
description: This workshop invites you to participate in a discussion about Internet security revolving around one question: How do we close the gap between the theory of security and the daily practice of what is in effect insecurity by design? The Dynamic Coalition on Internet Standards, Security and Safety (DC-ISSS) focuses on the topic that has been identified as a hugely important driver for establishing a safer and more secure Internet: the widespread global adoption of existing, security related Internet standards and ICT best practices. Cyber security is an issue gaining more and more public and political attention due to the ever increasing number of cyber attacks and threats. Many experts discuss it, propose policies to proceed towards a safer Internet and digital environment, create new Internet standards and ICT best practices aimed at reducing existing vulnerabilities, etc.. Despite all these efforts the Internet and ICTs has not become significantly safer. There are hundreds if not thousands of these standards and best practices. Many organisations work actively to promote digital security but often with the focus on one specific component of digital security, where their specific competence and background makes them an expert. And then there is the end user who is faced with all these threats. How can the end-user protect his or her privacy and security online? It is time to look at the whole picture and acknowledge that there is a considerable gap between the theory of cyber security and the daily practice of insecurity by design. Many, if not all, vulnerabilities and threats can be prevented when the ICT industry develops and manufactures devices and applications based on secure by design principles, i.e. containing state of
preparatory_focus: To facilitate pre-discussion on the topic of Internet security standards and practices, and to prepare for the main IGF discussions by identifying gaps and recommendations for secure by design principles in ICT development.

title: IGF LAC Space
organizers: LACTLD
key_issues: Presentation of projects contributing to economic and social inclusion, human rights, and universal access; discussion of research on Internet use, development, evolution, and regulation in the region.
format: The session will be divided into a first part of presentations focused on projects carried out by organizations in Latin America and the Caribbean, and a second part of research presentations focused on issues of regional relevance. The final minutes of the session will be for questions and answers raised by the participants in order to encourage an open and informed dialogue.
description: The fifth edition of the IGF LAC Space will bring together organizations, stakeholders and researchers from the Latin America and Caribbean Internet community to present and share projects and research undertaken over the past year. During the first part of the session, organizations from the Latin American and Caribbean region will share their leading projects and how these have contributed to economic and social inclusion, advanced human rights and ensured universal access. The second part of the session will be dedicated to presenting and discussing research papers that have addressed the use, development, evolution and regulation of the Internet in Latin America and the Caribbean. The session will thus seek to foster informed discussion and new opportunities for regional collaboration. The session will be divided into three different parts: 1) project presentations, 2) research presentations, and 3) time for questions and discussion. This way, the time allocated for presentations and the time allocated for questions and discussion will be clearly defined. The session moderators will be responsible for sticking to the agenda and organizing the participation of speakers and attendees in order to meet the objectives of the session and foster informed regional dialogue in an online environment.
preparatory_focus: To prepare for the main IGF event by facilitating regional dialogue and collaboration through the presentation of projects and research on Internet governance issues relevant to Latin America and the Caribbean.

title: Exploring Co-Regulatory Mechanisms on Platform Governance in the Indian Policy Context
organizers: University College London - Department of Science, Technology, Engineering and Public Policy (STEaPP)
speakers: Siddhant Chatterjee, University College London (UCL), Academic
key_issues: Discussion on problematic provisions of India’s Intermediary Rules, concerns about free speech, privacy, and the impact of regulations on innovation and the internet economy. Critique of self-regulation by intermediaries and the need for adaptive, multi-stakeholder approaches.
format: Presentation (20 - 22 mins) followed by a Q/A session (10 - 8 mins)
description: The recent iteration of India’s Intermediary Rules have been widely touted to be problematic by stakeholders across the spectrum. With concerning provisions on content takedowns, timeframes and traceability that are detrimental to free speech, expression and personal privacy of users, these regulations might have the potential to not only threaten their digital freedom, but also endanger the concept of an Open Internet. While the State’s intent behind these regulations might be constructive; to prevent harms and mitigate instances of mis/disinformation and hate speech, the efficacy and impact of policy instruments deployed for the same, are debatable. Further, some of these provisions can stifle innovation and retard the internet economy in the country. Self-regulation by intermediaries — the other alternative here, has also failed to find ground in India. Such a policy standoff demands the need for adaptive, smart and multi-stakeholder driven collaborativ
preparatory_focus: To provide pre-discussion on co-regulatory mechanisms in platform governance within the Indian policy context, contributing to the main IGF discussions on internet governance.

title: IGF 2021 Day 0 Event #2 IFIP 60th Anniversary: Future of Information Processing
organizers: IFIP
key_issues: Digital education in a rapidly evolving digital environment needs to be both sustainable and adaptive. Technologies change, but learners' and educators' needs are paramount and tend to be more stable. Digital education concerns all levels of education and all subjects, but a strong basis is computer science and computational thinking is important.
policy_recommendations: Policy makers in educational fields need to realise access for all people to well-founded digital education. Educators and researchers need to base their resources and activities on the needs of learners, instead of just following the pace of technological changes.
description: The International Federation for Information Processing (IFIP) provides policy-makers with an unbiased source of evidence-based knowledge and expertise in the field of information and communication technology (ICT). To celebrate IFIP's 60th anniversary, its members and affiliates will address the future of information processing with a focus on the intersection between information technology and society. This session will publicise the main outcomes of a series of events addressing educational and social challenges to achieving “Sustainable Education in a Digital Age of Rapidly Emerging Technologies,” and how to overcome them. This session is under the umbrella of the IFIP TC3 Zanzibar Declaration, which began in March of 2021 and will continue until November of 2021.
preparatory_focus: To prepare for discussions on digital education and its challenges in the context of rapidly emerging technologies, as part of the IFIP TC3 Zanzibar Declaration initiative.

title: Constitutionalising the Digital Frontier: Past, Present, and Future
organizers: Research Program on Digital Constitutionalism, Institute for Internet & the Just Society, Berlin
key_issues: Discussion on constitutionalising the digital frontier, exploring past, present, and future developments, with sub-questions on the proposal for a Day 0 Event, ongoing projects, and ideas for further discussion.
subtheme: Constitutionalising the Digital Frontier: Past, Present, and Future
format: Roundtable Discussion followed by a Q&A from the Audience
description: A Roundtable Discussion followed by a Q&A with the audience around the theme 'Constitutionalising the Digital Frontier: Past, Present, and Future'. The session will include sub-questions provided to speakers in advance, with each participant having 5 minutes to present thoughts and research. The moderator will open up the floor for a conversation on all ideas presented.
preparatory_focus: To organise a Roundtable Discussion followed by a Q&A with the audience around the theme 'Constitutionalising the Digital Frontier: Past, Present, and Future' as a preparatory event for the main IGF.

title: Advancing Internet Universality ROAM principles and Indicators (IUIs) for the Internet United
organizers: UNESCO, IGF Dynamic Coalition of Internet Universality ROAM-X indicators project
key_issues: Showcasing the overall achievement of Internet Universality indicators project and presenting national implementation progresses.
description: UNESCO, jointly with IGF Dynamic Coalition of Internet Universality ROAM-X indicators project, is organizing a 3-hour special pre-event on Internet Universality ROAM-X Indicators (IUIs) at IGF 2021 from Day 0, on December 6th 2021 to conduct its annual showcasing the overall achievement of Internet Universality indicators project and presenting national implementation progresses.
preparatory_focus: To conduct its annual showcasing of the Internet Universality indicators project and present national implementation progresses as a preparatory event before the main IGF 2021 meeting.

title: Ensuring Diversity in the AI World
organizers: UNESCO
key_issues: Significant lack of diversity in the field of AI, gender and ethnic/cultural biases in AI technologies, negative impacts on accuracy, reliability, and harmful consequences.
description: This session aims to address the significant lack of diversity in the field of AI and propose solutions for tackling it. Currently, the teams developing AI technologies are predominantly males, and much of AI technologies is produced by a few companies concentrated geographically in a limited number of countries. This has led to well-recorded gender and ethnic/cultural biases in these technologies, which negatively affect their accuracy and reliability and often result in harmful consequences that are disproportionately bor
preparatory_focus: Focus on pre-discussion themes related to AI diversity and biases, preparing for broader discussions on AI governance.

title: IGF 2021 Day 0 Event #3 GigaNet Annual Symposium 2021
organizers: GigaNet
key_issues: Discussion on platform regulation, including the paradox of platform monopoly between Tencent and Facebook, and the Telegram ban as an example of censorship 'made in Russia' facing a global internet.

description: GigaNet Symposium at IGF – 6 December 2021 Join the debate on our live tweeting-> #GigaNet2021 Program (all times indicated below are in CET) Register to get your Zoom link for Symposium HERE ! 14.00-14.05 Introduction and Welcome Dmitry Epstein, GigaNet Chair Roxana Radu, Program Chair 2021 14.05-15.35 Parallel Sessions 1 PANEL 1A: PLATFORM REGULATION The Paradox of Platform Monopoly between Tecent and Facebook :Theory, Practice and Governance , Tianchan Mao and Yu Wen The Telegram Ban: How censorship “made in Russia” faces a global Internet , Ksenia Ermoshi
preparatory_focus: Capacity building and pre-discussion on internet governance themes for the main IGF event

title: Youth Perspectives on Digital Civility
organizers: Microsoft and NetMission
key_issues: Discussion on digital civility, safer online interactions, youth perspectives, and the role of various stakeholders in promoting online safety and responsible behavior.
policy_recommendations: The session emphasized the importance of youth participation in shaping digital civility and online safety policies, and highlighted the need for collaborative efforts between private sector, civil society, and media to foster safer online environments.
format: Moderated discussion with Q&A from the Audience (in-person and online)
description: In 2017, Microsoft launched its inaugural Council for Digital Good, a group of 15 teens from across the United States that worked to advance digital civility and safer online interactions. The Council released a 15
preparatory_focus: This session served as a preparatory event to gather youth perspectives on digital civility and online safety, providing input for future discussions and policy development at the main IGF event.

title: APAC Collaborative Governance for Better Connectivity
organizers: Korea Internet & Security Agency(KISA)
speakers: SHI YOUNG CHANG, Deputy General Researcher, Korea Internet & Security Agency(KISA) / .KR ccTLD registry
Leonid Todorov, GM, Asia Pacific Top Level Domain Association(APTLD)
key_issues: DNS as critical internet infrastructure, challenges in DNS governance in Asia-Pacific, increasing DNS queries from abroad, cost of expanding DNS root servers
description: Background Information : Domain Name System(DNS) is one of the essential Critical Internet Infrastructures because website problems based on DNS error lead to stop core businesses of the company, and causes significant harms to end-users(e.g. Dyn DDoS attacks). Now, the Internet users in Asia-Pacific region have steadily increased over the years with IoT growth and the COVID19 pandemic; and, DNS queries originated from abroad have significantly increased in recently. However, DNS policies of ccTLD managers in Asia-Pacific region have been operated separately with each ccTLD’s national legislation. Moreover, current status of simply increasing physical DNS root servers costs a lot of money to build and operate the DNS system; and, ccTLD
preparatory_focus: Focus on DNS governance and collaborative approaches to improve internet connectivity in the Asia-Pacific region as a preparatory discussion for main IGF events

title: Cyber Stability Games: Learning the Complexities of Technical Attribution
organizers: Anastasiya Kazakova, Senior Public Affairs Manager, Kaspersky (Eastern European Group); Pierre Delcher, Senior Security Researcher, Global Research and Analysis Team (GReAT), Kaspersky (Western European Group); Vladimir Radunović, Director, E-diplomacy and Cybersecurity Programmes, DiploFoundation (Eastern European Group)
speakers: Anastasiya Kazakova, Senior Public Affairs Manager, Kaspersky (Eastern European Group)
Pierre Delcher, Senior Security Researcher, Global Research and Analysis Team (GReAT), Kaspersky (Western European Group)
Vladimir Radunović, Director, E-diplomacy and Cybersecurity Programmes, DiploFoundation (Eastern European Group)
regional_focus: Eastern European Group, Western European Group
key_issues: The session focused on technical attribution, cyber threats, and the importance of international cooperation in responding to security events. It emphasized the need for technical analysis and evaluation to maintain stability in cyberspace.
policy_recommendations: The session recommended capacity building through interactive training exercises like the Cyber Stability Games to improve technical attribution skills and cyber defense strategies.
format: Cyber capacity building exercise in the format of simulation/gamification based security training
description: Cyber Stability Games is a capacity building exercise organized by DiploFoundation and Kaspersky to help all professionals who do not have a technical background learn the complexities of technical attribution. The session is interactive and involves participants in a simulated environment where they face a series of unexpected cyber threats while trying to maintain confidence. The training uses Kaspersky Interactive Protection Simulation (KIPS) to teach players how to build a cyber defense strategy by making choices among the best proactive and reactive controls available.
preparatory_focus: This session was designed as a preparatory event to build capacity in technical attribution and cyber defense strategies for professionals without a technical background, serving as a pre-discussion theme for the main IGF event.

title: Internet Governance Challenges in Crisis Periods; Covid 19
organizers: Rwenzo Green Associates Ltd
key_issues: The session discusses the challenges faced by educational institutions during the Covid-19 pandemic, the shift to online learning, and the role of EdTech start-ups in addressing these challenges. It also covers the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and challenges of e-learning modes during crises.
policy_recommendations: The session suggests that academic institutions should adopt flexible and blended learning approaches, invest in EdTech solutions, and develop policies that support online learning and lifelong education.
description: The session explores the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic on education, the transition to online learning, and the growth of EdTech start-ups. It discusses the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and challenges of e-learning modes during crises, as well as the importance of policy support for online education.
preparatory_focus: This session serves as a preparatory event to discuss the challenges of internet governance during crisis periods, particularly focusing on the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic on education and the role of online learning in crisis management.

preparatory_focus: Focus on capacity building, training, or pre-discussion themes related to digital identity and gender equality for policy making and practice.

organizers: GEODE - Kaspersky - CIGREF

description: The session included a presentation of multi-stakeholder collective work within WG6 on key initiatives for ICT supply chain security, and a panel discussion with a broader audience.

title: Who is coding it and deploying it? | Internet Governance Forum
organizers: Alliance for Inclusive Algorithms
key_issues: Exploring the ideas behind Feminist AI and the concept of using AI & Algorithmic Decision-Making (ADM) to deliver equality outcomes designed with inclusion at the core to create new opportunities & proactive, innovative correction of inequities

format: Four regional panels of 45 minutes each. 180 minutes.
description: Sharing the current state of Feminist AI focussed on economic and social inclusion and human rights, an interactive panel taking a tour of Latin America & the Caribbean, Asia, and MENA region, exploring the ideas behind Feminist AI and the concept of using AI & Algorithmic Decision-Making (ADM) to deliver equality outcomes designed with inclusion at the core to create new opportunities & proactive, innovative correction of inequities -- and how research, policy & technology investment and intervention could open an era of unprecedented gender inclusion
preparatory_focus: Pre-discussion theme for main IGF event on Feminist AI and algorithmic decision-making

title: Are we shaping the digital market to all citizens?
organizers: ECHAlliance – European Connected Health Alliance
speakers: Charalampos Vassiliou, BYTE Computer (H2020 SmartWork project)
Claudia Fernandez Rivera, Technological University Dublin (Interreg EU_SHAFE project)

Alexander Peine, Ultrecht University (H2020 Gatekeeper project)
Marie Kannampuzha, UN Global Pulse Finland
key_issues: The session discusses the implementation of the sustainable digital European society, focusing on digital access and inclusivity in research and innovation projects. It addresses the challenges of making digital solutions accessible to all, including older adults, persons with disabilities, and unprivileged groups, and the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on digital transformation and access to services.
policy_recommendations: The session emphasizes the need for designing accessible ICTs, increasing digital literacy, and ensuring equal opportunities in digital access. It highlights the importance of stakeholder collaboration to address the digital divide and its implications for participatory democracy and public services.
description: The European vision for 2030 is a digital society where no-one is left behind. This is the cornerstone of the Digital Compass 2030, recently launched by EC President von der Leyen... (full description as provided in the text)
preparatory_focus: To prepare for the main IGF discussions by exploring the practical implementation of digital inclusion and accessibility in European research and innovation projects, and to highlight the importance of addressing the digital divide in the context of the pandemic.

title: Biotechnology and Cybersecurity. The Post-Pandemic Cooperation
organizers: centurialabs.org
key_issues: Analysis of international standards relating to biotechnology and laboratory instruments, examination of generic and cyber threats, analysis of biotechnology threats from targeted cyber attacks, discussion on bioterrorism, and importance of international cooperation.
description: The analysis focuses on the study of international standards relating to biotechnology and laboratory instruments. Some types of generic threats and cyber threats are analyzed. Then we go to analyze the threats of biotechnology that come from targeted cyber attacks. Some hints on bioterrorism. Finally, some observations on the importance of international cooperation. Participants will be able to ask questions at the end of each speaker's speech. There is also a space dedicated to questions. All speakers indicate contacts and can deliver materials to all participants. IGF's platform will be used, but attendees can ask the speakers questions and contact them later. In addition, one of the speakers could be present on site.
rapporteur: Costanza Matteuzzi, Willian Nonnis, Giovanni Caria
preparatory_focus: Focus on capacity building and pre-discussion themes related to biotechnology and cybersecurity cooperation in the post-pandemic context.

title: Internet Commons Forum
organizers: FGV, ISOC, APC, Centrum Cyfrowe and Free2Air
speakers: Yu Ping, Office of the UN Secretary-General's Envoy on Technology
Lucy Harris, UNICEF / Digital Public Good Alliance
key_issues: The structures of the Internet affect us more deeply than ever before, reaching out to all aspects of our lives, from our societies and cultures to our finances and politics – to our very individual human behaviours and identities. This event will explore different views of Internet Commons, Digital Commons, and Digital Public Goods, exploring strategies for a less concentrated Internet.
policy_recommendations: The 'Digital Commons' and 'Digital Public Goods' are powerful concepts to operationalize digital rights. However, there is a need to improve the mechanisms through which they are organised and put into practice. Initiatives that can be initially commons-oriented might suffer proprietary capture through market forces, especially from large internet platforms that act as intermediaries.
subtheme: Digital Commons and Digital Public Goods
description: The structures of the Internet affect us more deeply than ever before, reaching out to all aspects of our lives, from our societies and cultures to our finances and politics – to our very individual human behaviours and identities. This event will explore different views of Internet Commons, Digital Commons, and Digital Public Goods, exploring strategies for a less concentrated Internet. The Internet Commons Forum (ICF) has been jointly organised by FGV, ISOC, APC, Centrum Cyfrowe and Free2Air, since 2019. The ICF aims at gathering thinkers and doers that are developing ideas and solutions for a less concentrated and more just Internet. See http://www.intcomforum.org/ Internet Commons Forum | #ICF | For a more just Internet The structures of the Internet affect us more deeply than ever before, reaching out to all aspects of our lives. The Internet Commons Forum aims at gathering thinkers and doers that are developing ideas and solutions for a less concentrated and more just Internet. www.intcomforum.org The ICF will feature well-respected thinkers and doers exposing their ideas and innovative approaches to digital commons, with regard to the development of Internet access infrastructure, digital platforms, digital policies and data. This workshop will aim at fostering a collaborative discussion with the participants in order to identify concrete actions and strategies for collaboration and implementation of digital commons. Organisers will make use of a variety of social networks to encourage and diversify participation
preparatory_focus: Focus on capacity building, training, or pre-discussion themes related to Internet Commons and Digital Public Goods to prepare for the main IGF discussions.

title: Our Internet Voices: Designing Inclusive Spaces
organizers: Emerging Youth Initiative
regional_focus: Africa, Europe, Latin and Caribbean, America
key_issues: Challenges and opportunities of designing inclusive online events, tools and platforms for open online events, ensuring safety and meaningful participation in online events
subtheme: Inclusive Design Practices for Online Events
description: A practical session to look at the challenges and opportunities as events increasingly move online. It's not enough to assume that online events will be more inclusive, they need to be designed with inclusion in mind. We will share experiences and then facilitate attendees to engage with case studies so they can test methods of designing inclusive online spaces. We aim to extract objective experiences from participants by giving them questions on pressing matters and key scenarios as internet leaders to see their thinking and solutions in creating equal online spaces and a well-distributed fair internet ecosystem.
sdgs: SDG 8: Decent Work and Economic Growth
preparatory_focus: To prepare participants for the main IGF event by providing tools and methods for designing inclusive online events, facilitating case study analysis, and encouraging collaborative problem-solving around inclusion challenges.

title: Technological assistance emphasis on teenagers during the pandemic — is it fair to distribute resources in such a way?
organizers: Chinese YMCA of Hong Kong
key_issues: Discussion on the distribution of technological resources during the pandemic, focusing on whether teenagers should be prioritized over other vulnerable groups such as the elderly and people with disabilities.
policy_recommendations: Agreed consensus on how to properly distribute technological resources to ease the digital gap among different vulnerable groups.
description: There has always been a huge digital gap between the youth and the elderly. This has become more significant during the COVID-19 pandemic when governments emphasize online education materials for students. Some argue that there is a lack of resources and support in terms of device and literacy programs from governments to meet the demand for technological assistance for adults, elderly, and people of disabilities. Meanwhile, some believe that technical assistance to teenagers’ learning should be prioritized. In this session, the current situation of technological support by government and different parties will be introduced. Whether or not support should be equally provided and how to be equally provided will also be discussed. It is hoped that after the session, a clear message on how technological resources should be properly distributed to ease the digital gap among different vulnerable groups can be obtained. This session focuses on the diverged views on whether teenagers are better than other generations in adapting to new technologies, and our focus is on youth and digital inclusion.
online_moderator: CHENG Yee Him, LEUNG Huen Hei, CHAU Tsz Chun Anthony
preparatory_focus: To prepare for discussions on equitable distribution of technological resources during the pandemic, focusing on youth and digital inclusion as a pre-discussion theme for the main IGF event.

title: Polylateralism and Geneva: how communities shape Internet Governance
organizers: Internet Governance Forum (IGF)
speakers: Open to anyone interested to speak about Geneva.
key_issues: Understanding how Geneva serves as a hub for Internet community discussions and tactics for better advocacy and policy.
description: The event will be hybrid and help newcomers understand how Geneva is a place concentrating many possibilities for the Internet community trying to shape Internet-related issues. With experienced advocates and practitioners, it will unlock tactics for better advocacy and policy. We will have online only session.
preparatory_focus: To help newcomers understand Geneva's role in Internet governance and prepare for discussions on advocacy and policy tactics.

title: Civil Society Pre-event: Internet Governance in times of Crisis
organizers: Internet Governance Caucus
themes: Economic and social inclusion and human rights
key_issues: Discussions around the impact of the pandemic on civil society, digital divide, fake news, data protection, and post-covid challenges.
policy_recommendations: Gather input from Civil Society Organizations and activists about remedies to pandemic-introduced issues and inequalities, and new ways of organization.
description: With more than one year since the beginning of the covid-19 pandemic, civil society has gone almost entirely online and so has advocacy and activism. Internet Governance is a topic that gathers both national and global aspects and relies entirely on proportionate participation from all interested stakeholders and their participation. In 2021 and past the vaccine rollout - in some parts of the world - people are preparing themselves for resuming at least some level of onsite activities. From enhancing the already existing differences imposed by the digital divide, the fake news pandemic and also newly-introduced data protection discussions in light of the need to facilitate data collection from citizens regarding their travel histories and their contacts with others, the post-covid world will have to deal with a lot of challenges. The goal of this pre-event session is, therefore, to gather input from Civil Society Organizations and activists about remedies to the pandemic-introduced issues and inequalities, as well as the new ways of organization we have all been forced into. We plan to gather the Internet Governance Caucus members and other interested individuals for a conversation about the post-covid world as the past year and a half presented very few opportunities for CSOs to gather and discuss alternatives out of this crisis. Lastly, it is important to mention this session holds connection to the 'Economic and social inclusion and human rights' and 'Universal access and meaningful connectivity' main focus areas for this year's Internet Governance Forum
preparatory_focus: To gather input from Civil Society Organizations and activists about remedies to pandemic-introduced issues and inequalities, as well as the new ways of organization we have all been forced into.

title: Youth IGF: Tutorial on the DNS Root
organizers: ICANN Technical Community, WEOG
speakers: Fred Baker, Internet Systems Consortium (ISC) Board Member, Technical Community, United States
Ken Renard, US Army Research Laboratory, Cyber Security Researcher, Academia, United States
Lars-Johan Liman, co-founder Netnod, Private Sector, Sweden
key_issues: Understanding the DNS root zone, its role in internet infrastructure, governance framework, and its importance for policy-making.
description: More and more governments around the world are beginning to legislate around components of the Internet in order to promote local policy goals. For these activities, it is essential that future policy makers and future parliamentarians understand what the DNS root zone is, the role it plays in how the Internet functions, which organizations operate the root, and how it is governed. Understanding these elements helps to better inform policy, which in turn, helps ensure the fundamental operation of the Internet. This will be a 60-minute tutorial session intended to help participants understand what the DNS root is and why it’s so important.
preparatory_focus: To provide foundational knowledge on DNS root infrastructure and governance for participants, enabling them to engage more effectively in the main IGF discussions on internet policy and regulation.

title: Digital policy making from below -- Ask the impacted sectors first
organizers: Just Net Coalition
key_issues: The session focused on digital policy making from the perspective of impacted sectors, emphasizing the importance of involving frontline communities in the policy-making process.
policy_recommendations: The session recommended that policymakers prioritize engaging with impacted sectors and adopting participatory approaches in digital governance.
description: The event brought together experts and frontline representatives from various sectors to discuss digital policy making from the perspective of impacted communities, emphasizing the need for inclusive and participatory approaches in governance.
preparatory_focus: To facilitate pre-discussion on digital policy making and to highlight the importance of involving impacted sectors in the policy process before the main IGF event.

title: The Rising of Techno Authoritarianism: when the employment of technology is an enablers of Human Rights Abuses
organizers: Data Privacy Brasil Research Association
key_issues: Risks of state surveillance, rise of technoauthoritarianism, tech-enabled human rights abuses by governments, data protection and privacy frameworks compliance
policy_recommendations: Strategize against tech-enabled human rights abuses, conceptualize a new agenda for Privacy in the digital age focused on new technologies, share Techno-Authoritarianism Map with participants
description: Over the past few years, governments and authoritarian actors all over the world are increasing their reliance on personal and sensitive information under the banner of improving public policies and services. The result is a widespread use of biometric data (including for mandatory identity cards), facial recognition in combination with the monitoring of public spaces, centralized databases of citizens personal data, among others technologies and practices. Technologies and practices that can pave the way for tech-enabled human rights abuses, one of the main outcomes of a process called tech-authoritarianism. And they also raise concerns about the disproportionate collection and processing of personal data by governments that are not compliant with data protection and privacy frameworks. The result of which may be health indicators being used to identify and capture groups that deviate from gender or political norms, e.g. LGBTQI people, and the use of other kinds of data to apply some measurement of political censorship or doxxing practices directed at anti-fascist groups.
preparatory_focus: Facilitate exchange of perspectives among Civil society organizations and activists about risks of state surveillance and rise of technoauthoritarianism, and strategize against such practices to conceptualize a new agenda for Privacy in the digital age focused on new technologies

title: AfICTA - Driving the Digital Potential of Africa

Ulandi Exner, AfICTA, Private Sector, Africa
Thabo Mashegoane, AfICTA, Private Sector, Africa

description: The Africa Information & Communication Technologies Alliance (AfICTA) is a concerned private sector led alliance of ICT Associations, Multi-national Corporations, Companies, Organisations and individuals in Africa. The intent of our day 0 event is to host a collaborative discussion of interested stakeholders on the needs, challenges, and drivers towards achieving a digital Africa and unlocking the digital potential of the continent. Session will be conducted in a sort of round table "On Line" meeting with AfICTA regional chairs providing a regional insight in to the ICT related matter following by an open session of interactive dialogue with the participants. The idea is not to be prescriptive but to let the meeting flow with the view to bringing forward new ideas and suggestions that might influence the future work of the alliance.
preparatory_focus: To host a collaborative discussion of interested stakeholders on the needs, challenges, and drivers towards achieving a digital Africa and unlocking the digital potential of the continent as a preparatory event for the main IGF

title: Internet governance, with and for the citizens
organizers: Missions Publiques
key_issues: Discussion on digital identity, disinformation, internet environment, and the role of citizens in internet governance. Highlighted the importance of education for online human rights and the need for global inclusion in internet governance.
policy_recommendations: The findings from the We, The Internet Dialogues emphasize the importance of education for online human rights and the need for global citizen inclusion in internet governance. There was a call for collaboration to become a national partner in Australia and implement similar deliberative processes.
format: Interactive presentation and exchange between speakers and attendees
description: We the Internet is the first debate of its kind to engage a coalition of strategic stakeholders brought together by Missions Publiques and representing the key players in the field: international organizations (UNESCO, European Commission, Council of Europe) governments (Germany, Switzerland), the private sector (Google, Facebook, Mozilla), civil society (The Internet Society, Web Foundation, Wikimedia Foundation, Particip’action), and the scientific community (WZB Berlin, Arizona State University for example). In 2020 we are scaling up the process in more than 100 countries, with discussions held on a single day and following a single method. In addition to the citizens’ forums, there will also be workshops with stakeholders as part of the UN High Level Panel process. “We the Internet” has proven that the future of Internet is a subject to be debated with citizens. The outcome of the preliminary dialogues in 2018 put the participants’ agenda on the table. That year, the participants brought up the question of the environment and this has now been officially added to the agenda of the Global Internet Governance Forum to be held in Poland in 2021. The pilots run in 2019 produced some clear results on the issues of digital identity and disinformation while showing the state of internet in different part of the world. We will show to and with the attendees what a deliberative process is and what kind of output it can bring, even on a topic which is difficult to tackle as Internet. It will be an interactive session where staff members will interact directly with attendees and then compare the results of the session with the large-scale event that we run in 2020.
preparatory_focus: To engage strategic stakeholders in pre-discussion themes, scale up deliberative processes globally, and prepare for the Global Internet Governance Forum in Poland 2021 by incorporating citizen voices and findings from previous dialogues.

agenda: Panel debate discussing regulation of blockchain, decentralization, integration into economies, and governance challenges.

title: AI in the public service: combating disinformation and fighting with the pandemic
organizers: Center for International Relations
key_issues: Discussion on how AI and big data analysis can help counter cybersecurity threats, fight the pandemic, and combat disinformation while promoting media literacy. Focus on AI applications in public policy, health sector, and social impact analysis.
policy_recommendations: Need for public policies to act as a buffer in AI implementation, ensuring good analysis and recommendations to avoid negative social consequences. Emphasis on regional cooperation and knowledge sharing between Poland, Czech Republic, and other Central and Eastern European countries.
description: The aim of the debate is to present how solutions based on the use of Artificial Intelligence algorithms and big data analysis help counteract key challenges of our time, such as cybersecurity, fighting the pandemic or combating disinformation combined with building media literacy among the citizens. The subject and scope of the debate results from several years of cooperation between the Center for International Relations and its partners as part of international projects implemented in Poland and EU countries (especially the Visegrad Group and other Three Seas countries) as well as the activities of the Observatory for the Social Impact of Artificial Intelligence - run by the THINKTANK center and its partners. The composition of speakers proposed in the debate is the result of several years of contacts between Centre for International Relations and THINKTANK with foreign partners from the region - representatives of non-governmental organizations, think tanks, academia and business. Thanks to the cooperation with the Institute of Political Innovation in Vienna, we also have examples of solutions used in public policies in various EU countries based on AI. The reason for the subject of the debate is the apparent increase in interest in solutions based on Artificial Intelligence in Poland and other countries in the region. In December 2020, Centre for International Relations, together with ASPEN CEE in Prague published an analysis comparing Poland and the Czech Republic in this regard (as part of a project financed by the Polish-Czech forum). In 2020, THINKTANK published THINK-BOOK "Artificial Intelligence in 2025" and a report on the applications of artificial intelligence in the public sector in Poland. The reports describe, inter alia, solutions in the health sector and in the area of combating disinformation. The broader context of the debate is the fact that Central and Eastern Europe has a great opportunity to use AI for its civilization and material advancement, but it should do it wisely so as not to cause negative social consequences. Public policies should act as a buffer in this process, but they need good analysis and recommendations.
onsite_moderator: Małgorzata Bonikowska, PhD - President of the Center for International Relations Foundation
preparatory_focus: To provide a platform for pre-discussion on AI applications in public service, especially in combating disinformation and pandemic response, and to inform the main IGF discussions through regional cooperation and knowledge sharing.

title: Ocean of Changes
organizers: Institute of Oceanology Polish Academy of Sciences
key_issues: Exploring methods and strategies of environmental education using ICT, digital resources, community involvement and cooperation via the Internet.
description: 2021 begins the United Nations' Ocean Decade Its vision assumes the cooperation of all stakeholders, including scientists and decision-makers, who will work together for the benefit of ecosystems and, consequently, society. An important area of activities under the Decade is the development of methods of modern environmental education, using information and communication technologies, digital resources, methods of community involvement and cooperation via the Internet. The proposed workshop aims to explore the methods and strategies of environmental education on the example of ocean science. The workshop is focused on enabling the exchange of information between those who are not indifferent to the fate of natural resources, including our seas and oceans. We want to build a community whose representatives recognize the sense of the implementation of the UN Sustainable Development Goa
preparatory_focus: To prepare for discussions on ocean-related internet governance issues during the main IGF event by exploring environmental education methods and strategies through ocean science examples.

title: Making smart cities happen – navigating through the web of paradoxes
organizers: Union of Entrepreneurs and Employers
key_issues: Challenges in smart city development including rapid urbanization, population growth, climate change, ageing population, and the paradoxes of efficiency vs. resource consumption, interoperability vs. resilience, and privacy vs. security.
description: By 2050, more than two-thirds of the world's population is projected to live in urban areas. Rapid urbanization, population growth, climate change and an ageing population are challenges that public policy must address. The answer to these challenges can be found in the digitalization and development of smart cities. The smart city idea is more than two decades old and is widely recognized as a goal towards which we should strive. However, despite several large-scale projects and widespread consensus, relatively little has been achieved on this topic so far. The reasons why smart cities are not advancing at a sufficient pace can be found in a web of paradoxes. Jevons' paradox says that the more efficiently we use a resource, the more its consumption increases. At the level of smart cities, we need to consider what can be done to ensure that the efficiency gains achieved through smart solutions are not offset by increased resource consumption. Further conflicts may arise between interoperability and resilience of systems and between privacy and security of residents. During this roundtable, we will invite panellists and the audience to discuss the reasons why smart cities are not growing as fast as we could wish and how we can change this situation. It is important to note that the panellists have been selected to represent a variety of environments related to innovation and smart growth, i.e.: government organizations, funding, academia, Big Tech companies and startups. Audience contact and feedback will be a very important part of the debate, so we anticipate using interactive tools at every stage of our discussion.
preparatory_focus: To facilitate pre-discussion on smart cities development challenges and paradoxes before the main IGF event.

title: Internet in 10 years from now – where is it going? Let’s check together!
organizers: National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC)
themes: Trust, security and stability - Cybersecurity practices and mechanisms
key_issues: Predictions about development directions of the Internet, cybersecurity, social media and technologies from 10 years ago, and audience's visions of key issues in 2031.
format: online quiz with a comment by the moderator
description: A brilliant workshop in the form of a quiz (stationary and online) that will be a logical experiment referring to IGF2021 issue area: "Trust, security and stability - Cybersecurity practices and mechanisms". The presenter will provide everyone with a QR code leading to a secure website created by the National Cyber Security Centre, where everyone will be able to answer a series of questions. The presenter will initially conduct a kind of intellectual warm-up for the audience, based on a few tricky questions with non-obvious, surprising answers from various areas of life in order to explain the formula of the workshop in a practical form. Then he will go to the main parts of the quiz. The first part of the quiz will be devoted to predictions about development directions of the Internet, cybersecurity, social media and technologies, which were formulated 10 years ago, and which were then truly difficult to predict. The second part of the quiz will cover the audience's visions of key issues with the subject of the first part, i.e. the functioning of the Internet, cybersecurity, social media and the development of technology in 10 years’ time, i.e. in 2031. Each time, after a series of questions, the presenter will formulate a thesis and interpret the results. The entire workshop will lead to conclusions about the exponential development of the Internet as a whole and each specific field, as well as about the unpredictability of the directions of changes even within the short time horizon.
online_moderator: Ms Karolina Drozdowska - NCSC senior specialist
preparatory_focus: Capacity building and pre-discussion on cybersecurity practices and mechanisms for the main IGF2021 issue area.

This time we would like to take advantage of the Internet Governance Forum 2021 event in Katowice, Poland, and invite representatives of leading think-tanks from around the world to discuss the values that should guide the development of the Internet and new technologies.

title: In the search of a golden mean – different perspectives on the regulation of digital markets
organizers: Union of Entrepreneurs and Employers
key_issues: Regulation of digital markets, finding a balance between regulation and innovation, perspectives of different stakeholders
description: Regulation of the digital economy is currently high on the agenda of major global organizations, including the World Trade Organization, the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, and the European Union. Recently, at the level of the European Union alone, several regulations have been created to adapt regulations to changing technological and economic realities and to regulate the digital economy in its broadest sense. However, it is important to remember that over-regulation can limit growth and innovation in the digital sector, which is uniquely important to economic recovery from the coronavirus pandemic. As stated by the OECD, we should also not forget that the digital economy is increasingly becoming a proper economy. Therefore, we believe that it is necessary to find a golden mean when it comes to regulating digital markets that allow for innovation and a greater diversity of business models. However, finding this balance is only possible if we take into account the perspectives of different parties.
preparatory_focus: To facilitate a discussion on finding a balanced approach to regulating digital markets by considering different stakeholder perspectives, in preparation for main IGF discussions on digital economy regulation.

title: Global Road(s) to Digital Sovereignty
organizers: The Kosciuszko Institute Association
speakers: Capitaine Romaric Agbagla, Chief Technology Officer, Togo Digital Agency
Nathália Lobo, Director of Sector Policy of the Secretariat of Telecommunications of Brazil
Ang Peng Hwa, Director of the Singapore Internet Research Centre, Wee Kim Wee School of Communication and Information, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore
Paul Timmers, Research Associate, Oxford University; Prof, European University Cyprus
key_issues: Regional perspectives on digital sovereignty, models of internet governance, universal values for digital sovereignty
policy_recommendations: Agreement on universal values that can be incorporated into digital sovereignty concept by every country
description: Over the last years digital sovereignty has become a central element in political discussion on digital issues across the globe. This term has a variety of meanings influenced by the regions and culture, and it’s not limited to control of a state of critical digital systems but also touches the broader scope of economy, society and rule of law. Today, the issue of digital sovereignty has become a much more encompassing concept focusing on wider digital transformation of societies, oftentimes used to present an ordered, value-driven, reasonable and secure digital world. Digital sovereignty can be used to solve the problems of individual rights and freedoms, fair economic competition or political and legal enforceability. However, the problem is that regional perspectives differ on the issue of digital sovereignty and even contradict each other. But the problem of development of ethical technology will challenge every country and the values based digital sovereignty will be profitable to everyone. The panel intends to spark a discussion on regional approaches to digital sovereignty, identifying similarities and main differences. Since values-based digital world is desirable, the panel looks for the universal values, which can be incorporated into digital sovereignty by every country.
rapporteur: Maciej Góra - Project Coordinator, the Kościuszko Institute
preparatory_focus: To prepare for discussions on digital sovereignty in the main IGF event by exploring regional perspectives and identifying universal values that can be incorporated into digital sovereignty concepts.

title: Harass me not
organizers: SFLC.in
speakers: Radhika Jhalani, Legal Counsel SFLC.in, Civil Society, India
Hija Kamran, WRP and GenderIT coordinator and Editor APC. Pakistan
Afra Suci Ramadhan, Regional Project manager, Digital Defenders Partnership
Ellen Kusuma, Head of Digital at At-Risks, SafeNet
key_issues: Online harassment as a barrier to freedom of expression, targeting of women and marginalized communities, role of state actors and platforms in creating safe spaces, challenges faced by digital rights defenders.
policy_recommendations: Need for stronger policies to address online harassment, increased accountability of state actors and platforms, support for digital rights defenders, promotion of safe and inclusive online spaces.
description: Online Harassment has been identified as a major cause for curbing freedom of expression in the digital space and making it inaccessible. This harassment takes multiple forms like sending threatening messages, verbal abuse, sexual abuse, doxxing etc. More often than not the harassment is targeted at women and women belonging to marginalised communities. These are also aimed at prominent individuals who represent and express the concerns and narratives of this community. The result of such harassment is exclusion of some the most vulnerable sections of the society from the digital space. SFLC.IN has written a report on Online Harassment which can be accessed here: https://sflc.in/report-online-harassment-form-censorship . We also have a Free Speech Tracker which records instances of Free Speech violations by state actors. This helps us understand the broader issues revolving around freedom of speech and expression in the digital space. We would like to discuss our work so far, and how it can contribute to the existing discourse on online harassment and freedom of speech and the way forward. The session aims to identify the forms of harassment that take place online especially at the intersection of women and marginalised communities. How identity and the victim's relation to that identity is used by harassers. Further, the session will discuss the role of state actors and online platforms in creating safe spaces online. We plan to conduct this meeting in an hybrid format, to enable greater participation for south Asian actors in participating in the conversations.
preparatory_focus: To prepare for the main IGF discussions on online harassment and freedom of speech by sharing research, identifying key issues, and exploring policy recommendations.

title: Global governance of a digital society: Examining different approaches and models
organizers: Transnational Institute (TNI)
key_issues: The session discussed the paradigm shift in the digital age, the social and political changes brought by data-based intelligence, and the challenges in global digital governance. It highlighted the need to reinvent connections between nation state-based political organisation and global co-existence. The session also addressed the cross-cutting nature of digital governance and the need for forward-looking governance mechanisms for issues like data governance, platform governance, AI governance, Web3, and Metaverse.
policy_recommendations: The session emphasized the need for reinventing global digital governance mechanisms, addressing the cross-cutting nature of digital governance, and developing forward-looking governance frameworks for emerging technologies. It called for exploring the social aspects of digital governance and how they differ from technical aspects.
subtheme: Connecting All People and Safeguarding Human Rights
description: The industrial age triggered many social and political changes – from nuclear families becoming the norm to the rise of the nation state. While mechanisation was at the heart of this shift in the industrial age, data-based intelligence becomes central to production in the digital age, superseding the role of machines and even IP. A paradigm shift is evidently underway, as data redefines the economic and material infrastructure of society. The social, political and economic tensions arising from this shift are all around us – the pervasive impacts of social media on our societies or of platformisation of the economy on labour rights. These new challenges have also exposed the weak links in global governance of the digital phenomenon, calling ever-more attention to the need to reinvent the connections between nation state-based territorial political organisation and global co-existence. Global digital governance (a more appropriate name for what has been called as global internet governance) involves both technical and social aspects. It is a cross-cutting phenomenon that impacts all sectors, and partly, its governance may be seen as belonging to the respective sector. Yet, there are vital horizontal issues, from management of the internet to data governance, platform governance and AI governance, not to mention Web3 and Metaverse, that also require forward looking governance imaginations and mechanisms. Global digital governance therefore stands at a cross-roads, seeking its basic moorings and appropriate institutional forms. There are many questions that need to be addressed in this regard: • How are the social aspects of digital governance different from those of the technical? • How can current UN based governance models in areas of health (WHO), food and agricultu
preparatory_focus: This session served as a preparatory event for the main IGF 2022, focusing on exploring different approaches and models of global digital governance, and setting the stage for discussions on the social, technical, and institutional aspects of internet governance.

title: IGF Women Summit

organizers: Hacklab Foundation
key_issues: Reimagining youth participation in internet policy spaces, addressing digital literacy needs, and designing inclusive participation experiences for diverse personas.
policy_recommendations: Agreed consensus on the importance of digital literacy, inclusive policy design, and open intellectual property to ensure equitable internet access and participation.
subtheme: Connecting All People and Safeguarding Human Rights
description: We are beyond the initial phases of technology adoption and internet revolutions, its integration into the business of society is intertwined with survival itself. Culturally we are united, content-wise divided. Policy now is a gateway to improving how we connect and safeguard people. Our session uses the available framework of equal access to diversity of people, inclusive in its design to reimagine mindsets and policy design on core matters that made the internet a successful venture, openness redefined to save us from the splinternet, open intellectual property and access to objective information. In the end we need to have access to the reasoning, facts, and institutional ties to translate what openness means in the age of decentralized innovations that are people-centric and secure in its design. We will draw inspiration from these core pillars and open up a methodology of meaningful participation in the digital markets, decision making, and independent thought literacy needed for policy reform and structural rebuild for a more stable and equal network, ours is a free and open space of reasoning and dialogue much needed at this critical juncture where our decisions, activism and multilateral collaboration can either lead to a vicious cycle of a broken, insecure authoritaria
preparatory_focus: To prepare for discussions on youth participation in internet policy spaces by exploring digital literacy needs, inclusive participation models, and policy frameworks that support equitable internet access and open innovation.

title: Global Peace Tech Atlas
organizers: Global PeaceTech Hub, European University Institute, New York University, CEPS, University of Lucerne
key_issues: Mapping and analyzing PeaceTech initiatives, exploring transnational governance models for technology use in peacebuilding, addressing ethical and legal challenges in deploying technologies for peace.
policy_recommendations: Proposing concrete solutions for responsible use of technologies like AI, blockchain, and e-identity systems to support peace and cooperation at the transnational level.
description: The session will represent the first public launch of the ‘Global PeaceTech Atlas’ a global mapping of PeaceTech topics, initiatives, and case studies. Peace-oriented technologies are becoming an ecosystem, not only an academic discipline, consisting of NGOs, start-ups, and companies. The deployment of technology for peace entails legal, political, economic, and ethical dilemmas that transcend national borders and require new models of transnational governance. Our aim is to study these models, highlight existing practices, and propose concrete solutions to promote the responsible use of technologies such as Artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, blockchain, technical architectures for e-identity, and many more, in support of peace.
preparatory_focus: To contribute to SDGs by mapping, assessing, analysing and recommending policy on different technologies for peace, supporting practitioners in reducing violence and promoting responsible technology use.

title: IGF 2023 Day 0 Event #105 The Digital Justice House: labour rights and the internet
organizers: Team Community
speakers: Danae Tapia Director of community strategy at Team Community Civil Society GRULAC
Francisco Vera Program officer at Open Society Foundations Civil Society WEOG
key_issues: Psychosocial research has demonstrated a severe crisis of emotional health in the digital rights space. The session discusses structural issues of the industry, specifically labour rights, as crucial to tackle this problem. It highlights the lack of instances to reflect on labour rights and the need for better holistic conditions for participants in the 2023 IGF.
policy_recommendations: The session proposes three policies: a four-day work week, the right to disconnect, and unlimited vacations as effective implementations that advance SDGs 3 and 8. It aims to provide a safe space for discussion, promote collective strategies between digital rights defenders, funders, and other stakeholders to make the right to decent work a standard for the industry.
description: Psychosocial research has demonstrated a severe crisis of emotional health in the digital rights space. At Team Community (TCU), we propose that structural issues of this industry, specifically labour rights, are crucial to tackle this problem, and in the recent months we have been sharing in different spaces the Digital Justice Every Day pamphlet with concrete organisational policies to tackle this crisis that not only affects the wellbeing of our community members but also impacts in the quality of the work we produce. In this activity we want to provide a safe space to discuss labour rights affairs, we have noticed the lack of instances to reflect on this topic and this gathering will be a necessary moment to assess and promote better holistic conditions for the different individuals participating in the 2023 IGF. We will also advance towards collective strategies between digital rights defenders, funders and other stakeholders to make the right to decent work a standard for our industry.
preparatory_focus: To provide a safe space for discussing labour rights in the digital rights space, promote better holistic conditions for participants, and advance collective strategies between digital rights defenders, funders, and other stakeholders to make the right to decent work a standard for the industry.

title: DNS: Foundation for Safe, Secure and Interoperable Internet
organizers: IGF Secretariat, ICANN
speakers: David Huberman, ICANN, Technical Community, WEOG
key_issues: Understanding DNS technical operations, DNS resolution, routing, IP addresses, and the role of DNS in Internet governance and infrastructure development.
policy_recommendations: Promote quality, reliable, sustainable, and resilient Internet infrastructure; broaden participation of developing countries in Internet governance; encourage collaboration among regional and international stakeholders; ensure access and use of the Internet in developing countries.
description: Participants in the Parliamentarian Track are invited to join us for an engaging session, co-organized with the IGF Secretariat, that offers valuable insights into the Domain Name System (DNS), a critical component of the Internet's foundation. In this session, participants will gain a comprehensive understanding of the DNS and its significance in supporting Internet functionality. They will explore the key players in the Internet ecosystem and discover recent initiatives that impact Internet governance. The session will delve into the technical operations of the Internet, covering topics such as DNS resolution, routing, and IP addresses. Through this exploration, participants will develop a deeper comprehension of the mechanisms behind these technical operations, providing them with insights into the functioning and governance of the Internet. Furthermore, the session will foster discussions on the dynamic interplay between policy and technology, highlighting its implications for Internet governance. By actively participating in this session, attendees will have a unique opportunity to enhance their knowledge and gain comprehensive insights into the DNS and its governance framework. They will engage in meaningful discussions and exchange ideas on the evolving landscape of the Internet ecosystem. Through this exploration of technical operations, participants will gain a better understanding of how these operations shape the Internet and contribute to its overall functionality.
preparatory_focus: Provide foundational knowledge on DNS and its role in Internet governance, preparing participants for deeper discussions on Internet infrastructure and policy in the main IGF event.

The session discusses SDG Goal 9's target 9c on universal Internet access in LDCs, SDG Goal 3 on digital inclusion and health services, and SDG Goal 4 on education and lifelong learning.

title: Consumer data rights from Japan to the world
organizers: Consumers International
key_issues: Cross-border Data Flows and Trust, Data Free Flow, Data Privacy and Protection
policy_recommendations: Enabling the data governance frameworks that builds consumer trust are central elements of the development of transborder digital infrastructure (SDG 9.1) and allow for small companies in developing countries to be part of global value chains (SDG 9.3). Enabling the participation of consumer groups and civil society (SDG 17.7), and particularly from developing countries (SDG 18.8) in global data governance can drive more effective cross-border redress when data flows across jurisdictions (SDG 16.3) and consumers always know who is responsible and can help them with any issues (SDG 16.6). The input of civil society groups from Asia Pacific countries towards global data governance will improve the quality and coherence of policy (SDG 17.14) while respecting the diversity of approaches (SDG 17.15) and will also enable the trust required to generate more data that can then be disaggregated and used to inform policy (SDG 17.18).
format: A gathering where plenary discussions will be divided into several discussions with short presentations by speakers on the key topics followed by discussions, some of these in smaller breakout groups. title: Transforming technology frameworks for the planet
organizers: Association for Progressive Communications (APC)

Jaime Villareal, May First Movement Technology, Civil Society, GRULAC

key_issues: Extractive business models in the technology sector pose a serious threat to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals. Alternative models exist, and must be supported, in line with SDG9 target b: 'Support domestic technology development, research and innovation in developing countries, including by ensuring a conducive policy environment for, inter alia, industrial diversification and value addition to commodities'.
policy_recommendations: Support alternative models and frameworks that shape the technology sector. Encourage cooperative and collective models that support participatory decision-making by workers and members.
format: This pre-event to the global IGF aims to support a facilitated discussion with speakers and participants. Speakers in the pre-event will share their experiences in working through cooperative and collective models, and reflect on questions that will guide a facilitated discussion with participants. Participants will be invited to pose questions and share reflections on the discussion throughout the event.
description: In 2022, the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), in a report on the practical application of the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights to the technology sector, stated that when a company cannot prevent or mitigate human rights violations within the framework of existing business models, those models may need to be adapted or even transformed. This statement reflects the need to collectively interrogate extractive business models in the technology sector, and support alternative models and frameworks that shape the technology sector. Alternatives models in the technology sector exist in many forms - including cooperative and collective models that support participatory decision-making by workers and members. Technology cooperatives and collectives face significant challenges in operating in a sector dominated by large technology companies that seek to extract and monetize our experiences and engagement with technology. Efficiency and scalability are often cited as requirement for digital technologies to meaningfully contribute to sustainable development. As a result, technology cooperatives and collectives are often ignored, and their potential to contribute to accelerate the realization of development goals is restricted.
preparatory_focus: This pre-event to the global IGF aims to support a facilitated discussion with speakers and participants. Speakers in the pre-event will share their experiences in working through cooperative and collective models, and reflect on questions that will guide a facilitated discussion with participants. Participants will be invited to pose questions and share reflections on the discussion throughout the event.

description: Most stakeholders will agree with the need to connect “the other half”, as the Internet enables the exercise of Human Rights, including Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, and Civil and Political Rights. However, there is much less consensus regarding how to bring the underserved communities online. Many have pointed out to infrastructure as the main barrier to universal connectivity, with the resulting problem of economic incentives, especially regarding communities that inhabit areas far from the big urban centers, which are often impoverished communities as well. Many of the unconnected communities are traditional communities. To reduce the discussion to the technical and economic from a Global North/Western approach, not only lacks a deep understanding of the problem, but is also carries the dangers of colonialist oppression. Instead of imposing one single access model to the Internet, it is necessary to listen to the local communities, their needs and desires, in order to create solutions with them.
preparatory_focus: To explore different alternatives to connectivity in the Amazonian region, with a focus on the experiences of the people that inhabit it, and to discuss how to achieve universal connectivity without disrupting the relationship that communities have with the environment.
