title: Legal and policy challenges to Surveillance through Spyware
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: State surveillance, issues and concerns surrounding Pegasus spyware, legal accountability, indictment of NSO Group, privacy laws, mass surveillance, spyware manufacturers accountability, strategic litigation and policy advocacy to challenge unlawful surveillance, transparency and accountability.
policy_recommendations: Summarizing key policy recommendations, setting the stage for a policy brief and future advocacy efforts. Policy interventions to strengthen privacy laws, prevent mass surveillance, hold spyware manufacturers accountable for human rights violations. Strategic litigation and policy advocacy as tools to challenge unlawful surveillance, ensure transparency, and hold governments and private entities accountable.

title: IGF 2025 WS #39 Multistakeholder Collaboration in AI Regulatory Sandboxes
organizers: Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: Discussion on AI Regulatory Sandboxes (AIRS), challenges in inclusive and participatory approaches, confidentiality, trust, capture and efficiency, strategies to address these obstacles, and how the multistakeholder model of Internet governance can inform the design and implementation of AI Regulatory Sandboxes.
policy_recommendations: Exploration of successful participatory methods in AI Regulatory Sandboxes, analysis of challenges such as confidentiality, trust deficits, and process complexity, and how the multistakeholder model of Internet governance can enhance collaboration, inclusion, and accountability in AI Regulatory Sandboxes.

title: Digital Inclusion 4All: Digital Competences 4Future
organizers: Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Digital literacy programs for vulnerable groups, online safety for children and seniors, cross-sector collaboration for cybersecurity awareness
policy_recommendations: Strengthen digital literacy programs, develop policies for online safety, enhance cross-sector collaboration for cybersecurity resilience
networking_goals: Partnerships, collaboration, knowledge exchange
agenda: Brief presentations (20 min), facilitated discussion (50 min), actionable conclusions (20 min)
collaboration_outcomes: Meaningful policy recommendations and future collaborations

title: IGF 2025 WS #391 Intermediary liability: lessons from legal to regulatory
organizers: Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: Balancing regulation of online harms with freedom of expression, addressing misinformation and AI challenges, promoting international harmonization of intermediary liability rules while respecting local contexts.
policy_recommendations: Generate recommendations for the IGF and other Internet governance processes through collaborative knowledge construction.
key_takeaways: The importance of a multi-stakeholder approach in balancing regulation, freedom of expression, and innovation while promoting international harmonization of intermediary liability rules.

title: LEO Satellites, Global Connectivity and Sustainability
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Government, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: The session addresses the technical, regulatory, and socioeconomic implications of LEO satellite mega-constellations, focusing on universal Internet access, environmental sustainability, global space governance, connectivity in remote communities, and the balance between security, digital sovereignty, and innovation.
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain a comparative understanding of the impacts of LEO satellite mega-constellations on Internet infrastructure in Brazil, Germany, Nigeria, and the Dominican Republic. The discussion will provide an interdisciplinary analysis of regulatory, socioeconomic, and environmental challenges, with a focus on digital sovereignty, sustainability, and universal access. It will facilitate a multistake, exchange of perspectives on spectrum governance, economic feasibility of satellite connectivity, and technological autonomy in different regional contexts. Attendees will explore collaborative tools, including a public repository to further research and inform policy discussions.

title: IGF 2025 WS #394 Katutura Community Networks as a Utility: A Sustainable Mode
organizers: Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: Policy fostering multistakeholder collaboration among governments, civil society, ISPs, and tech innovators to advance digital inclusion through community networks as a utility; policy frameworks supporting capacity building for local communities to manage, maintain, and expand their networks; incentivizing private and public investment in community-based connectivity projects.
policy_recommendations: Advocate for a 'Community Networks as a Utility' model that redefines connectivity as a human right; showcase proven CN models integrating solar-powered infrastructure, wireless mesh networking, and open-source solutions; advocate for regulator support for community networks as a utility.
networking_goals: Partnerships, collaboration, knowledge exchange on community networks as a utility for digital inclusion and rights advocacy.
agenda: Short demonstration (15 minutes), experience of community network sharing by stakeholders or attendees (15 minutes), development of best practices for community networks as a utility in rural areas and informal settlements (20 minutes).
collaboration_outcomes: Advocacy for regulatory support for community networks as a utility; showcasing proven CN models; exploring ways to incentivize private and public investment in community-based connectivity projects.

title: Applying International Law Principles in the Digital Space
organizers: Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Intergovernmental Organization, Asia-Pacific Group
speakers: Francisco Brito Cruz , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Nieves Molina , Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Chantal Joris , Civil society, Western European and Other Group (WEOG)
Nadim Nashif , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: How do existing international law obligations provide a regulatory framework for the protection of individuals and communities for conducts related to incitement to violence in the digital space? How can we balance Article 19 (freedom of expression) and Article 20 (prohibition of incitement) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights? What are the sovereignty implications of cross-border digital interventions?
policy_recommendations: Provide clarity on the state of international law interpretation when applied to conducts in the digital space and their effects on individuals and communities. Develop global legal principles on existing international law obligations and responsibilities to counter human rights harms in the digital civic space.

title: Gendered impacts of tech: moving from Harm to Accountability
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Eastern European Group
key_issues: How are tech companies impacting gender equality across their value chain—from workplace policies to supply chains, product design, and end-use effects? What should tech companies be doing to fulfil their responsibilities under the UN Guiding and Principles on Business and Human Rights (UNGPs)? What actions need to be taken to ensure that tech companies are held accountable for their gendered human rights impacts?
policy_recommendations: Participants will leave with having: - Garnered a deeper understanding of gendered impacts of the tech sector across the value chain. - Insights from case studies on gender-responsive human rights due diligence from different sectors. - Contributed concrete strategies for companies, investors, policymakers, and civil society to drive systemic change.

title: Regional Orgs Bolster Public Interest AI
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group; Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: How can regional organizations integrate human rights and digital public goods into AI development frameworks? What are the key challenges and opportunities in implementing digital rights plans across regional contexts? How can international cooperation among regional organizations enhance public interest AI development globally?
policy_recommendations: The workshop aims to facilitate a comprehensive discussion on how regional frameworks can ensure AI is developed ethically, sustainably, and inclusively. It will highlight best practices and challenges in implementing these plans across diverse regions. The session will provide a platform for stakeholders to share insights on the intersection of AI governance and human rights, emphasizing the, importance of collaborative governance in ensuring AI benefits are equitably distributed.

title: IGF 2025 WS #399 Global South: Collaboration Activists Digital safety
organizers: Intergovernmental Organization, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: A. Beyond Borders: How Can Governments, Tech Companies, and Civil Society Ensure Activists’s Digital Safety in the Global South? B. What are the Global Solutions: Cross-Border Collaboration for Activists’s Digital Safety C. How can we implement these solutions?
policy_recommendations: Inspire new approaches and solutions. Engaging discussion that underscores the power of collective action and shared knowledge in addressing this pressing issue.
networking_goals: Enhance Activists's digital safety through collaborative efforts, knowledge sharing, and partnerships.
agenda: 1. Opening 10 mins 2. Challenges, problems 15 mins 3. Approaches 20 mins 4. Questions 15 mins, for the online interaction will be 8 mins
collaboration_outcomes: Hybrid Format: After discussion, we will open the questions and notes Then networking.

title: IGF 2025 WS #40 Boosting innovations from and for communities
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: Policy frameworks and funding mechanisms to support sustainability and scalability of community networks; role of community networks in digital rights; influence of community-led initiatives on economic and development policies.
policy_recommendations: Actionable insights, policy recommendations, and a deeper appreciation for community-led digital initiatives in fostering inclusion and rights-based connectivity.

title: Instantiation of the Digital Public Infrastructure
organizers: Civil Society, African Group; Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Access to information and services in the digital age as a human right, current practices and their limitations, collaboration to realize DPI through CL3 and RCC approaches
policy_recommendations: Collaboration to realize DPI through various approaches like CL3 and RCC, multi-stakeholder discussions on local adaptations of global initiatives like GIGA, frameworks for DPI implementation, partnership development strategies, and implementation steps for CL, RCC concepts
networking_goals: Foster collaboration, partnerships, knowledge exchange, leveraging international university networks for sustainable digital inclusion
agenda: Icebreaker, brainstorming, problem solving, interactive activities, feedback & reflection, discussions on DPI approaches, exploration of affordable access models like AA4EDU, examination of local adaptations of global initiatives like GIGA, sharing of practical tools and frameworks
collaboration_outcomes: Collaboration to realize DPI through various approaches like CL3 and RCC, multi-stakeholder discussions on local adaptations of global initiatives like GIGA, frameworks for DPI implementation, partnership development strategies, and implementation steps for CL, RCC concepts

title: Digital Rights and Online Disinformation Resilience
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Balancing protection of vulnerable communities from harmful content with freedom of expression and access to information; implementing Global Digital Compact principles on information integrity through collaborative governance; mechanisms for collaboration between government, civil society, media, and technology sectors to improve information integrity without creating barriers to digital access.
policy_recommendations: Practical methodologies for designing inclusive interventions; diverse perspectives on balancing security concerns with freedom of expression; assessment frameworks adaptable to different regional contexts; insights into successful capacity-building approaches that improve digital literacy.
networking_goals: Partnerships, collaboration, knowledge exchange between government, civil society, media, and technology sectors.
agenda: Presentation of the Disinformation Resilience in Israel (DRI) project as a case study; discussion on vulnerabilities in minority groups, religious communities, and digitally marginalized populations; sharing of practical methodologies from the DRI project's experience; emphasis on balancing regulatory frameworks with democratic values.
collaboration_outcomes: Successful capacity-building approaches that have enhanced digital literacy and verification skills among journalists and vulnerable communities.

title: IGF 2025 WS #402 Heritage Site Interactivity
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
speakers: Allen Hyde , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Robert Adams , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Shadi Alathamneh , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Junshan Liu , Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Maria Jose VIÑALS , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: 1. How can virtual experiences of heritage sites be accessed through online platforms without compromising site safety and security or infringing upon sacred sites or intangible heritage? 2. How can reality captures showcased online and on-site community-based tourism fortify local expertise and build entrepreneurialism? 3. How can digital monitoring systems in heritage sites help mitigate risks related to climate change?
policy_recommendations: This workshop will explore applications and considerations for documentation and analysis techniques at other threatened World Heritage sites, especially those under mounting pressures from climate change and overtourism. The workshop will present a balanced perspective to the widespread socio-economic impacts of heritage tourism, questioning how digital tours can improve access and augment on-site entrepreneurship. Additionally, continuous digital sensor-based monitoring through secured online platforms for remote access can responsibly support and protect sites, augmenting disaster and emergency planning and implementation. This focus on protecting cultural heritage underscores the importance of safeguarding sites for sustainable development and integrated growth. The team will present methods for the promotion of cultural heritage that can contribute to economic growth and social cohesion.

title: IGF 2025 WS #403 Deepseek and AI Democratization
organizers: Private Sector, Asia-Pacific Group
speakers: Wolfgang Kleinwaechter , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Kilnam Chon , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
Anriette Esterhuysen , Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: Designing a global AI governance framework that supports technological democratization while mitigating accountability gaps from decentralized innovation; exploring if the non-Silicon Valley model (Deepseek) can offer an alternative pathway for AI development in the Global South and how to adjust international strategies for technical assistance and investment; balancing open collaboration with national security concerns (e.g., critical infrastructure protection, geopolitical competition).
policy_recommendations: Publish 'AI Democratization and Global Governance: Challenges and Opportunities from the Deepseek Case' summarizing technical analyses, regional impact assessments, and policy recommendations; promote the establishment of an 'AI Democrat, Innovation Alliance'

title: IGF 2025 WS #405 Deepseek and Straw-man Fallacy
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
speakers: Wolfgang Kleinwaechter , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Kilnam Chon , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
Anriette Esterhuysen , Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: 1. How to prevent the "Straw-man Fallacy" from distorting global AI governance policies? 2. Can technological competition and governance cooperation coexist? 3. Who should lead the formulation of global AI rules?
policy_recommendations: Release the policy brief titled "Logical Pitfalls in AI Governance: Analysis of the Deepseek Incident," summarizing the core points of contention and recommendations from the conference.
initiative_or_product_name: Logical Pitfalls in AI Governance: Analysis of the Deepseek Incident
launch_purpose: To analyze the Deepseek incident and its implications for global AI governance, focusing on the Straw-man Fallacy and its impact on policy formulation.
target_audience: Experts, policymakers, and stakeholders involved in AI governance, particularly those from the United States, China, and Europe.
stakeholders_involved: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), African Group, United States, China, Europe
impact_expectation: Provide a fresh perspective on China's AI capabilities and contribute to the development of effective mechanisms and proactive advancements in global AI governance.

title: Multistakeholder Solutions for Building Digital Trust
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Challenges to strengthening multistakeholder engagement in the Global Majority, ensuring balanced and meaningful participation from various stakeholder groups under authoritarian contexts, possibilities offered by international human rights frameworks for rights-centric and truly multistakeholder approaches to technology governance in the Global Majority, and how international multistakeholder standards can strengthen the participation of the Global Majority in key internet governance processes.
policy_recommendations: Exploring adaptations of multistake, international multistakeholder standards such as the NETmundial principles for Global Majority contexts and discussing ways to strengthen Global Majority participation across regional and global internet governance processes.

title: American Denial: Digital Exclusion for Vulnerable Groups
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: Structural and policy barriers preventing marginalized communities from accessing digital government services, the impact of unstable housing and unreliable connectivity on digital exclusion, redesigning digital government initiatives for accessibility and participation, roles of governments, private actors, and technical community in addressing digital exclusion.
policy_recommendations: Concrete recommendations for governments and private actors to enhance accessibility, participation, and data security; advocacy strategies to bridge gaps in digital inclusion; governance models prioritizing equity, digital rights, and inclusive infrastructure.

title: IGF 2025 WS #408 The weaponization of the Internet and the future of openness
organizers: Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: A. How can Internet blocking be prevented from becoming a tool for censorship or suppression of dissent, particularly in regimes with weak democratic safeguards? B. How can technical standards be leveraged to preserve user autonomy while addressing legitimate concerns around illegal content? C. Given divergent national laws, how can technical and legal cooperation reduce Internet fragmentation while respecting local contexts?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain a clear understanding of how Internet blocking and filtering work at a technical level, including the specific methods employed and their potential for unintended consequences. Furthermore, they will gain insight into the motivations behind blocking and filtering, encompassing the diverse range of actors involved and the legal and political contexts in which these actions occur. In addition to this, they will acquire a deep understanding of the human rights implications of Internet blocking, particularly its impact on freedom of expression, access to information, and the right to privacy. Moreover, the session will provide participants with the opportunity to engage in direct dialogue with experts and stakeholders from diverse backgrounds, fostering collaboration and identifying common ground. Finally, the session will explore and analyze the risks of blocking orders originating from a top-down perspective, assessing the potential for abuse and the need for safeguards.

title: Digital Inclusion of Indigenous Communities in APAC
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: 1. Do rural development programs incorporate digital development for indigenous communities? 2. How can local governments and civil society collaborate with international organizations to advance SDGs (1, 4, 8, 9, 10) by ensuring equitable internet access and meaningful connectivity for indigenous communities? 3. What does connectivity mean for for-profit ISPs in rural areas, and how can policies and partnerships address unfavorable cost-to-benefit ratios to serve marginalized and indigenous communities? 4. How can digital literacy and skills initiatives promote socio-economic growth while preserving cultural diversity and fostering online multilingualism in low-resource settings?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain insights into issues and challenges faced by indigenous communities, socio-economic effects of digital seclusion, how meaningful connectivity can drive sustainable development, the importance of digital access and literacy for cultural identity, and relevant cases of digital development efforts in APAC.

title: IGF 2025 WS #41 Unifying Digital Efforts: Strengthening Multistakeholder Par
organizers: Intergovernmental Organization, African Group; Intergovernmental Organization, African Group; Intergovernmental Organization, African Group; Technical Community, African Group; Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernment, Organization; Technical Community, African Group; Technical Community, African Group
key_issues: How can multistakeholder partnerships enhance digital cooperation to bridge connectivity gaps and promote inclusive digital growth? What role can youth play in shaping digital policies and fostering cross-border cooperation for a more inclusive digital ecosystem? What are the key challenges and opportunities in building sustainable digital partnerships between governments, private sector, and civil society?
policy_recommendations: Insights into successful digital cooperation models and best practices. Diverse perspectives from policymakers, industry leaders, and youth advocates. Actionable strategies for bridging digital divides and fostering collaboration. Youth-centered approaches to innovation, policy, and digital inclusion.
networking_goals: Networking opportunities to build global and regional partnerships
agenda: Roundtable format with a 60-minute duration fostering dynamic, inclusive dialogue among diverse stakeholders. Encourages equal participation, open interaction, allowing for a free flow of ideas, collaboration, and problem-solving.
collaboration_outcomes: Attendees will gain insights into scalable strategies for digital cooperation, leaving with actionable takeaways to build more inclusive and resilient digital ecosystems.

title: Digital Literacy for All: Equitable Access via No-Code Tools
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: How can internet governance frameworks better integrate digital literacy as a core component of equitable access? What role do multi-stakeholder partnerships play in designing inclusive tools and policies that empower non-technical users? How can we ensure that the development and deployment of digital technologies align with the principles of The Tech We Want—transparency, accessibility, and fairness?
policy_recommendations: Participants will leave the session with a clear understanding of how no-code tools like the Open Data Editor work, including a live demonstration of its features and how it can enhance digital literacy in non-technical communities. They will get access to a roadmap for building a community of practice around digital literacy, including templates for organizing local workshops and training sessions. Attendees will benefit from a governance checklist for inclusive technology, outlining key principles such as accessibility, transparency, and sustainability, which participants can apply to their own projects or policies. They will learn about case studies and success stories from the Open Knowledge Foundation’s The Tech We Want initiative, showcasing how inclusive tools and governance frameworks have been successfully implemented in diverse contexts.

title: Truth Under Siege: Tools to Counter Digital Censorship
organizers: Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Legal protections for journalists and sources, role of public funding in supporting secure communication tools, digital literacy education in national policies
policy_recommendations: Establish legal protections for journalists and sources, support public funding for secure communication tools, incorporate digital literacy education into national policies

title: Global Action for Local AI Innovation: The Role of Open-Sour
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: How can open-source AI projects democratise AI innovation and ensure equitable access to AI-driven solutions in developing countries? What are the key trade-offs for policymakers, developers, and civil society when developing or using open-source AI for sustainable development? What policies and regulatory frameworks are needed to address emergent challenges?
policy_recommendations: What capacities, resources, and institutions are required in order to support and scale emergent best practices to ensure that open-source AI development supports individual and community rights? What will participants gain from attending this session? Participants will gain a more nuanced understanding of the trade-offs inherent in open-source AI development and use for advancing the SDGs in the Global South. It will also help participants understand how global actions and frameworks shape possibilities for local innovation. Participants will get concrete examples of best practices to address emerging challenges around open-source AI. This will help them identify actionable insights and advocate open AI practices within their contexts. This includes strategies for effective data governance, open-source adoption and maintenance, support for community innovation and participation and policy recommendations to guide governments and organisations in creating inclusive and sustainable technological ecosystems. Participants will also hear a variety of viewpoints from experts in academia, industry, and civil society, as well as from different geographies. This will help understand how various stakeholders approach the balance between open and closed AI and how this debate differs across local contexts.

title: Enabling collective redress online for communities at risk
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: How can access to collective redress be operationalized by the communities at risk inside and outside the EU? What are the main obstacles to accessing effective remedies for at-risk communities against platforms' unjustified restrictions? What are the eligibility requirements for CSOs to defend the collective interest of communities at risk? How has enforcing Articles 20 and 86 of the DSA worked so far, and what needs strengthening? Can this new mechanism under the DSA also empower communities at risk outside the EU? How can public regulators, such as Coimisiún na Meán in Ireland, help at-risk communities ensure online safety?
policy_recommendations: The participants will gain a mutual understanding of persistent issues that HRDs face when being silenced or discriminated against by online platforms, for instance, by content policies and their arbitrary enforcement, either by automated content moderation or content recommender systems. By raising these issues, the moderated dialogue will raise awareness among HRDs living in exile, who may defend themselves against this arbitrariness with the support of specialized civil society organizations representing their interest. Second, the community of invited stakeholders will discuss and agree on the main points for the future joint strategy on leveraging new DSA measures for collective redress in the EU. Even if the DSA applies only in the EU jurisdiction, such measures' outcomes may positively shape global redress mechanisms. Finally, the workshop will facilitate joint conversations with relevant stakeholders, including the EU External Service, the European Commission, the Appeals Centre Europe, and national Digital Service Coordinators.

title: Patients with Tech will replace clinicians
organizers: Private Sector, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Discussion on the evolving relationship between technology and clinical care, exploring whether digital health innovations empower patients to replace or complement traditional healthcare providers. Engagement with diverse perspectives from clinicians, digital health entrepreneurs, policymakers, and patient advocates.
policy_recommendations: Policy implications of digital health innovations, challenges in cross-border data flows for law enforcement access to digital evidence, and the role of data and AI in addressing sustainability issues such as climate change, biodiversity, conservation, and water scarcity.

title: Personal AI to Empower Citizens and Consumers
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Discussion on international principles and ethical frameworks for personal AI development, regulatory support for ethical ecosystems, competition between small businesses and big tech in personal AI, and multistakeholder collaboration for personal AI services.
policy_recommendations: Facilitate multistakeholder collaboration towards the realization of personal AI services, align incentives across public administrations, individual consumers, and business actors, and explore specific use cases for personal AI.

title: Strengthening Digital Resilience Through Civil Society
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group; Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group; Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
regional_focus: Asia-Pacific; Latin American and Caribbean; African
key_issues: How can governments and policymakers support and scale civil society-led media literacy and fact-checking initiatives to enhance digital resilience while safeguarding freedom of expression? What policy frameworks and regulatory measures are needed to strengthen collaboration between civil society, technology platforms, and governments in combating misinformation, particularly in the Global South? How can funding and institutional support for civil society interventions be improved to address challenges such, as outreach limitations, scalability, and the evolving nature of misinformation, including deepfakes?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain practical insights, research-based knowledge, and collaborative opportunities to enhance their efforts in countering misinformation. Through discussions with experts from civil society, government, and the private sector, they will explore the effectiveness, challenges, and scalability of different interventions, including media literacy programs, fact-checking initiatives, and digital tools for misinformation detection. By engaging in interactive dialogue and peer-to-peer learning, participants will exchange experiences, reflect on successful and failed interventions, and identify gaps in cu

title: Platform Accountability Failures: Perspectives from ARISE
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Systemic challenges of platform accountability, regional disparities in digital governance, labor rights, data access, regulatory protections, monopolistic practices, and the impact of platform economies on governance structures.
policy_recommendations: Reimagining platform accountability frameworks to prioritize user rights, addressing regional disparities in digital governance, fostering collaboration among governments, platforms, and civil society to create inclusive and equitable digital ecosystems, and developing policies that prevent monopolistic practices and protect marginalized communities.

title: IGF 2025 WS #418 Trustworthy AI in the public sector
organizers: Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Discussion on conditions for public sector to lead in defining trustworthy AI, mechanisms for trustworthy communication with embedded AI, and interoperability across countries and legislations.
policy_recommendations: Bridging regulatory viewpoints with technical viewpoints to address various ideas on mitigating trust risks in AI usage in communications.

title: IGF 2025 WS #42 Teaming Up to Create a Stronger Multistakeholder Dialogue
organizers: Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Intergovernmental Organization, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: What prevents multi-stakeholder dialogue from taking place? Can we identify the key obstacles? What roles do different stakeholders play, and how can they leverage their positions to foster a global multistakeholder dialogue? What steps can we take to ensure a sustainable and effective multi-stakeholder dialogue? How do we start and how do we secure that process?
policy_recommendations: We want everyone to walk away with a sharper understanding of roles, possibilities, and a solid game plan for creating real, impactful conversations.

title: Truth, Trust & Tech: Defending Democracy from Digital Threat
organizers: Government, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: Balancing free speech with limiting misinformation, regulations to prevent AI from spreading misinformation, media trust amid deepfakes and AI narratives, government actions to protect elections from disinformation, global governance of digital threats while respecting rights
policy_recommendations: Actionable strategies for strengthening information resilience, approaches to combat misinformation, safeguarding digital platforms, ensuring fair electoral processes, and multidisciplinary solutions to digital threats to democracy

title: Digital Leap: Leading CASA from Isolation to Connection
organizers: Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: How can policymakers and regional Internet governance organizations enhance cross-border collaboration to lower Internet transit costs and improve connectivity across CASA? What strategies can governments adopt to attract private investment for fiber-optic, 5G, and satellite-based infrastructure? How can policies and programs be aligned across CASA to improve affordable access and regional harmonization?
policy_recommendations: Participants will understand the current state of CASA connectivity, explore policy and regulation for digital inclusion, discuss technologies and digital CASA, and explore regional collaboration and economic impact.

title: IGF 2025 WS #423 Algorithmic Diplomacy: Better Negotiations?
organizers: Civil Society, Eastern European Group
speakers: Nicolas Fiumarelli , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
James Nathan Adjartey Amattey , Private Sector, African Group
Arevik Martirosyan , Civil Society, Eastern European Group
Yee Man Ko , Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Ethical integration of AI in diplomacy, risks/benefits of algorithmic diplomacy in global governance, ensuring equity and transparency in AI-driven diplomatic tools
policy_recommendations: Promote equitable, transparent, and sustainable use of AI in multilateral settings; explore ethical, practical, and geopolitical implications of algorithmic diplomacy

title: Online Safety for Kids: Implementable Lessons for SIDS
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: How can SIDS and economies of the Global South demand that social media giants apply a more equitable approach to appropriating resources, for example, content moderation, to provide coverage for their territory? What creative funding mechanisms can be used to ensure monies are dedicated to social protection for kids from online risks in parallel with the thrust towards resilient digital infrastructure and digital transformation advancement? How can we ensure that interventions are customized to consider the cultural diversity of the region where they shall take place and stakeholders are receptive to, and trust, both the message and messenger?
policy_recommendations: Attendees will get an understanding of the severity of online threats, including cyberbullying and financial sextortion which may lead to teen suicide. Emerging threats will also be examined. Speakers will engage and discuss where responsibilities lie across several actors to ensure social protection of vulnerable age groups – examining role of the state, social media giants, telecoms and parents. Can banning kids from social media until they reach a certain age be a possible solution or does this bring about other risks for children that may rely on the Internet given their circumstances? Understanding the digital rights of children is critical. We intend to dissect approaches for delivery of interventions and examine the need for customized content for the intended stakeholders. Finally, we shall examine the issue of funding comprehensive safety programmes at a national/regional level and again examine how responsibilities may be linke

title: IGF 2025 WS #426 Ensuring Equitable and Innovative AI Through Inclusive Data
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: How can inclusive data governance frameworks mitigate risks of information dominance while promoting equitable and local AI development? What strategies can ensure AI systems are trained on diverse, representative, and high-quality data to support public interest objectives? How can data governance practices enhance content integrity, media resilience, and inclusive information ecosystems?
policy_recommendations: Participants will learn about how different jurisdictions govern data in AI systems and the implications for sustainable innovation in which the benefits accrue to a wide array of stakeholders. They will gain a deeper understanding of data governance strategies that promote quality and inclusive information ecosystems. It will present research on AI and copyright and AI governance frameworks from Brazil, Europe, Japan, Indonesia, South, Africa, the UK and the US on practical frameworks that prevent power consolidation, as well as examples of inclusive data governance initiatives that support innovative and sustainable AI. Attendees will also acquire actionable ideas for building AI systems that reflect diverse voices, ensuring public interest outcomes in the digital landscape.

title: Holding environments for multi-stakeholder DPI governance
organizers: Intergovernmental Organization, Technical Community, Intergovernmental Organization
key_issues: Role of holding environments in making DPI governance safe and inclusive; embedding holding environments in policy-making for safe and inclusive DPI; examples of multi-stakeholder governance for operationalising holding environments
policy_recommendations: Operational understanding of holding environments, ecosystem mapping framework for reviewing multi-stakeholder collaboration in DPI-related policy processes, contributing insight to operationalisation of holding environment concept
target_audience: Participants in DPI-related policy processes
stakeholders_involved: Intergovernmental Organizations, Technical Community, Civil Society
impact_expectation: Help governments cultivate effective multi-stakeholder governance mechanisms for digital public infrastructure, ensuring diverse perspectives in the development of holding environments

title: IGF 2025 WS #428 Bridging Digital Gaps in Multicultural Societies
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Digital gaps in multicultural societies, intersecting barriers (geographic, linguistic, socioeconomic), digital literacy disparities, online safety challenges, and community-based digital literacy programs.
policy_recommendations: Develop culturally sensitive digital literacy initiatives, implement data-driven policy solutions for multicultural contexts, and adopt inclusive strategies to enhance universal access and online safety.

title: AI, Gender & Climate Justice: Intersectional AI Governance
organizers: Technical Community, African Group, Civil Society, African Group, Civil Society, African Group
regional_focus: African Group, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: How can AI governance frameworks integrate principles of sustainability and gender justice to prevent long-term social and environmental harms? What regulatory and policy gaps exist in addressing AI’s environmental footprint and its potential to reinforce historical gender biases, and how can they be closed? How can policymakers, technologists, and advocates collaborate to ensure AI governance is intersectional, balancing innovation with ethical, gender-responsive, and sustainable approaches?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain a critical understanding of how AI governance can integrate principles of sustainability and gender justice, ensuring policies proactively address environmental and social risks. They will leave with: Insight into AI’s environmental and gendered impacts, including how existing governance frameworks may reinforce biases and inequalities. Diverse perspectives from policymakers, AI ethicists, and activists on regulatory gaps and best practices for intersectional AI governance. Actionable strategies to advocate for policies that embed sustainability and gender equity in AI decision-making. A deeper awareness of the long-term consequences of AI governance, helping them critically assess emerging policies to prevent future harms. This session will equip attendees with the knowledge and tools to push for AI policies that do not just mitigate risks, but actively build a more just and sustainable future.

title: IGF 2025 WS #43 Lessons in Bridging the Digital Divide in Times of Crisis
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: How can international bodies like the ITU and governments ensure and protect internet and telecommunications access in conflict zones, especially where ICT infrastructure is deliberately targeted? What immediate and long-term solutions exist for restoring internet access and building resilient ICT infrastructures in crisis-affected regions, and what barriers prevent their implementation? What role can multistakeholder advocacy—civil society, private sector, and policymakers—play in promoting the recognition under international law that deliberately disrupting or preventing people's access to the internet violates human rights?
policy_recommendations: Policy recommendations on regional and global level to strengthen protections for digital access in conflict zones.
networking_goals: Networking opportunities with cross-sector experts and organizations working on similar contexts in geographically distant locations.
agenda: A 90-minute session provides the necessary time for in-depth discussion and interactive engagement, including regional case studies, advocacy lessons, and technical solutions. The additional time ensures that online and onsite participants have space to contribute meaningfully. This duration will allow real-time interaction between remote and in-person attendees without compromising depth or inclusivity.
collaboration_outcomes: Technical knowledge of solutions used in recent crisis settings to reconnect people. Common advocacy strategies to hold stakeholders accountable for restoring telecom access.

title: IGF 2025 WS #430 How 'Meaningful' is Disability Inclusion in Digital India?
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Scaling assistive technologies and inclusive digital ecosystems. Strengthening policies and DPDP Act implications. Digital accessibility in education and employment. Entrepreneurship and ICT adoption for PwDs.
policy_recommendations: Policy recommendations and best practices for scaling digital accessibility. Public-private collaboration for inclusive digital ecosystems.

title: Am I Addicted? Exploring Screen Dependency and its Risks
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, African Group, Civil Society, African Group, Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: The session will discuss the risks of screen dependency, including cybersecurity threats, mental health challenges, algorithmic harm, and the mental health impacts of excessive screen exposure, particularly among children and adolescents. It will also explore how public policies can promote technological innovation while protecting individuals from these risks.
policy_recommendations: The session will create a space for exchange between experts and the audience, allowing participants to gain practical knowledge applicable to their daily lives. Strategies for a more balanced use of digital technologies will be discussed, along with recommendations to reduce both individual and collective risks, fostering healthier digital habits.

title: IGF 2025 WS #432 Augmenting Security through Threat Intelligence
organizers: Private Sector, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Assessing the motives, strategies, methods, and procedures (TTPs) of international cyber threat actors; Engaging in cybersecurity threat intelligence training and educational initiatives to build a trained workforce; AI automating vulnerability assessment and identification to find and correct flaws before exploitation
policy_recommendations: Publications of research papers in C

title: Open Climate Governance: Beyond Closed-Door COP Processes
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: How can commons-based governance ensure that climate information is accessible to all? What role can open data and open knowledge initiatives play in holding decision-makers accountable? How can we collectively advocate for more inclusive and transparent COP processes?
policy_recommendations: Participants will leave the session with a clear understanding of how commons-based governance models can democratize access to climate-related information and foster transparency in global climate discussions. They will learn–and possibly join– about the work and advocacy of the Open Goes COP coalition, including their efforts to promote open knowledge, equitable access to information, and inclusivity in COP processes. Attendees will connect with like-minded individuals, organizations, and experts working on open climate governance, fostering potential collaborations and partnerships. They will acquire participation skills and learn how to effectively engage in high-level climate discussions, such as COP processes, and amplify marginalized voices in these spaces. By attending, participants will help build concrete steps and recommendations for advancing open climate governance, including how to leverage open data and open knowledge initiatives.

title: IGF 2025 WS #434 Innovating Submarine Cable Resilience for a Connected Africa
organizers: Civil Society, African Group, Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Technical Community, African Group, Intergovernmental Organization, African Group
key_issues: Regulatory frameworks for cross-border collaboration, private sector involvement in cable networks, government role in cable redundancy, cybersecurity frameworks for cable protection, climate resilience in cable planning, and addressing geopolitical/regulatory challenges impacting Africa's submarine cable infrastructure.
policy_recommendations: Actionable policy recommendations for governments, regulators, and the private sector to foster a resilient regulatory environment, incentivize investment, and address cybersecurity risks.
networking_goals: Collaborative networking opportunities to build partnerships for enhancing submarine cable resilience, connect with key stakeholders, and develop regional cooperation strategies.
agenda: Interactive roundtable session promoting collaboration, knowledge-sharing, and actionable outcomes to address submarine cable infrastructure challenges in Africa.
collaboration_outcomes: Developing regional cooperation strategies and governance frameworks, and contributing to strategic action plans for regional collaboration.

title: Co-Governing the Digitalisation of Work
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Discussion on inclusive governance of AI systems in the workplace, AI literacy initiatives, co-governance models between employers and employees, risks and harms of algorithmic management systems, and the need for transparency, explainability, and worker rights protection.
policy_recommendations: Presentation of the Co-governance Guide, discussion on mutually agreed solutions for managing AI technology in workplaces, and exploration of initiatives to enhance AI literacy and ensure responsible development and use of AI systems.

title: Empowering Youth IGFs: Overcoming Barriers for Impact
organizers: Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group; Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group; Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group; Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group; Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG); Technical Community, African Group; Civil Society, African Group; Technical Community, African Group
key_issues: Challenges faced by Youth IGF (YIGF) initiatives including leadership transitions, sustainable impact, and overcoming institutional barriers. Discussion on policy questions related to institutional resilience, impact and value creation, and support for youth-led initiatives in regions with institutional barriers.
policy_recommendations: Develop governance structures for YIGF initiatives to survive leadership transitions and maintain organizational memory. Transition from short-term projects to sustainable, long-term programs influencing policy at national and global levels. Support youth-led initiatives in regions with institutional barriers through regional and global IGF communities.

title: Hacking the Future: Rebuilding the Open Internet
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: The session will explore the tension between the original vision of a free and open internet and the current reality marked by the consolidation of power in the hands of 'Big Tech.' It will analyze how the evolution of the internet from a space of citizen empowerment to a geopolitical battleground poses significant challenges to democracy. The discussion will cover the influence of Big Tech in shaping society, from mass surveillance to manipulation of public opinion, algorithmic amplification of content, and commercialization of attention. It will also address the erosion of the free and open internet, once a bastion of free speech and access to information, and the strategies employed by Big Tech companies to create 'walled gardens' that limit competition.
policy_recommendations: The session seeks to encourage participants to critically reflect on the role of large technology companies in society and politics, their challenges to democracy, and the idea of an open and free Internet. Ideas will be offered to strengthen the democratic governance of the Internet and promote open innovation. The session will inspire participants to engage in community action and policy advocacy and even develop new ideas that contribute to reconstructing the concept of a free and open Internet from their areas of action.

title: Digital Dilemma: AI Ethical Foresight vs. Regulatory Roulette
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
speakers: von Knebel Moritz , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)

Saba Tiku Beyene , Technical Community, African Group
Alexandra Krastins Lopes , Private Sector, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)

key_issues: Key loopholes in AI regulations, ethical foresight in AI governance, cross-border regulatory cooperation, inclusion of marginalized communities in AI policymaking
policy_recommendations: Develop recommendations to balance ethical principles and AI regulation, identify novel approaches for cross-border cooperation, ensure accountability for digital platforms, and enhance participation of marginalized communities in AI governance
format: Classroom session with expert scene-setting, guided small-group discussions (online and onsite), constructive dialogue to develop recommendations
key_takeaways: Understanding AI governance challenges, exploring regional approaches to ethical foresight, strategies for cross-border collaboration, proactive models for adaptable governance, and practical approaches to bridge gaps between stakeholders

title: IGF 2025 WS #439 Update Required: Fixing Tech sector’s Role in Conflict
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
speakers: Gayatri khandhadai , Civil Society, African Group
Jalal Abukhater , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
Kiran Aziz , Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Why are we failing despite international attention on conflicts? To answer this question, we need a multistakeholder solution oriented dialogue, one that accounts for all perspectives. The aim is to have an interactive discussion garnering insights from all the participants. A round table format will let us have the following session plan: 1. 3, 30 minutes of introductory interventions by the different speakers 2. 30 minutes of discussion on gaps in the current initiatives to hold companies accountable for violations in conflict zones 3. 30 minutes of discussion on what concrete recommendations we can make to companies, states and to international mechanisms. We need this to be a collaborative exercise and a round table will facilitate that.
policy_recommendations: What policies and due diligence requirements should be enforced to ensure tech companies do not enable rights abuses in conflict zones? How can responsible disengagement be structured to prevent complicity in war crimes while minimizing harm to affected populations? What mechanisms can strengthen corporate accountability for tech companies operating in conflict-affected areas under international humanitarian law?

title: Digital Trade Agreements: Bridging Internet Fragmentation
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: Challenges in aligning trade and digital policies, legal and policy frameworks beyond international economic law to address internet fragmentation, and how digital trade agreements interact with broader internet governance principles.
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain insights into the Policy Network on Internet Fragmentation (PNIF) framework, including the state of internet fragmentation, key elements of digital trade, and the role of international public law in digital regulation. Through real-world examples, they will examine how trade provisions impact cross-border data flows, net neutrality, cybersecurity cooperation, AI governance, and interoperability. The session will highlight best practices from digital trade agreements and global regulatory frameworks.

title: Tracking online risks and barriers to digital rights
organizers: Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: AI-driven risks in online safety, successful interventions in Southeast Asia, policy and governance gaps in AI accountability for child protection, algorithmic biases, recommender systems, GenAI in spreading misinformation, deepfakes, and exploitative content, youth perspectives on digital security, digital literacy programs, regulatory gaps, AI ethics, platform accountability
policy_recommendations: Develop rapid-response strategies and policy recommendations for AI governance, platform accountability, and digital literacy; create ethical AI guidelines to prevent exploitation; design AI systems for children’s safety and sustainable funding; address GenAI, algorithmic manipulation, deepfakes, and AI-driven misinformation while safeguarding digital rights; examine regulatory gaps, AI ethics, and policy solutions for platform accountability
talk_topics: AI-driven risks in online safety (e.g., algorithmic biases, recommender systems)
Successful interventions in Cambodia, Thailand, Vietnam, and the Philippines
Policy and governance gaps in AI accountability for child protection
format: Phase 1: Expert lightning talks (20 mins) Three experts from civil society, industry, and academia will deliver 5-minute presentations on: AI-driven risks in online safety (e.g., algorithmic biases, recommender systems) Successful interventions in Cambodia, Thailand, Vietnam, and the Philippines Policy and governance gaps in AI accountability for child protection These concise talks will establish a strong knowledge foundation. Phase 2: Real-world scenario simulation (20 mins) Participants, divided into stakeholder groups (policymakers, regulators, youth advocates, educators), will analyze AI-driven safety challenges, assessing risks, ethical dilemmas, and systemic barriers. Phase 3: Multi-stakeholder response & policy sprint (30 mins) Groups will develop rapid-response strategies and policy recommendations, with live expert feedback ensuring feasibility. Phase 4: Collective debrief & call to action (20 mins) Teams will present solutions, followed by a moderated discussion, synthesizing key takeaways into concrete recommendations for AI governance, platform accountability, and digital literacy.
key_takeaways: Understanding AI-driven risks in online platforms and their implications for children and young people; examining AI personalization, recommender systems, and Generative AI (GenAI) in spreading misinformation, deepfakes, and exploitative content; highlighting youth perspectives on digital security and real-world interventions in Cambodia, Vietnam, and Thailand; gaining insights into algorithmic biases in content moderation and exploring effective digital literacy programs that build trust and resilience, especially for marginalized communities; showcasing diverse global and regional perspectives on AI governance, examining regulatory gaps, AI ethics, and policy solutions for platform accountability; through multi-stakeholder collaboration, developing strategies and recommendations for AI governance, platform accountability, and digital literacy.

title: AI in Warfare - Role of AI in upholding International Law 2.0
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Challenges and opportunities with AI in improving targeting, data training monitoring at national level, developments in International Humanitarian Law on AI use in military context, linkages to debates at the Group of Governmental Experts on Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons
policy_recommendations: Checklist/recommendations of IHL compliance by design to promote AI for Good, actionable strategies for responsible AI development and deployment
networking_goals: Knowledge exchange, collaboration, mutual respect and trust, in-depth exploration of complex issues
agenda: Roundtable discussion on AI in warfare, exploring challenges and opportunities, data training monitoring, developments in International Humanitarian Law, linkages to debates at the Group of Governmental Experts on Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems, practical understanding of AI governance in warfare, insights into translating legal principles into technical specifications, real-world case studies of AI deployment
collaboration_outcomes: Equipping participants with actionable strategies for promoting responsible AI development and deployment, contributing to a safer and more ethical digital future in armed conflict

title: Preserving Encryption in a Changing, Risky World
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group; Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Discussion on how lawmakers can ensure proportionate measures to preserve encryption while fulfilling national security/CSAM prevention mandates, alternatives to anti-encryption mandates, regulation flow for communications security, impact of breaking encryption on different stakeholders, and the interplay between regulatory action, user harms, and platform roles.
policy_recommendations: Opinions on encryption from industry specialists, regulators, civil society, and experts. Views from both the global north’s and global south’s experience with encryption and regulatory mandates. Insight into commonalities and future plans of action. Importance of encryption for protecting free speech and privacy. The interplay between regulatory action, user harms, and the roles that platforms can play in this regard.

title: AI in Cyber Warfare: A Double-Edged Sword
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group, Government, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Private Sector, African Group
key_issues: Impact of cyber warfare on AI and its weaponization by state and non-state actors; ethical considerations for AI-powered cyber defense systems; bilateral and multilateral cooperation for cross-border collaboration and information-sharing in real-time cyber defense
policy_recommendations: Exploration of how AI is both a weapon and a shield in cyber warfare; understanding AI-driven cyber risks; learning about global efforts to regulate AI in cybersecurity; strategies for fostering international cooperation on digital resilience

title: When Open Isn't Open: The AI Governance Dilemma
organizers: Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group; Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group; Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG); Civil Society, African Group
regional_focus: Asia-Pacific; Western European and Others Group (WEOG); African Group; Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: The session addresses debates around the Open Source Initiative’s draft definition of Open Source AI, highlighting that AI systems are inherently more complex than traditional FOSS, making it easy to abuse 'open source AI' through open-washing proprietary technologies. It explores governance challenges of empowering LLMs with destabilization risks and the need for stakeholder engagement in the ecosystem.
policy_recommendations: Policymakers and AI practitioners should consider the complexity of open source AI compared to traditional FOSS when defining and employing it. Open source AI frameworks should promote rapid development while ensuring transparency, safety, and ethical governance. Stakeholders must balance the benefits of open access with risks like misuse, bias, and data security.

title: IGF 2025 WS #449 Rebuilding Trust Online: Human Rights-Centered Provenance
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
speakers: Jacco-Pepijn Baljet , Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Mallory Knodel , Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Mevan Babakar , Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Souza Michel , Intergovernmental Organization, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Jacobo Castellanos Rivadeneira , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: Policy Question(s) --> What should governance frameworks (for standardization, regulation or product policy) include to ensure that digital provenance systems serve human rights rather than undermining privacy or creating inequitable information ecosystems? --> How can we balance the technical standard, of provenance systems with the need for inclusive design that addresses diverse global needs and protects vulnerable populations? --> How should provenance systems distinguish between and appropriately handle the continuum of content—from fully human-created to hybrid human-AI collaboration to completely AI-generated material—while maintaining trust without stifling innovation or expression?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain a comprehensive understanding of the current provenance landscape, including key standardization efforts, regulatory frameworks, and real-world examples of these systems in action today. Speakers will provide frameworks that will help understand how provenance infrastructure reshapes how we consume content online and how trust is established. These insights will enable participants to evaluate how these technologies might impact vulnerable individuals and communities, and to identify strategies and actions for mitigating potential harms. Attendees will also be invited to explore constructive approaches to designing and governing provenance systems that not only rebuild trust but also strengthen our collective information ecosystem. By the session's end, participants will be equipped with the knowledge to meaningfully contribute to ongoing discussions about human rights-centered approaches to digital provenance in our increasingly complex online environment.

title: IGF 2025 WS #45 Unlocking Digital Opportunities for Marginalized Communities
organizers: Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: Harmonizing sector policies to enhance data value and promote economic development in Nigeria; challenges and opportunities for implementing effective data governance policies in Nigeria; promoting transparency, accountability, and trust in government and private sector institutions through data governance policies.
policy_recommendations: A coordinated approach to data governance in Africa, providing a framework for addressing challenges related to data governance.
networking_goals: Establishing connections with peers and stakeholders in the data governance ecosystem; networking opportunities for professionals working in data governance and policy development.
agenda: Interactive discussions, collaborative problem-solving, sharing experiences and expertise to address data governance challenges; focused discussions to maintain engagement.
collaboration_outcomes: Framework for addressing data governance challenges in Africa; practical guidance on developing and implementing effective data governance policies.

title: IGF 2025 WS #450 AI Sovereignty for Whom? Large Platforms, States or People?
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
speakers: Vittorio Bertola , Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Melody Musoni , Civil Society, African Group
Bianca Kremer , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: What is AI Sovereignty and how can people can be AI Sovereign? How does platform power shape governance models, particularly in the Global South? How can AI sovereignty be enjoyed without exacerbating internet fragmentation?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain a nuanced understanding of AI sovereignty and platform power from a Global South perspective, exploring how governance frameworks shape digital autonomy. Attendees will engage with critical discussions on how Global South nations navigate dependencies on dominant platforms and their controlling companies’ technological strategies and portfolios, platforms’ structural power as forms of quasi-state capacities, the intersection between platform choices in AI systems that dictate the flow of information and their ability to govern ecosystems, and strategies for regulatory and technological self-determination. The session will provide fresh insights into power asymmetries in platform regulation and AI diffusion, offering comparative perspectives on policy approaches and governance models. Participants will leave with a deeper awareness of the risks and opportunities associated with platform governance and AI governance, as well, as practical strategies for fostering more equitable and sovereign digital ecosystems in their respective contexts.

title: IGF 2025 WS #451 Between personal data sovereignty and strategic autonomy
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
speakers: Christian REIMSBACH-KOUNATZE , Intergovernmental Organization, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)

What policy mechanisms can balance individuals' control over their data with the need for secure and efficient cross-border data flows?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain a nuanced understanding of how personal data sovereignty can serve as a lever for enhancing strategic autonomy at both national and regional levels. The session will present concrete examples of emerging technologies—such as feder, trusted data intermediaries, and privacy-enhancing technologies—that empower individuals to control their data while supporting broader digital sovereignty objectives. Attendees will benefit from diverse perspectives, including insights from policymakers, industry leaders, academics, and civil society representatives from different regions, highlighting varied approaches and challenges. The interactive format will encourage exchange of ideas on aligning individual rights with geopolitical resilience, equipping participants with fresh policy insights and potential strategies adaptable to their local contexts. Ultimately, attendees will leave with actionable knowledge on how personal data governance can strengthen digital sovereignty, mitigate geopolitical risks, and foster a more open, secure and equitable global digital ecosystem.

Attendees also gain practical knowledge on how to leverage interdisciplinary expertise and cross-sectoral partnerships to enhance global digital cooperation. Attendees will also explore practical tools, case studies, and collaborative strategies for implementing sustainability-driven digital solutions. Through interactive discussions, they will leave with actionable recommendations, fresh ideas, and a broader network to drive responsible innovation in their respective fields.

Emmanuel Niyikora , Technical Community, African Group
Dina Santana Santos , Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: Policy Question(s) How can governments and regulatory bodies strengthen digital policies, such as Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) and the right to repair, to ensure sustainable e-waste management? What role should technology companies and manufacturers play in reducing e-waste, and how can digital policies incentivize sustainable design, recycling, and reuse? How can multistakeholder collaboration drive effective implementation of circular economy principles in digital technology production and disposal?
policy_recommendations: Participants will leave this session with a deeper understanding of how digital policies shape sustainable e-waste management solutions and why frameworks like Extended Producer Responsibility and the right to repair are critical. Through expert insights and real-world case studies, they will gain practical knowledge of policy-driven solutions, industry best practices, and grassroots initiatives that promote circular economy principles. They will gain insights into global and regional policy frameworks, industry best, practices, and innovative approaches to e-waste reduction, including design-for-recyclability strategies, sustainable business models, and regulatory mechanisms that hold the different actors accountable. The session will provide actionable tools and recommendations to help policymakers, businesses, and civil society integrate responsible e-waste management into their strategies, and advocate for stronger digital policies within their organizations and communities, empowering them to contribute to a more sustainable digital ecosystem.

title: IGF 2025 WS #461 Exploring Enhanced Cooperation Within the IG Ecosystem
organizers: Civil Society, Eastern European Group; Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Key challenges faced by enhanced cooperation as a follow-up process related to Internet governance, mechanisms for regional and global levels to facilitate enhanced cooperation, whether enhanced cooperation remains a standing commitment or if progress made so far is sufficient, frameworks and modalities for enhanced cooperation, and whether the IGF and enhanced cooperation can co-exist.
policy_recommendations: Gain a foundational understanding on enhanced cooperation, its history and its process. Insights into past activities related to enhanced cooperation and the key reasons behind it. Exposure to diverse stakeholder perspectives of enhanced cooperation. Ability to understand why some views support it and who finds it important and who find it less relevant and for what reasons. Opportunity to interact directly with the panelists who were involved in the enhanced cooperation process. Ability to critically assess and develop their own informed perspective on enhanced cooperation by the end of the workshop.

title: Bridging the Compute Divide: A Global Alliance for AI
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Geopolitical and technical barriers to equitable access to computational power for AI development, lessons from global public goods initiatives, Global South leadership in AI governance and infrastructure policies
policy_recommendations: Design a multilateral framework for fair distribution of compute resources, reduce dependence on foreign compute providers, build sustainable local AI capacity, and create a Global Alliance for Computational Power
format: 75-minute roundtable with interactive discussion, structured around policy questions, including speaker presentations and real-time exchanges
key_takeaways: Understanding of geopolitical and technical challenges in AI development, insights into current approaches' limitations, exploration of international cooperation for sustainable and equitable solutions, introduction of the Global Alliance for Computational Power concept

title: IGF 2025 WS #463 Cloud Infrastructures, Sovereignty, and Multistakeholderism
organizers: Private Sector, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC); Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC); Government, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
speakers: Ricardo Campos , Private Sector, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Tania Cosentino , Private Sector, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Marilia Maciel , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Ignacio Sánchez González , Civil Society, Latin, American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: Impacts of cloud infrastructure on internet architecture and sectors, strengthening digital sovereignty in ICT, emerging technologies, and services like AI, IoT, and big data; cybersecurity, operational risks, and stability concerns for public policies and online services; cloud regulation and its impact on users' fundamental rights and internet governance principles; role of States as regulatory actors and stakeholder collaboration.
policy_recommendations: A-What are the impacts of cloud infrastructure on internet architecture and sectors, and how can it strengthen digital sovereignty in ICT, emerging technologies, and services like AI, IoT, and big data? B-What are the cybersecurity, operational risks, and stability concerns for the continuity and efficiency of public policies and online services in the context of public digital infrastructures? C-How should cloud regulation be proposed, and how might it impact users' fundamental rights and internet governance principles? D-What is the role of States as regulatory actors, and how can stakeholders collaborate democratically and multistakeholder-wise?

title: IGF 2025 WS #464 Navigating A Changing Digital Landscape
organizers: Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: How can governance frameworks evolve to address AI’s integration into broader sociotechnical and institutional systems rather than focusing on isolated risks? How can sound and thoughtful safeguards and standards ensure secure interoperability while fostering responsible AI innovation? What mechanisms are needed to ensure AI systems can anticipate failures, recalibrate responses, and function effectively within complex governance structures? How can policy, technical standards, and operational oversight be better aligned to create a more adaptive and effective AI governance model?
policy_recommendations: Gain actionable insights into how AI governance works today and can be strengthened and aligned. Contribute to shaping policy recommendations that address AI’s societal impact, ensuring ethical, secure, and sustainable AI deployment. Engage with leading experts and decision-makers from government, industry, and academia to explore innovative solutions for AI governance, climate-conscious digital transformation, and critical infrastructure resilience.
