title: Judging in the Digital Age: Cybersecurity & Digital Evidence
organizers: Technical Community, African Group
key_issues: How can judicial systems ensure the integrity, authenticity, and admissibility of digital evidence, while safeguarding due process and defendants' rights? What cybersecurity measures should courts and judicial institutions implement to protect sensitive legal data, prevent cyber threats, and maintain public trust in digital justice systems? How can international legal frameworks and cross-border cooperation be improved to address the challenges of digital evidence, cybercrime, and jurisdictional conflicts in an increasingly interconnected world?
policy_recommendations: Provide diverse perspectives from judges, legal experts, cybersecurity professionals, and policymakers, offering a multidisciplinary understanding of legal and technological intersections. Attendees will explore strategies for judicial training and capacity-building, enabling courts to adapt to emerging digital challenges. Additionally, participants will receive practical tools and policy recommendations to strengthen legal frameworks, promote international cooperation, and enhance digital trust within the judiciary.
key_takeaways: Judicial systems must adapt to cybersecurity threats and digital evidence challenges, ensuring legal integrity and due process while promoting international cooperation and digital trust.

title: Cybersecurity Odyssey: Securing Digital Sovereignty & Trust
organizers: Civil Society, African Group, Technical Community, African Group, Government, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: The design of cybersecurity governance frameworks influencing resilience, sovereignty, and trust in digital infrastructures, particularly telecom and critical sectors; core principles for effective cybersecurity policy development; harmonization of global standards in cybersecurity governance and the role of the Global Digital Compact.
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain insights into cybersecurity-national security intersections, actionable strategies against AI-powered attacks, quantum encryption threats, telecom vulnerabilities; practical tools for cyber resilience and policy responsiveness; understanding of security-by-design and digital sovereignty; methods for multistakeholder collaboration; advocacy for inclusive cybersecurity policies; contribution to defining global standards aligned with the Global Digital Compact.

title: Connected Resilience: Policy Actions for Women in Digital
organizers: Civil Society, African Group; Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: How can national and regional digital policies more effectively integrate gender-responsive approaches to address systemic barriers, such as affordability, infrastructure gaps, and socio-cultural constraints, that hinder women’s digital inclusion and participation in the digital economy? What role should multistakeholder partnerships have in ensuring that digital inclusion policies translate into implementation for meaningful connectivity for women, particularly in underserved communities? What are the biggest barriers in the effective implementation of existing policies/strategies for digital gender empowerment and how to overcome the gap between policy and tangible actions?
policy_recommendations: Cross-regional knowledge-sharing among participants to generate actionable policy recommendations. Practical insights on gender-inclusive policy development process from Africa and Asia.

title: IGF 2025 WS #195 Roles and Responsibilities across the AI value chain
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Private Sector, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
speakers: Laura Galindo Romero , Private Sector, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Thomas Schneider , Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Umair M.Imam , Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Lorrayne Nalwoga , Technical Community, African Group
Lorray, Porciuncula , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: A. What are the types of cross-value chain feedback loops in open source AI contexts? and how can actors cooperate? B. How do AI Incident reporting frameworks work and how can cooperation across actors be supported? C. What are the AI liability questions that arise?
policy_recommendations: Participants will learn about AI value chains in an open source environment and the different types of opportunities and challenges that arise across sectors. Participants will come away with a deeper understanding of roles and responsibilities of actors across the AI value chain and ideas for how to support cooperation. In terms of tools, participants will be equipped with practical examples of how AI value chains can manifest in health care and agriculture and a roadmap for supporting collaboration and common taxonomies to balance AI innovation with addressing risks and harms.

title: Trust in the Digital Age: How Secure DNS Protects Users
organizers: Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: How can policymakers balance user privacy with the need for law enforcement access to DNS data? How can Secure DNS help prevent phishing, malware distribution, and other cyber threats? How can governments, private sector actors, and civil society collaborate to promote Secure DNS while respecting internet openness?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain a comprehensive understanding of how Secure DNS enhances online safety and trust. They will explore the critical role DNS security plays in protecting against cyber threats such as phishing, DNS spoofing, and man-in-the-middle attacks. Through real-world examples and best practices, attendees will learn how to safeguard personal and organizational data, ensuring a more secure digital experience. The session will provide actionable insights and practical strategies that can be implemented to strengthen cybersecurity measures.

title: IGF 2025 WS #197 Addressing Bloatware and Coding Inefficiency in AI and Cloud
organizers: Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: The session will discuss the role of coding efficiency in software, applications, AI models, and cloud computing in addressing sustainability and environmental concerns, the role of the software development industry, steps that can be taken from the user side, and how policymakers and governments can incentivise efficient and sustainable coding practices.
policy_recommendations: The workshop will provide an opportunity for stakeholders to come together to understand their respective expertise and contributions to sustainable coding practices, and to brainstorm complementary solutions to adopt computing practices that are efficient and sustainable.

title: Using digital platforms to promote info integrity
organizers: Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: How do inter-governmental and civil society actors reach new audiences and share trustworthy information by using digital platforms? How do inter-governmental and civil society actors navigate the complexities and challenges of engaging online and promoting information integrity?
policy_recommendations: Deliver actionable learnings from speakers on their use of digital platforms to share credible information, promote information integrity and reach new audiences. Open up space for a conversation on the complexities and challenges of using these platforms as part of intergovernmental or civil society work and share strategies to overcome these challenges.

title: IGF 2025 WS #2 Using AI in courts and safeguards of the right to Justice
organizers: Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: The session will discuss potential concerns from AI-induced biases and their implications for a defendant's right to a fair trial, and seek to reach essential principles and safeguards for using AI in courts to guarantee and protect the right to justice and fair trial.
policy_recommendations: The session seeks to reach out a number of recommendations, guiding principles and safeguards of fair trial when using AI systems in the courts. Exchange the experience with audience is essential to reach out the concrete principles.

title: IGF 2025 WS #200 WSIS+20: Setting the path for digital governance
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: How do we ensure protection, promotion and respect for human rights as core value across the implementation of all WSIS Action Lines, with a view to achieving the people-centred, inclusive and development-oriented information society envisaged by the WSIS? What role should the WSIS agenda play in the broader digital governance environment, including the GDC and ongoing global dialogues on AI and data governance? How can we ensure meaningful, sustained and diverse multi-stakeholder participation in Internet and digital governance processes in line with the NETMundial+10 Multistakeholder Guidelines?
policy_recommendations: Participants will come away with an understanding of priorities and common objectives of relevant stakeholders for the WSIS+20 review. They will be able to contribute to formulating concrete recommendations to the WSIS+20 review process, drawing from their own unique national, regional, and stakeholder perspectives.

title: IGF 2025 WS #201 For a multistakeholder Global Digital Compact
organizers: Intergovernmental Organization
key_issues: How can the multistakeholder model of digital cooperation support the way forward for the Global Digital Compact - and viceversa? Which are the priority areas/actions where stakeholders' contribution can help Governments and the UN deliver?
policy_recommendations: Elaborate a one-page document on traceability and transparency of GDC actions/commitments - Define how stakeholders can be involved in specific follow-up actions to the GDC; Hybrid Format: We will use the same format for GDC Townhalls used, e.g. at IGF2024, Paris AI Summit etc., that is 1. We prioritize interventions from online participants to make sure they are engaged 2. We will have an online moderator that can reply to queries in the chat 3. We may use Menti or other polling tool, as available

title: IGF 2025 WS #202 How to AI Impact Assessment - An Intro Manual
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Balancing innovation and risk management in AI systems, ensuring meaningful stakeholder participation, particularly youth and marginalized groups, and standardizing AI Impact Assessments globally.
policy_recommendations: Develop actionable strategies for responsible AI practices, ensure stakeholder participation in policy shaping, and establish standardized AI Impact Assessment frameworks that address ethical implications, accountability, and transparency.
networking_goals: Fostering cross-sector collaboration and exchange of views on responsible AI practices through direct interaction and debate among diverse participants.
agenda: Interactive learning through real-world AI use cases, in-depth exploration of AI ethics concepts, and guided exercises for practical application of skills.
collaboration_outcomes: Potential for cross-sector collaboration and exchange of views on responsible AI practices.

title: IGF 2025 WS #203 Protecting Children from Online Sexual Exploitation including in livestreaming spaces: Technology, Policy, and Prevention
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Technical Community, Eastern European Group, Intergovernmental Organization, Eastern European Group
speakers: Awo Aidam Amenyah , Civil Society, African Group
Pratishtha Arora , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
Robbert Hoving , Intergovernmental Organization, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Sean Litton, President and CEO, Tech Coalition
Sabine Witting , legal academic based at Leiden university
Kate Ruane , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: How can technologies to prevent CSEA on livestreaming platforms be integrated into trust and safety systems in a way that protects and promotes children's rights and how effective are these tools for children from specific communities (e.g., those that speak certain languages, or from different cultures)? How can we promote cross-platform efforts to prevent the spread of CSEA content—including when livestreaming is used to drive traffic elsewhere? How can national and international policies be strengthened to address emerging forms of abuse, such as self-generated content and online coercion? What preventative measures, including education and digital safeguards, can empower children to recognize and respond to online sexual exploitation?
policy_recommendations: Tools to support collaboration between governments, platforms, educators, and civil society. Actionable recommendations to improve platform safeguards, reporting systems, and policy frameworks.
target_audience: Participants in the session, including governments, platforms, educators, and civil society
stakeholders_involved: Civil Society, Intergovernmental Organization, Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Eastern European Group, Tech Coalition, Leiden University
impact_expectation: A deeper understanding of the intersection of livestreaming, digital platforms, and child sexual exploitation and abuse. Practical knowledge on current technologies and their impact on privacy, safety, and children’s rights. Insights into emerging trends such as self-generated content and sextortion. Approaches to integrating digital literacy and online safety into national curricula and parenting resources.

title: Closing digital divides by universal access & acceptance
organizers: Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Technical Community , Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
speakers: Sabrina Wilkinson , Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Allison O'Beirne , Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Steinhauer-Mozejko Phil , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Andrew Mwanyota Lewela, CEO, Kenya Network Information Centre (KeNIC), technical community
key_issues: How can governments develop and implement policies that ensure equitable access to high-quality internet infrastructure in rural, remote and Indigenous communities? What role can multistakeholder partnerships play in accelerating the deployment of digital infrastructure in underserved areas? What progress has been made towards Universal Acceptance, what challenges remain, and what further opportunities are there to promote linguistic diversity and inclusion on the internet?
policy_recommendations: A better understanding of how diverse stakeholders have closed digital divides by advancing universal access and a multilingual internet, as well as what challenges remain; An identification of what solutions the various stakeholder groups can apply in their local contexts; A chance to connect and meet with stakeholders from different regions with shared goals.

title: IGF 2025 WS #205 Getting the UN Cybercrime Convention Right(s respecting)
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: The session will discuss lessons from the UNCC negotiations, how the UNCC affects law enforcement authorities, and key issues remaining to be decided regarding the Convention's implementation and human rights implications.
policy_recommendations: Encourage stakeholder engagement in Ad Hoc Committee discussions and domestic debates on ratification and implementation of the UNCC.

title: AI for All: Policies and Practices to Enhance AI Innovation
organizers: Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Policies and governance structures to promote comprehensive AI development, addressing AI biases, ensuring transparency and accountability in AI-driven decision-making, and enabling equitable AI through government, private sector, and civil society collaboration.
policy_recommendations: Collaborative policymaking, investment in digital infrastructure, skilling, and innovation-friendly regulations to bridge the AI divide.
networking_goals: Networking and knowledge-sharing to contribute to shaping comprehensive AI policies and initiatives within their own organizations and countries.
agenda: Roundtable discussion with open communication, interactive dialogue between moderators and speakers, in-depth discussion, and a constructive Q&A section to address audience questions, feedback, and thoughts.
collaboration_outcomes: Exploring real-world case studies and best practices for ensuring AI benefits are equitably distributed across all regions and communities.

title: IGF 2025 WS #207 Placing Human Rights at the Center of Multilateral Consensus
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
speakers: in ’t Veld Sophie , Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Anstis Siena , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Elizabeth Kolade , Civil Society, African Group
David Kaye , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
André Lucas Fernandes , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: A. How can international law balance the need for national security with the protection of civil liberties in the regulation of spyware, and what role do multilateral bodies play in creating global standards? B. What are the key challenges in developing inclusive global standards for spyware regulation, and how can we ensure that the voices and needs of the Global Majority are adequately represented in multilateral discussions? C. How can technology developers be held accountable for ensuring transparency and ethical practices in the design and deployment of surveillance technologies, while addressing concerns of national security and international cooperation?
policy_recommendations: Participants in this session will gain a deeper understanding of the complex intersection between human rights, national security, and technology regulation in the context of spyware. They will learn how international law can be leveraged to promote ethical practices and protect civil liberties while ensuring national security needs are met. Attendees will also gain insight into the challenges and opportunities of creating inclusive global standards for spyware regulation, especially from the perspectives of both the Global North and Global Majority. Additionally, participants will have the chance to contribute to an interactive dialogue, sharing diverse viewpoints and helping to shape concrete, practical solutions for strengthening multilateral cooperation and advancing ethical, effective, and transparent spyware regulations.

title: IGF 2025 WS #209 Lessons Learned for Ensuring Inclusive UN Cyber Processes
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
speakers: Ellie McDonald , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Vera Toro Catalina , Government, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Raman Jit Singh Chima , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
Oluseyi Oyebisi , Civil Society, African Group
Suto Timea , Private Sector, Eastern European Group
key_issues: This session will explore how UN cyber processes have shaped stakeholder engagement and what lessons can be applied to future processes. It will address three main questions: (1) What lessons can be learned from past and present UN cyber processes about implementing a multistakeholder approach? (2) Which stakeholder engagement mechanisms from these processes should be integrated into future UN forums, including the permanent mechanism and work under the UNCC? (3) How can the modalities of these processes ensure meaningful multi-stakeholder participation, which leads to outcomes that respect human rights and enhance global trust and resilience?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain an understanding of how UN cyber processes have facilitated or limited multistakeholder participation and how these lessons can inform future structures and processes. Governments and representatives from international organisations will leave with practical insights on integrating multistakeholder input into the design of processes and policymaking, particularly in shaping the forthcoming permanent UN cyber mechanism and under the UNCC. Civil society and the technical community will gain strategies to demonstrate the benefits of human rights-based and multistakeholder engagement in relevant processes, helping them advocate more effectively for inclusive decisionmaking. The private sector will better understand its role in building resilience and supporting rights-respecting policies through constructive engagement.
target_audience: Governments, international organisations, civil society, the technical community, and the private sector
stakeholders_involved: Civil Society, Government, Private Sector, International Organisations
impact_expectation: To equip diverse stakeholders with the tools to strengthen the modalities of UN cyber processes, as well as contribute to international cooperation, reinforcing the need for an inclusive and resilient global cybersecurity ecosystem.

title: Global Perspectives on Governing AI for Children’s Rights
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
speakers: William Bird , Civil Society, African Group
Maria Góes de Mello , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Hazel Bitaña , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: The session will address common expectations children have for policymakers and tech companies, establish global minimum standards for AI systems impacting children, and explore how companies can design AI that upholds children's rights. It will also emphasize the importance of children's voices in AI governance and the need for a coherent approach across jurisdictions.
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain insight into a path forward grounded in existing frameworks such as the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and General comment No. 25, demonstrating that responsible innovation and child protection are not mutually exclusive.

title: IGF 2025 WS #211 Children's Rights and EdTech
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: How can we ensure EdTech products prioritise pedagogical value and children's best interests over engagement metrics and commercial interests? How can we ensure EdTech companies are held accountable for systematically violating children’s rights, and how can these requirements be effectively implemented across different educational contexts and jurisdictions? How can governments and regulators fulfil their responsibility to protect children’s rights in the digital world with regards to education by shifting responsibility from schools to EdTech companies?
policy_recommendations: Participants will develop a greater understanding of the issues surrounding EdTech, including relevant risks relating to children’s privacy and safety and the unproven pedagogical efficacy of these services. They will also gain appreciation for how Ed, impacts vary across different socioeconomic environments, with particular attention to digital divide concerns across different global regions. They will deepen their understanding of how children's rights to privacy, protection, and quality education should inform EdTech design, procurement, and classroom implementation. Finally, the session will equip participants with knowledge of emerging best practices for business conduct in the EdTech sector which respects children’s rights, including safety- and privacy-by-design approaches. The session will also set out governments’ role in protecting children’s rights in EdTech.

title: Empowering Youth-led SMEs in the Digital Economy
organizers: Private Sector, African Group; Technical Community, African Group
speakers: Ida Padikuor Na-Tei , Private Sector, African Group
Athanase Bahizire , Technical Community, African Group
Stephen Samuel Kwame Jaja , Private Sector, African Group
Abdulrahman Abotaleb , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Policy frameworks and regulatory reforms to improve access to finance, digital infrastructure, and market opportunities for youth-led SMEs; collaboration between governments, private sector, and financial institutions to create inclusive digital ecosystems; role of digital platforms and emerging technologies in fostering sustainable innovation.
policy_recommendations: Actionable recommendations on financial inclusion models, digital upskilling programs, regulatory frameworks for SME growth; collaboration between governments, investors, and technology providers to remove barriers for youth-led enterprises.
networking_goals: Knowledge exchange, collaboration between stakeholders to support youth-led SMEs, sharing of successful case studies and practical solutions.
agenda: Opening remarks & context setting (10 minutes); Panel discussion with experts and youth entrepreneurs (3,0 minutes); Q&A and audience interaction (15 minutes); Wrap-up and key takeaways (5 minutes).
collaboration_outcomes: Multistakeholder perspectives on enabling youth-driven digital innovation; actionable recommendations for inclusive policies and collaboration frameworks.

title: IGF 2025 WS #214 AI Readiness in Africa in a Shifting Geopolitical Landscape
organizers: Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Government, African Group, Intergovernmental Organization, African Group, Private Sector, African Group, Civil Society, African Group
speakers: Mlindi Mashologu, Deputy Director General, Department of Communications & Digital Technologies
Neema Iyer, Founder and Executive Director, Pollicy
key_issues: Developing AI governance capacity: How can African institutions ensure that AI development serves public interest and safeguards democratic principles and fundamental rights? Reducing dependency on foreign AI systems: What policy, infrastructure, and investment strategies can strengthen Africa’s digital sovereignty? AI and digital colonialism: How can Africa ensure control over its data, algorithms, and AI infrastructure and design AI systems that reflect African values, ethics, and culture?
policy_recommendations: The session will provide a deeper understanding of opportunities and challenges of AI governance made in Africa and its implications for digital sovereignty. Speakers from various stakeholder groups and regions will bring different perspectives, and common solutions and the way forward will be identified. The session will explore practical strategies for local AI ecosystems while addressing the risks of dependency on foreign technologies and external governance models. Participants will gain insights into: Regulatory approaches that balance innovation with the protection of human rights and democratic governance Strategies for reducing reliance on foreign AI models and infrastructure The role of African cultural and normative frameworks in shaping AI governance.

title: IGF 2025 WS #215 Moving from commitments to actions on digital governance
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Discussion on the implementation of digital governance commitments and frameworks at national and regional levels, inclusive digital governance, and the role of civil society and multistakeholder partnerships in translating global commitments into practical solutions.
policy_recommendations: Exploration of how to sustain the multistakeholder model, enhance civil society engagement, leverage technology for implementation, and foster inclusive digital governance and accountability through cross-regional and cross-expertise discussions.

title: Leveraging and protecting knowledge for bottom-up AI
organizers: Civil Society, Eastern European Group; Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG); Civil Society, Eastern European Group
key_issues: What governance models can ensure fair compensation and attribution when AI systems leverage individual and community knowledge? How to protect community and individual knowledge from exploitation in AI training while fostering local innovation? What mechanisms can be put in place to empower local communities, SMEs, research institutions in shaping bottom-up AI? How to create enabling environments to support the development of bottom-up AI that leverages localised knowledge, particularly in developing / least developed countries? How can digital governance frameworks better incorporate the distinction between data, information, and knowledge to ensure that AI development respects and amplifies human and communal insights?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain: Insights into the distinction between data, information, and knowledge, and how this distinction impacts AI development and governance. Insights into how localised knowledge can be leveraged for sustainable innovation while addressing ethical and governance challenges. Exposure to diverse perspectives on protecting community knowledge from exploitation, fostering inclusive AI ecosystems, and empowering local actors to drive AI innovation. Exposure to practical approaches to fostering bottom-up AI development while ensuring knowledge protection and fair attribution. Exposure to an experimental cognitive proximity approach for institutional AI adoption (developed by the organisation behind this proposal). SDGs 8.2 8.3 9.2 9.5 9.b

title: IGF 2025 WS #218 Strengthening Cybersecurity for Nonprofits
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Intergovernmental Organization
key_issues: Cybersecurity challenges for nonprofits, digital resilience for sustainability, multi-stakeholder collaboration, innovative tools for cyber protection
policy_recommendations: Increased awareness of cybersecurity risks for nonprofits, knowledge of collaborative efforts and available resources, practical strategies for sustainable cybersecurity measures

title: IGF 2025 WS #219 Generative AI & LLMs in Content Moderation: Rights & Risks
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
speakers: David Sullivan, DTSP, Executive Director, WEOG
Dhanaraj Thakur, CDT, Research Director, WEOG
Marwa Fatafta, Access Now, MENA Policy and Advocacy Director, MENA
key_issues: How can automated content moderation be designed and developed to respect different cultural norms and values across the world, especially in the Global Majority? What are some human rights risks specific to LLM-driven content moderation? Should there be any specific regulation of automated content moderation, including LLMs? If so, what international legal instruments or norms would we want to protect human rights in this context?
policy_recommendations: This multistakeholder, interactive session invites participants to collaboratively examine the human rights impacts of GenAI systems and LLMs, while exploring strategies for prevention, mitigation, and remedy in line with evolving regulations and transparency obligations. A key focus is the importance of demographic and regional diversity within AI development teams, and we look forward to learning from participants across sectors and disciplines. The session also underscores the vital role of civil society and marginalized communities in shaping AI-driven content moderation, particularly in the Global Majority. We encourage attendees to share insights from their local contexts, especially in high-risk situations such as conflict or crisis. Importantly, this space is designed to support activists and community members in strategizing effective advocacy and organizing efforts. By fostering dialogue and collaboration, we aim to strengthen civil society’s influence in AI governance and ensure technology upholds human rights and civic space.

title: IGF 2025 WS #220 Empowering Rights: AI, Data Literacy & Digital Inclusion
organizers: Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
speakers: KEIKO TANAKA , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
Mirco Schoenfeld , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Israel Cedillo Lazcano , Private Sector, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: Integration of data literacy into public policies to protect fundamental rights, regulatory and educational mechanisms for AI transparency, collaboration among stakeholders for inclusive digital governance aligned with human rights principles.
policy_recommendations: Actionable insights on data literacy application, strengthening global cooperation on responsible AI use, practical approaches to digital capacity-building, and fostering inclusive, equitable, and ethical digital ecosystems.

title: Digitizing Agricultural Communities with Internet Backpacks
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, African Group, Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Technical Community, African Group, Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: Policy frameworks for integrating digital connectivity and clean energy in agriculture; incentivizing digital tool adoption in African rural farming; privacy, security, and data governance in digital agriculture; multi-stakeholder partnerships for scalable solutions; strategies for women and marginalized farmers in digital agriculture.
policy_recommendations: Actionable policy recommendations for governments, industry, and civil society; addressing SDGs related to food security, climate action, and rural development.
talk_topics: Internet Backpack technology and clean energy solutions in agriculture
format: Lightning Talks: Short, impactful presentations introducing the Internet Backpack technology and clean energy solutions in agriculture. Panel Discussion: A blend of experts from agriculture, technology, energy, and policy will engage in a robust discussion on the key issues, opportunities, and barriers for digital agriculture solutions. Interactive Q&A: Participants will have the opportunity to ask questions, share experiences, and offer insights, fostering a collaborative atmosphere. Closing Remarks & Policy Takeaways: Key points will be summarized, with actionable policy recommendations for governments, industry, and civil society.
key_takeaways: Digital agriculture enhances food security, combats climate change, boosts productivity; renewable energy supports sustainable agriculture; successful case studies improve crop yields, market access, reduce post-harvest losses; collaboration opportunities for scaling solutions in rural communities.

title: IGF 2025 WS #222 Impact of Internet fragmentation on digital rights
organizers: Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group; Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
speakers: Farzaneh Badii , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
William Drake , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Sheetal Kumar , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
regional_focus: Asia-Pacific Group; Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Forms of fragmentation posing risks to digital rights, potential positive impacts of fragmentation, alternative ways for policymakers to meet goals without fragmentation
policy_recommendations: Categorization of fragmentation types, discussion of offline human rights in digital space, impact of fragmentation on human rights, ways to avoid/mitigate fragmentation's impact on digital rights and universal access.

title: IGF 2025 WS #224 Deterring Child Sexual Exploitation and Abuse on Livestreams
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
speakers: Dhanaraj Thakur , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)

Sabine Witting , Technical Community, African Group
Lauren Tharp , Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Colm Gannon , Private Sector, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: The session will help participants to gain an understanding of the unique trust and safety challenges that lie at the intersection of livestreaming and CSEA. Some approaches we will cover include design based friction or verification measures, AI based content analysis, and analysis of metadata and other behavioral characteristics to flag potential bad actors/content. Participants will understand the perspectives of those working on child safety online and those working on livest, including those from civil society.
policy_recommendations: The discussion can inform the work of those working on policies on children's safety online, social media regulation, and AI based regulation.

title: IGF 2025 WS #225 Bridging the Connectivity Gap for Excluded Communities
organizers: Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: Policy and regulatory frameworks to support last-mile connectivity initiatives, leveraging emerging technologies like Low Earth Orbit satellites, 5G, and Television White Spaces to bridge the connectivity gap sustainably, and the role of public-private partnerships and community-driven models in ensuring affordable, long-term access to the Internet.
policy_recommendations: Identification of key policies and strategies that can accelerate last-mile connectivity solutions, enhanced collaboration between governments, private sector actors, and community networks, and policy recommendations to be shared with IGF stakeholders and other decision-making bodies.

title: Strengthening Multistakeholder Participation
organizers: Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Technical Community, African Group, Technical Community, Intergovernmental Organization
key_issues: Ensuring underrepresented communities have a meaningful role in technical Internet governance, fostering cross-sector collaboration for diverse participation, addressing challenges of inclusive digital cooperation, integrating underserved communities into technical Internet governance, and exploring governance mechanisms to prevent AI from contributing to linguistic homogenization.
policy_recommendations: Concrete recommendations for strengthening multistakeholder collaboration and knowledge sharing through partnerships between governments, academia, industry, civil society, and indigenous communities to co-create sustainable, community-driven language solutions, while gathering valuable feedback from the Internet governance community on UNESCO's newly developed Roadmap on Language Technologies and Multilingualism.
networking_goals: Partnerships, collaboration, knowledge sharing, community building, and co-creating sustainable, community-driven language solutions.
agenda: A 60-minute session designed in a classroom-style format, blending expert insights with collaborative exercises to deepen understanding and equip participants with strategies for effective engagement in global technical internet governance, with a well-structured flow.
collaboration_outcomes: Developing governance mechanisms to ensure AI does not contribute to linguistic homogenization, and gathering feedback on UNESCO's Roadmap on Language Technologies and Multilingualism.

title: IGF 2025 WS #227 Charting Global AI Dialog & Governance: Where Do We Go?
organizers: Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: A. How can international cooperation be strengthened to address the ethical, legal, and social implications of AI? And what mechanisms can be established to ensure transparency and accountability in AI development and deployment? B. How can stakeholders from different regions and sectors collaborate to bridge the digital divide and promote inclusive AI governance? C. What kind of cooperative mechanisms are needed for future global AI dialogue and governance?
policy_recommendations: The workshop will produce the post-event report summarizing key outcomes of the workshop, including viewpoints and recommendations, and submit to the IGF to be included in the summary report of IGF 2025. The outcomes will serve as a valuable reference for policymakers, researchers, and practitioners in the field of AI governance.

title: IGF 2025 WS #229 Responsible AI Innovation: Ethical Governance & Collaboration
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: 1. How to design innovation standards that are acceptable to multiple stakeholders and avoid unfair distribution of digital dividends while balancing diverse needs? 2. How can global governance integrate ethical values throughout the AI innovation cycle to achieve the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals? What mechanisms can ensure that AI solutions are ethically rooted, socially inclusive and risk resilient through collaborative governance?
policy_recommendations: The forum will invite experts from universities, industry organisations and companies from different regions to share and discuss. The forum will explore how to achieve social and ethical goals in the innovation process and provide morally acceptable, socially acceptable, and developmentally sustainable solutions to the significant societal risks posed by AI applications through multi-party collaborative mechanisms, inclusive frameworks, and common practices.

title: Digital Cooperation in a Fragmented World
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Balancing national sovereignty with cross-border digital cooperation, risks and benefits of multilateral versus multistakeholder approaches, practical steps to prevent Internet fragmentation while respecting national digital policies and cybersecurity concerns
policy_recommendations: Developing practical strategies for addressing Internet fragmentation, preserving digital trust, navigating national sovereignty and global cooperation, and contributing to shaping inclusive and sustainable digital policies

title: IGF 2025 WS #231 Address Digital Funding Gaps in the Developing World
organizers: Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group
speakers: Franz von Weizsaecker , Economic Development & Digital Transformation Lead, GIZ, Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Maarten Botterman, Director, Board of Directors, ICANN, Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)

Sabhanaz Rashid Diya, Executive Director, Tech Global Institute
key_issues: How can the funding community contribute toward development in LDCs, LLDCs, and SIDs, to meet their connectivity and meaningful access targets? How can the funding community work together to create collective impact, contribute to replicating and scaling innovation, and avoid duplication of efforts? How can funding toward Internet and digital development ensure that economies are able to achieve human development goals and socio-economic progress?
policy_recommendations: This workshop aims to provide a space for funders, donors, investors, and businesses to come together and identify gaps that persist with respect to connectivity, meaningful access, and knowledge in the developing regions. Speakers and the audience in attendance, including civil society, technical community, will have an opportunity to explore creative finance mechanisms to brainstorm refreshed approaches to establish a collective impact framework in the developing regions.

title: IGF 2025 WS #232 Rule of law for personal information protection in AI era
organizers: Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group; Government, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: How can existing legal frameworks be adapted to effectively regulate AI-driven personal data processing while ensuring innovation and fundamental rights protection? What are the key challenges in enforcing personal information protection laws across different jurisdictions, and how can international cooperation address regulatory gaps? How can AI governance models balance transparency, accountability, and data privacy to build public trust in AI systems?
policy_recommendations: This workshop aims to bring together global stakeholders-including government entities, civil society, technical communities, and the private sector-from Asia, Africa, Europe, and the Americas. Participants will engage in discussions on the development and evolution of AI and personal information protection, assess key concerns and challenges in this field, and explore legal frameworks and best practices for personal information protection in the AI era.

title: IGF 2025 WS #233 Political economy of DPIs: Universal highways, local streets
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group, Private Sector, Asia-Pacific Group
speakers: Luca Belli , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Smriti Parsheera , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
Keith Breckenridge , Technical Community, African Group
Armando José Manzueta Peña , Government, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)

policy_recommendations: Participants will gain insight into the political and economic forces shaping DPI trends in different jurisdictions and be equipped with critical policy questions for aligning DPI outcomes with principles of inclusion and equity.

title: IGF 2025 WS #234 AI, digital exclusions and equitable governance - do we need
organizers: Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
speakers: Ana Ruelas , Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization

policy_recommendations: Policy interventions to address algorithmic bias and data gaps, integrating gender as a core concern in regulatory frameworks, and strengthening efforts to build a plural and resilient information ecosystem that ensures women's digital human rights.

title: Exploring Alternative Models for Internet Governance
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: What is the appropriate model for Internet Governance? What is the value of multistakeholderism in Internet Governance? What will participants gain from attending this session? An understanding of the issues that alternative models for Internet governance may face An appreciation of the advantages and disadvantages of multistakeholder governance, as opposed to other models
policy_recommendations: Broader community understanding of the value of multistakeholderism. The intention is also to draft a workshop report that will then be disseminated to the various stakeholder groups.

title: IGF 2025 WS #237 CLARITI-fying ICT Accountability: A DIY Human Rights Audit
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: How can civil society organizations (CSOs) effectively assess and engage tech and telecom companies on human rights risks, particularly in restrictive environments in Asia? What mechanisms can ensure that tech sector policies align with the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (UNGPs) and uphold freedom of expression and privacy? How can access to transparent research and collaborative networks like ETIF strengthen governance and digital rights advocacy in the Asia-Pacific region?
networking_goals: Join the ETIF community, benefiting from ongoing knowledge sharing and networking
agenda: Provide key insights into digital rights challenges, including privacy, surveillance, misinformation, and governance issues, equipping participants with tools for advocacy, government and corporate engagement, and policy recommendations.
collaboration_outcomes: Participants will gain access to documents, case studies, and reports on tech accountability, along with guidance on using CLARITI findings for advocacy, governance recommendations, and publications.

title: Digital Cooperation and Global South actors: Navigating Glob
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Significant changes in U.S. policy affecting global digital rights landscape, difficulties faced by digital rights organizations in the Global South, changing dynamics of digital rights in the Global Majority, addressing these through multi-stakeholder strategies involving governments, corporate sector, academia, and civil society
policy_recommendations: Examine and pinpoint possible areas of cooperation between Global South stakeholders in digital rights. Enhance understanding and awareness to guide future legislative choices and cooperative initiatives to defend digital rights in the Global South.

title: IGF 2025 WS #239 Prospects on the Global Digital Compact in the Global South
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: How will the process include different necessities of local contexts - avoiding to reproduce a model of 'one-size-fits-all'? What are the challenges for the full implementation of the Global Digital Compact in Global South countries? How are some GDC’s objectives related to national strategies and regulatory efforts? How can a multistakeholder approach contribute to the implementation process?
policy_recommendations: Attendees will gain insights from multistakeholder representatives from Global South countries. Additionally, it will be an opportunity to understand the demands of specific sectors, such as civil society, demands in specific contexts, as well, as the actions, opportunities, and challenges in the implementation process of the Global Digital Compact by government representatives. By integrating a comparative view of various countries and organizations in the Global South, it will be possible to understand the future obstacles and difficulties that the GDC may face in its implementation and encourage cross-learning from successful practices adopted in other jurisdictions.

title: IGF 2025 WS #24 Working together to fight online gender-based violence
organizers: Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Combating online gender-based violence, multistakeholder cooperation, cost-effective educational initiatives, regulatory measures, global governance standards
policy_recommendations: Strengthen multistakeholder cooperation, develop and scale educational initiatives, establish effective regulatory measures and global governance standards to address online gender-based violence.

title: Building resilience: how we fight disinformation

Unique concepts and work routines
Examples and work routines
Collaboration between Faktisk, Rappler, and Google to build resilience
key_takeaways: Building resilience against disinformation requires collaboration between fact checkers, media literacy initiatives, and technology platforms to create a comprehensive approach to combating misinformation and ensuring trustworthy information online

title: Balancing Acts 2.0: Can Encryption and Safety Co-Exist?
organizers: Civil Society, Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
regional_focus: Western European and Others Group (WEOG), African Group
key_issues: The session discusses the complex relationship between encryption and public safety, focusing on balancing privacy with the protection of vulnerable individuals, particularly children. It explores technical solutions for lawful access without compromising cybersecurity and collaborative strategies among governments, technology companies, and civil society.
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain practical, evidence-based insights to help shape encryption governance that prioritises both individual rights and public protection. The session aims to move beyond the debate towards real-world solutions and understand the implications of 'weaponisation of privacy' for child protection and public safety.
format: 75-minute classroom format with live Q&A, case studies, and moderated audience contributions
key_takeaways: The session emphasizes the need for collaborative strategies among governments, technology companies, and civil society to create rights-respecting encryption frameworks. It highlights the importance of moving beyond polarised debates to focus on practical solutions that protect both individual rights and public safety.

title: Strengthening Regional Governance & CyberDiplomacy in Africa
organizers: Intergovernmental Organization
key_issues: A. How can African RECs strengthen cyber diplomacy and regulatory harmonization to foster cross-border digital trade and cooperation while ensuring sovereignty and security in digital governance? B. What role can public-private partnerships play in expanding financial inclusion and digital economic resilience, particularly in mobile banking, blockchain-based financial solutions, and digital entrepreneurship? C. How can African governments and regional bodies collaborate to enhance cybersecurity measures, mitigate digital fraud, and protect digital assets while fostering innovation in the digital economy?
networking_goals: cross-sector collaboration, networking opportunities and knowledge-sharing platforms that will sustain engagement and momentum beyond IGF 2025
agenda: expert panel presentations, an interactive Q&A session and key recommendations. The extended duration also allows for in-depth analysis of key issues, ensuring participants leave with actionable insights and strategic takeaways.
collaboration_outcomes: strategic roadmap for enhancing digital governance, leveraging blockchain, AI and mobile banking for economic resilience.

title: IGF 2025 WS #243 An Inclusive Digital Future: Solutions, Policies, and Impact
organizers: Civil Society, African Group, Government, African Group, Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Digital accessibility policies to ensure inclusive and equitable access for all, particularly for people with disabilities, elderly groups and seniors, people with low digital literacy levels, and marginalized groups; regulatory challenges in the Middle East regarding digital accessibility; multi-stakeholder strategies to integrate digital accessibility into governance frameworks
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain a deeper understanding of digital accessibility as a fundamental pillar of inclusive digital environments and a driver for economic growth. They will explore diverse perspectives on accessibility challenges, particularly in the Middle East, and gain insight into regional and global legal compliance frameworks. Through discussions and expert insights, attendees will discuss solutions, policies, and best practices for integrating accessibility into digital governance. They will also discuss strategies to advocate for and implement inclusive digital policies, ensuring equitable access for people with disabilities, elderly groups and seniors, people with low digital literacy levels, and marginalized groups.

title: IGF 2025 WS #244 IDN & UA: Promoting Global Digital Inclusion
organizers: Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group; Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group; Government, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: How can cooperation between governments and the private sector in IDN promotion be facilitated to remove language barriers and promote universal access to the Internet? When formulating IDN-related policies, how can the relationship between technical standards, user needs and cultural diversity be balanced to ensure that policies are inclusive and operational? What is the specific role of IDNs in enhancing Internet access and use? How can digital economic development and social inclusion be promoted through IDNs?
policy_recommendations: Develop technical and policy recommendations on IDN rollout to inform governments, international organizations, and the private sector; raise public awareness of the importance of IDNs in Internet governance and their role in promoting digital inclusion.

title: IGF 2025 WS #246 Combating Disinformation and Rebuilding Trust in the AI Era
organizers: Civil Society, Intergovernmental Organization
key_issues: A. How do existing ethical AI regulatory frameworks (such as the EU AI Act) address/fail to address the blind spots in application of ethical AI to media and communications industry? B. What can policymakers learn from local and regional strategies for addressing AI-driven disinformation at a global/universal scale? C. What role can media regulations and policies play in advancing application of ethical AI across diverse media functions?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain the following insights and takeaways from the workshop: Examine AI’s Dual Impact: Understanding how AI technologies both enable and combat disinformation globally. Showcase Best Practices: Learning about successful tools and localized strategies from diverse regions to combat disinformation. Promote Ethical AI Use: Advocating for human rights-aligned, inclusive, and ethical AI practices to protect marginalized groups and enhance media integrity. Foster Collaboration: Encouraging global and cross-sector partnerships among media, tech, civil society, and policymakers to create scalable solutions. Develop Actionable Outcomes: Equipping participants with practical tools, strategies, and recommendations to counter dis,information effectively in their respective contexts.

title: IGF 2025 WS #248 Navigating Ethical Dilemmas in AI-Generated Content
organizers: Civil Society, Intergovernmental Organization
key_issues: Policy Question(s): How can public awareness initiatives and digital literacy programs empower audiences to critically assess AI-generated content and resist misinformation? What role should media organisations, technology companies, and policymakers play in preventing the misuse of AI in content creation while fostering innovation? How can ethical AI frameworks be integrated into national and international policies to safeguard digital platforms from misinformation and manipulation?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain critical insights into the ethical implications of AI in storytelling and content creation, directly linking to sustainable and responsible innovation. Through scenario simulations and discussions, they will explore how AI can be used ethically in digital media to safeguard public discourse and democracy. By contributing with feedback to the Ethical AI Checklist, attendees will develop practical tools to prevent misinformation, and manipulation. The session will highlight the importance of content authentication in maintaining the integrity of digital platforms and fostering audience trust. Participants will leave with a deeper understanding of how ethical AI practices can strengthen media credibility, ensuring transparency and accountability in AI-driven content creation. They will also be encouraged to share the finalized checklist with their network, contributing to a broader effort to promote responsible AI use in media and protect democratic values in the digital age.

title: IGF 2025 WS #249 Disinformation and Misinformation in Online Content and its
organizers: Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
speakers: Christine Strutt , Private Sector, African Group
Charles Shaban , Private Sector, Asia-Pacific Group
Sara Freixa Ruiz , Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: How can policy effectively balance freedom of expression with the need to mitigate the societal harms of disinformation? What regulatory frameworks can promote platform accountability while fostering innovation in combating online misinformation? How can public-private partnerships be leveraged to enhance digital literacy and build resilience against disinformation across diverse populations?
policy_recommendations: Attendees will leave with practical tools to identify and combat disinformation, including fact-checking techniques, media evaluation, platform accountability, and takedown strategies. They'll gain diverse perspectives from experts across disciplines, fostering a deeper understanding of the issue's complexities. Participants will learn to analyze the societal impact of eroded digital trust and discover innovative approaches to measure and rebuild trust. The session will enhance digital literacy, empowering them to navigate online information responsibly. They will also gain insight into the psychological and social mechanisms behind misinformation and build connections with others dedicated to a more trustworthy digital environment.

title: Governing national trustworthy digitization
organizers: Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group, Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Digitization processes and strategies in Norway. How resilience the society is in the face of increased cyber threats and digital uncertainty? The main requirements for building a trustworthy digital services and infrastructure. the role of different actors in the society to increase resilience and security in crisis and war. The foundations needed for establishing national digital sovereignty. SDGs 4. Quality Education 9. Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure
policy_recommendations: The main outcome is follow-up events to further discuss and develop action points resulted from the session.

title: Closing broadband connectivity divides for all
organizers: Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization
key_issues: What policies can help bridge connectivity divides? How can metrics tracking geographic connectivity divides between regions be used to inform policy? What hurdles exist to create accurate broadband maps that depict where broadband offers are accessible? How can they inform policy? What tools and models have emerged to close geographical broadband connectivity divides (e.g. infrastructure sharing models such as open access fibre networks, community-led networks)? How can policy support or encourage these tools?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain an understanding of the latest data measuring territorial gaps (urban/rural) on a range of broadband performance indicators for over 60 countries. In addition, participants will discuss possible policy tools to overcome disparities between and within countries and in which context these tools may be appropriate.
initiative_or_product_name: Closing broadband connectivity divides for all: From evidence to practice
launch_purpose: Contributing to the evidence base, the OECD will release the publication
target_audience: Governments and societies
stakeholders_involved: OECD
impact_expectation: Ensuring that everyone is connected “well” in terms of broadband availability, quality and affordability is a key policy aim. While there has been progress, persistent connectivity gaps exist between and within countries. As societies become more connected and adopt digital technologies, divides between rural and urban areas and differences in digital adoption between groups can perpetuate or even widen. Measuring these divides is critical to better understand the state of connectivity and to enable evidence-based policymaking.

title: Addressing the challenges of digital markets
organizers: Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernment, Organization
speakers: Elise Philips , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Sven Stevenson , Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Masha Oojievaar , Private Sector, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: How can regulators and authorities join forces across sectors and borders to coordinate and cooperate in addressing challenges stemming from digital markets and in anticipating them? What are the particular challenges developing and emerging economies may face in this context? What are the most urgent issues on which regulators should focus in their cooperation, for example privacy protection, AI, online safety, financial regulation?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain insights into the evolving intersection of privacy and competition, particularly in digital markets and learn from real-world case studies of cooperation, including the Dutch Digital Regulation Cooperation Platform and the South African Digital Regulators Forum. Experts from authorities, law firms, businesses, and civil society will share perspectives on balancing competition and privacy while ensuring transparency and accountability. The session will offer actionable takeaways for policy makers and practitioners to enhance international cooperation and multistakeholder governance frameworks.

title: IGF 2025 WS #253 Research to policy through open data access & visualisation
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: How can advanced data analysis and visualization methodologies help inform more evidence-based and future-proofed policies? How can they become more mainstream? How can policies support their broader adoption and open source access across regions and disciplines? How can global and civil-society-led initiatives - leveraging cutting-edge data analysis methods - help bridge the evidence-gathering gaps between Research, Advocacy and Policy work in different regions and contexts?
policy_recommendations: The session aims to disseminate and discuss methodologies and processes for research synthesis around information ecosystems – focusing on how to strengthen the link between research and policy to the benefit of evidence-based policy-making. Understanding, discussing, and taking part in shaping the future of a global civil society and academia-led effort to develop and govern a research to policy interface on information ecosystems. 2. Learning, training, and testing advanced methodologies for research synthesis, assessment and visualization including : - LLM based pipelines - Data extraction - Data visualization - Network analysis - Citation analysis

title: Digital Diplomacy: Global Perspectives on Tech Engagement
organizers: Government, Eastern European Group

How can countries ensure that digital diplomacy initiatives are inclusive and beneficial to all, bridging the digital divide and promoting sustainable development?
policy_recommendations: Attendees will gain a global overview of how digital diplomacy is evolving, including concrete examples of successful cooperation among governments, tech companies, and international organizations. They will learn practical strategies for negotiating digital issues, from cybersecurity frameworks to data protection and AI ethics, in ways that are inclusive and responsive to different national contexts. Additionally, participants will discover how to build multi-stakeholder partnerships that uphold transparency and innovation, take away best practices from diverse regions, and explore how smaller states or emerging economies can leverage digital diplomacy. Ultimately, attendees will gain actionable insights to enhance their own diplomatic efforts in the digital era.

title: Early Warning & Transformative Innovation amid global shifts

networking_goals: Facilitate multi-stakeholder dialogue, enhance trust-building, and support the development of balanced regulatory frameworks through direct engagement and open discussion.
agenda: Interactive roundtable discussions comparing regulatory approaches, cost-benefit analysis of minimal vs. strict regulation, exploration of implications for innovation, security, and stability in African member states.
collaboration_outcomes: Practical insights, policy recommendations, and strategic tools to shape Africa's regulatory framework; fostering partnerships and knowledge exchange among stakeholders.

Shortcomings of automated content moderation systems
Steps for companies and governments to improve content moderation
Labor conditions of moderators in non-English languages

title: Empowering Youth Online: Rights, Safety & Access

What tools, skills, and resources are needed by average citizens and NGOs to identify and report hate speech in the online space? What are the best practices for civil society to monitor and report Big Tech's activities that threaten democratic values, considering the different contexts of the EU and Global South?
policy_recommendations: Participants are not only audience members but actively participate in the workshop, learning practical techniques that they will use in their own work and sharing real-life case studies and experiences for the purpose of helping them improve their documentation of hate speech online. They are invited to bring along real-life examples of borderline or concerning content that they have come across in their own work. In this way, the most relevant content can be reviewed in the group and organisations and individuals receive tailored assistance with reporting content that concerns them.

title: Towards Smarter Governance: Lessons from AI Policy Learning
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: A. What lessons can be drawn from past governance challenges in digital technologies (e.g., internet regulation, data protection, and blockchain) to inform more effective and scalable AI governance strategies? B. What conditions enable policymakers and institutions to move from static rule-making to iterative, evidence-based policy learning in the face of rapidly evolving AI technologies? C. How can different institutional policy setting traditions (such as geographical ones) learn from each other?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain a hands-on understanding of policy learning in AI governance, experiencing how governance adapts to emerging challenges in real time. Rather than a traditional panel, this session invites active engagement, allowing attendees to explore AI policy dilemmas alongside experts from law, technology, ethics, and creativity. Participants will also explore how adaptive governance models reinforce societal resilience by empowering citizens with AI literacy, fostering public trust, and improving the public sector's capacity to respond to emerging challenges. By understanding how to integrate civic-driven values into AI governance, participants will leave equipped to develop policies that align technological innovation with social cohesion By interacting with a diverse set of perspectives, attendees will challenge assumptions, test governance strategies, and rethink policy learning as an ongoing, adaptive process—one that ensures AI governance remains flexible, inclusive, and future-ready.

Diverse perspectives—from UN policymakers to grassroots advocates—will deepen understanding of global vs. local approaches, sparking innovative thinking on digital governance and scalability. Participants will leave with actionable tools and a network to advance responsible tech innovation, aligned with WSIS C7 and SDG 9, fostering collaboration across disciplines and regions.

title: IGF 2025 WS #278 Strategies for Improving Submarine Cable Resilience
organizers: Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Multistakeholder cooperation for subsea cable resilience, common ground on subsea cable security, role of international actors (EU, ITU) in improving subsea cable security.
policy_recommendations: Deepen understanding of strategies for submarine cable resilience, overview of technological and operational aspects, geopolitical context, best practices, existing initiatives, and future expectations.
description: Submarine cable infrastructure is an essential part of international communication, as it carries most international data traffic. Submarine cables are also considered to be part of the core infrastructures ensuring that the internet is globally available. In a dynamic geopolitical world, their critical role can also mark them as a target for harm, and disruptions to submarine cable connections have the potential to create major issues for the provision of connectivity and internet services. Aside from purposeful attacks, submarine cables can be damaged naturally, and repairing the infrastructure can be costly and difficult. A recent string of incidents where cables were damaged in the Baltic Sea has further drawn attention to the potential problems damage can cause. Previously, incidents for example in the Suez Canal have led to serious disruptions. These developments have resulted in regional and international efforts to improve submarine cable resilience. European policymakers
preparatory_focus: Focus on capacity building, training, or pre-discussion themes related to submarine cable resilience and multistakeholder cooperation.

How can governments and educational institutions collaborate with industry leaders and civil society to improve information literacy skills and empower users to critically evaluate online content, especially AI-generated content?

Our experts will share perspectives on the technical, policy, and ethical dimensions of provenance, offering insights into its role in combating misinformation, ensuring transparency, and fostering trust in AI systems. Attendees will discuss the opportunities and challenges for implementing different provenance tools across different platforms, regulatory and business environments. The session will provide practical takeaways, including emerging policy frameworks, industry best practices, and potential governance models to enhance AI accountability and empower users to make decisions about content trustworthiness.

title: IGF 2025 WS #282 Ensuring an age-appropriate online experience for kids
