Jennifer Brody , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Rand Hammoud , Civil Society, Intergovernmental Organization
key_issues: Policy gaps in spyware regulation, lessons from existing initiatives, collaboration between civil society, journalists, and policymakers to enforce regulations and protect against surveillance abuses.
policy_recommendations: Identify strategies to close spyware-related policy gaps, build stronger global accountability mechanisms, and strengthen enforcement of spyware-related regulations.
networking_goals: Foster networking and collaboration, equip participants with new connections and concrete next steps to drive action within their respective fields.
agenda: Scene-setting with expert insights on spyware policy challenges, facilitated discussion on policy responses and advocacy strategies, open forum for participants to explore opportunities to leverage existing mechanisms.
collaboration_outcomes: Participants will leave with practical knowledge on existing legal and policy tools and ideas on how to strengthen accountability mechanisms and counter spyware abuses.

title: IGF 2025 WS #292 Journalism and AI: Regulation in the Global South
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Private Sector, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, African Group, Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Intergovernmental Organization, Civil Society, African Group, Civil Society, Intergovernmental Organization
key_issues: Platform governance promoting transparency and fairness in content distribution while safeguarding press freedom, regulatory frameworks protecting journalism sustainability against AI-driven disruptions and platform concentration, collaboration among Global South countries to shape international digital governance and media sustainability policies
policy_recommendations: A policy document outlining recommendations for media sustainability and platform governance, including content moderation, algorithmic transparency, regulatory responses promoting free and diverse press, and South-South cooperation strategies for media resilience and equitable digital policies

title: IGF 2025 WS #293 Addressing Technology-Facilitated Gender-Based Violence
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization
key_issues: How can governments integrate TFGBV protections into broader legislative frameworks (e.g., AI governance, cybersecurity, and data protection laws)? What are the key challenges in developing human-rights-based, survivor-centered legal responses to TFGBV at national and international levels? How can policymakers ensure that legislative responses to TFGBV are intersectional, inclusive, and do not inadvertently suppress free expression or digital privacy rights?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain a deeper understanding of how to effectively integrate protections against TFGBV into broader legal and policy frameworks, such, as AI governance, cybersecurity, and data protection laws. Through expert insights and real-world case studies, attendees will explore best practices for rights-based, survivor-centered, and intersectional legislative approaches. The session will also provide practical tools, including the Guiding Principles for Rights-Based Law Reform on TFGBV, to support policymakers, advocates, and digital rights defenders in crafting inclusive, effective policies. By engaging in a multi-stakeholder discussion, participants will leave with concrete strategies to balance safety from digital violence with the protection of fundamental rights, such as freedom of expression and privacy. Ultimately, this session will empower attendees to advocate for and contribute to more inclusive, gender-sensitive digital governance frameworks that ensure online spaces are equitable and safe for all.

title: IGF 2025 WS #294 AI Sandboxes: Responsible Innovation in Developing Countries
organizers: Civil Society, Intergovernmental Organization, Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
speakers: Lorrayne Porciuncula , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Lucia Russo , Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization
Meni ANASTASIADOU , Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Moraes Thiago , Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Jai Ganesh Udayasankaran , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
Cyril Seck, Private Sector, Africa Group
Alex Moltzau , Intergovernmental Organization, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: How can sandboxes for AI support innovation in developing countries while ensuring responsible AI governance and mitigating risks? What are the key challenges SMEs face in AI adoption, and how can sandboxes help overcome barriers such as regulatory complexity and limited resources? How can international organizations and governments collaborate to create AI sandbox frameworks that are adaptable to different regional contexts in the Global South?
policy_recommendations: A deeper understanding of sandboxes (regulatory, operational and hybrid) and their role in fostering responsible AI innovation in developing economies. Insights from responsible practices of global sandbox initiatives as well as highlights from sandbox implementation toolkits from leading institutions such as the OECD. Best practices from concrete examples of AI sandboxes implemented in developing countries, as well as practical examples of how AI sandboxes have been deployed to support SMEs, regulators, and policymakers. A roadmap for establishing AI sandboxes that balance innovation and protection in developing countries.

title: IGF 2025 WS #295 New Paradigm: Digital Assets & Blockchain
organizers: Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization
key_issues: Policy Question(s) 1. With countries and local governments integrating blockchain into finance, regulation, and voting, what policies are needed to promote interoperability, compliance, and public trust in digital assets? 2. How can governments ensure the secure and responsible adoption of blockchain and digital asset technology while mitigating risks such as fraud, volatility, and illicit activity? 3. What role does the Blockchain Maturity Model (BMM) play in establishing global standards for blockchain adoption across industries, and how can governments implement it effectively?
policy_recommendations: Attendees will learn about the massive opportunities for using blockchain, digital assets and cryptocurrency to solve public sector challenges. They will also learn about open-source guides and standards to support the development, investment, acquisition, and adoption of emerging technologies to support the UN SDGs.

title: Costs of Internet fragmentation
organizers: Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: What policies, regulations and technical practices drive Internet fragmentation? What are the broad economic consequences of Internet fragmentation? What are policies that drive Internet fragmentation - like network blocking, DNS interference, sovereign Internet models, and network fees - trying to accomplish? Are there any key themes or commonalities across the intent behind those policies? How should we evaluate the long term economic impact of those policies? What economic impacts of these policies have we already seen? What other technical, policy or legal impacts should we consider? What alternative approaches to these types of policy challenges mitigate potential adverse impacts?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain a better understanding of the regulatory and legal implementation of policies around the world that potentially cause Internet fragmentation. Participants will gain an understanding of the technical consequences associated with those policies, including at the infrastructure layers of the Internet. Participants will gain a better understanding of the economic costs of those policies, including unintended or less understood consequences like over-blocking, cloud service interruption, or other online disruptions.

title: Digital Sovereignty: Bridging the Digital Divide
organizers: Civil Society, Intergovernmental Organization, Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Collaboration between governments, private sector, and civil society to support Indigenous digital sovereignty; policies to protect Indigenous data sovereignty; integrating Indigenous perspectives into global digital governance discussions
policy_recommendations: Actionable policy recommendations for supporting Indigenous participation in digital governance, community-driven solutions for digital access, and ethical data governance frameworks

title: IGF 2025 WS #299 Emerging Technologies and the Evolution of Disinformation
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Emerging technologies impact the scale and sophistication of disinformation; regulatory measures to prevent misuse of emerging technologies for disinformation; challenges and opportunities in regional or global AI governance
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain understanding of how emerging technologies reshape the information landscape, explore advancements in detecting and mitigating disinformation, and insights into ethical and governance challenges of addressing disinformation while protecting free expression.

title: IGF 2025 WS #3 Right to seek asylum in the age of AI, risks and Safeguards
organizers: Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: Using AI systems in asylum contexts raises challenges regarding the legality of automated tools, responsible use of digital technologies in displacement, motivations behind AI deployment, human-centred approaches, and adverse impacts of machine decision-making on asylum seekers' rights.
policy_recommendations: The workshop aims to issue an article on the topic and organize capacity-building programs for actors in refugees and migration fields about AI's impact on refugees and their protection.

title: IGF 2025 WS #300 Information Integrity through Journalism & Alternative Platforms
organizers: Internet Governance Forum (IGF)
speakers: Anne Marie Engtoft Meldgaard, Denmark’s Tech Ambassador, Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Julia Haas, Adviser, OSCE, Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization
Beatriz Barbosa, Journalist, Coalition for Rights on the Net, Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Jan Lublinski, Head of Policy and Learning, Deutsche Welle Akademie, Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Magnus Ag, Head of Public Interest Tech, International Media Support, Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Maxence Melo, Executive Director, JamiiAfrica, Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: A. What role can independent journalism play to bolster information integrity and contribute to building healthy online information systems? B. How is information integrity conceptualized and addressed by different regulatory or developmental initiatives around the world? And what role can States play to bolster information integrity? C. How can multi-stakeholder collaboration contribute to scaling and replicating best practices to safeguard journalism in the digital age and promote alternative discussion platforms in other geographies, cultures and linguistic communities?
policy_recommendations: Participants will benefit from the discussion on the complex concept of information integrity through a multistakeholder perspective, and will explore different approaches to strengthening information integrity. The workshop discussion will not only identify the main perspectives around this topic and present policy guidance, but will also promote the exchange of concrete experiences and lessons learned about how different solutions have been applied. As we further seek to inspire the design of digital public (interest) infrastructure that services and is serviced by high-quality journalism, those attending will better understand the critical discussion around the concept of journalism as a public good. Those joining our session will have the opportunity to engage with high- and working-level stakeholders from tech, media, policy experts and government across the globe who are using their positions to (re)create a digital space that serves the public interest, not profits nor public figures.

title: Environment as Economy & Economy As Environment
organizers: Civil Society, Intergovernmental Organization, Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Integration of environmental sustainability into economic policies, policy frameworks for green economy transition, international cooperation and public-private partnerships for sustainable innovation.
format: Theater-style, 9, 90-minute session with structured format for expert insights, audience interaction, dynamic presentations, Q&A, and debate.
networking_goals: Cross-sector collaboration and knowledge exchange on the green economy’s role in shaping a sustainable future.
agenda: Structured format for expert panelists to present diverse perspectives, audience participation, high-impact storytelling, case study presentations, thought-provoking discussions, Q&A, and debate on policy frameworks, industry trends, and technological innovations.
collaboration_outcomes: Enhance adoption of sustainable innovation across industries and supply chains through international cooperation and public-private partnerships.

title: IGF 2025 WS #302 Upgrading Digital Governance at the local level
organizers: Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: How can multi-stakeholder collaboration—including governments, civil society, and private sector actors—strengthen local digital governance and improve municipal digital maturity? What are the key challenges and best practices in assessing and enhancing municipal digital maturity, and how can methodologies like LOSI be adapted to different regional contexts? How can digital cooperation at the municipal level contribute to more inclusive, transparent, and citizen-centric governance models?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain practical knowledge on how multi-stakeholder collaboration can improve local digital governance. They will explore Tunisia’s LOSI assessment methodology, learning how to evaluate and enhance municipal digital maturity. Attendees will be exposed to diverse perspectives from government, civil society, and international organizations on digital cooperation strategies, including public-private partnerships and community-driven digital initiatives. By the end, they will leave with insights on best, practices and tools for assessing and advancing municipal digital transformation in their own contexts.

title: Financing Self-Sustaining Community Connectivity Solutions
organizers: Civil Society, African Group; Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
speakers: Nathalia Foditsch , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Elmstam Carl , Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Claude Dorion , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Marie Lisa Dacanay, Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
Chris Locke , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Alessandra Lustrati , Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Community connectivity initiatives evolving to deploy blended and impact finance; learning from social and solidarity economy initiatives; innovative financing mechanisms to close the digital divide; stakeholder roles in implementing financial mechanisms.
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain understanding of alternative approaches to achieving self-sustainability in community connectivity initiatives; leveraging strategies for blended finance and innovative financial mechanisms; ensuring communities' communication needs remain central through experiences from social and solidarity economy initiatives.

title: IGF 2025 WS #306 Cyber interference with democracy
organizers: Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization
key_issues: Exploration of cyber interference with democracy, regulatory frameworks for digital platforms, freedom of expression, AI accountability, international cooperation mechanisms, and protection of democratic processes from digital threats.
policy_recommendations: Participants will explore specific instances of cyber interference, emphasize international cooperation and multi-stakeholder engagement, and engage in discussions on policy questions related to digital platform regulation, AI accountability, and protection of free expression in the context of cyber interference.

title: Digital Public infrastructure and Digital Rights
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Balancing data collection for DPI systems with privacy and security, recommendations for policy frameworks and regulatory measures to achieve this balance, practical insights into DPI models, and experiences from different regions.
policy_recommendations: Policy frameworks and regulatory measures to achieve a balance between data collection for DPI systems and privacy protection, recommendations for rights-preserving and innovation-enabling data governance systems, and case studies from different regions.

title: Digital Safety & Equality for Marginalized Girl and Children
organizers: Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: Digital risks faced by girls and children in marginalized communities, intersectional approaches to policy-making, role of digital literacy programs in empowering children, collaboration between governments and tech companies for safer online environments.
policy_recommendations: Actionable insights into digital risks, practical tools for policy implementation, examples of successful initiatives like Kenya’s Tuseme program and Brazil’s SaferNet, networking opportunities with global stakeholders.
networking_goals: Networking opportunities with global stakeholders committed to child safety and digital rights, knowledge exchange on innovative solutions and best practices, collaboration on policy frameworks and digital literacy programs.
agenda: Open dialogue and collaboration among diverse stakeholders, in-depth discussions on digital risks, interactive Q&A, development of concrete action points, exploration of innovative solutions like AI-driven safety tools and community-led digital literacy programs.
collaboration_outcomes: Potential collaboration on policy frameworks, digital literacy programs, and AI-driven safety tools to create safer digital environments for children, follow-up actions through networking and knowledge sharing.

title: Accessibility in Phygital Spaces: Barriers & Solutions
organizers: Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Defining vulnerability and accessibility needs in phygital environments, catering to transient access needs across physical, digital, and phygital environments, and defining roles and responsibilities for digital access rights across stakeholders.
policy_recommendations: Exploring new approaches to address accessibility challenges in phygital spaces, fostering collaboration among stakeholders to co-create solutions, and ensuring inclusive environments for diverse users.

title: Scaling normative social media & communication technologies
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization, Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: Growing global concerns over AI-driven misinformation, election interference, and youth exploitation on social media; problem framing, reimagining solutions, and showcasing alternatives; evidence on the harmful effects of social media platforms on individuals and societies; AI's influence on the landscape
policy_recommendations: Present and discuss evidence on the various inter-linked ways in which today’s big social media platforms are harming individuals and societies; explore how AI will influence this landscape; identify digital public goods and open source components relevant to a normative social media landscape

title: Eco-Design for a Sustainable Digital Future
organizers: Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: How can policymakers, businesses, and developers integrate eco-design principles into digital services to reduce their environmental footprint while maintaining innovation? What levers and frameworks could help promote the adoption of eco-design practices in digital services, and more largely, to build a sustainable future to the Internet? How can transparency and user awareness of the environmental impact of digital services be improved to encourage more sustainable consumption habits?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain valuable insights into the environmental impact of digital services and the role of eco-design in building a more sustainable digital ecosystem. They will: • Discover key data and trends on the energy and resource consumption of digital technologies, including AI and streaming services. • Explore practical eco-design strategies that can reduce the environmental footprint of websites, platforms, and digital applications. • Gain diverse perspectives from experts working at the intersection of digital innovation and sustainability. • Learn about real-world examples of eco-design in action and how it can contribute to extending device lifespans and optimizing resource use. • Leave with actionable knowledge and tools to integrate eco-design principles into their own digital projects, policymaking, or business strategies.

title: Future-Proofing Policy: Gender & Data Governance in Africa
organizers: Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: How can gender transformative approaches strengthen the African Union Data policy framework implementation and address systemic biases in data governance? What role does an evaluation framework play in measuring progress towards gender equitable data ecosystems across Africa? What is the role of multistakeholderism in ensuring data policies prioritise gender equity and amplify marginalized voices?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain practical insights and tools to implement gender-transformative data governance policies. They will engage with a structured evaluation framework designed to assess the effectiveness of national data systems, ensuring gender equitable outcomes that drive sustainable development. Participants will explore how Afrofeminist principles can be integrated into data governance to address systemic biases, power imbalances, and inclusion gaps Participants will be equipped with advocacy tools and policy strategies to drive institutional adoption of regular data policy audits to strengthen accountability, transparency and evidence-based decision making.

title: IGF 2025 WS #314 Bridging the Digital Divide for Children in Africa
organizers: Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: Balancing digital access for children with online safety, roles of governments, tech companies, and civil society in child protection policies, legal frameworks for child online protection in Nigeria
policy_recommendations: Practical recommendations for implementing child-friendly digital policies, strengthening regulatory frameworks, fostering cross-sector collaboration, access to guidelines and best practices for enhancing child safety in digital spaces

title: AI Regulation in East and West - Comparing new approaches
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: The workshop will provide participants with an overview of existing approaches in AI regulation, focusing on regulatory innovations addressing technical characteristics of AI systems. It will discuss implementation challenges, resources needed for effective regulation, and the transferability of AI regulation to other countries.
policy_recommendations: The workshop will discuss implementation challenges, particularly the resources needed to effectively regulate AI systems. It will also explore the transferability of AI regulation to other countries and provide participants with a better understanding of regulatory options and the conditions for their success.

title: Green Future: Reinforcing Green Economies
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: How do green technologies such as clean and modern energy solutions support a transformative digital economy? How can technology transform the green economy but, at the same time, ensure cost efficiency such, as integration of green technologies into infrastructure and industry? How can we enhance stakeholder collaboration in achieving integration of green technologies into infrastructure and industry for sustainable production processes? Through the acceleration of stakeholders collaboration, what would be the strategy in checking the progress and outcomes for resource resilience and investment in green technologies?
policy_recommendations: This session will offer the knowledge of green technologies and its application in the Global South. We invited speakers from relevant expertise who will be pleased to share their fields of expertise. We invited various yet relevant speakers who will have their take on carbon footprints, the adoption of green technologies and their impacts. The session will provide an in-depth understanding of how different sectors such as academia, civil society, the private sector, and technical experts address environmental technology and its innovation followed by its purpose of creating awareness to the participants. Through the roundtable discussion, attendees will engage with diverse perspectives, fostering experts' opinions on sustainability solutions for the future. Furthermore, the discussion will be made to support the interaction between speakers and participants, particularly equip participants with the knowledge of green technology and carbon footprints.

title: Mapping Equal and Decolonial Futures for Digital Autonomy
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Existing gaps in platform policies and conduct in accounting for the unique online experiences of marginalised groups, especially from the Global Majority; technological mechanisms and feedback processes to address challenges faced by such communities; public discourse and policymaking to enable fair and inclusive design and structures of redressal within online platforms
policy_recommendations: Generate a culturally nuanced understanding of challenges that marginalised communities experience in navigating access, autonomy and privacy online; deepen collective knowledge of systemic biases inherent in tech design/infrastructures; enable a collective reimagination of inclusive solutions and alternatives that recognise diverse experiences of autonomy online
target_audience: Low-income women, queer-trans persons, disabled individuals in the Global Majority
stakeholders_involved: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
impact_expectation: Develop a co-created resource focused on designing autonomy-enabling environments; co-strategise decolonising Big Tech; maximising opportunities created by these technologies and minimising risks imposed on marginalised Global Majority users

title: Data Commons: Global South Challenges & Solutions
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: Balancing national sovereignty with global interoperability, addressing legal fragmentation and weak enforcement in data-sharing frameworks, and empowering communities through decentralised stewardship like national data trusts.
policy_recommendations: Designing governance models that integrate open data licenses, AI licenses, and decentralized stewardship; fostering dialogue on sovereignty and governance across stakeholders; crafting actionable frameworks tailored to local contexts; strengthening a global network for data and digital infrastructure governance.

title: AI Innovation for Public Good: A New Policy Playbook
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
speakers: Burcu Kilic , Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Pranesh Prakash , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
Sanya Smith , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: How can industrial policies use national innovation systems to lessen reliance on Big Tech and boost local AI ecosystems? What strategies can align trade, competition, and R&D to ensure AI benefits society, not just a few firms? How should public institutions evolve for a whole-of-government AI approach that ensures sovereignty and local needs?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain actionable insights into reshaping AI development through national innovation systems. They’ll learn how strategic industrial policies can reduce Big Tech dependency, foster local AI ecosystems, and enhance technological sovereignty, drawing from a 2025 open-source AI breakthrough. Attendees will acquire new knowledge on aligning R&D investments, competition, and trade policies to address market concentration and support small innovators. Diverse perspectives from global policymakers, techn, and civil society will broaden their understanding of AI’s societal impact across regions. Through interactive breakout groups, they’ll gain practical tools to design context-specific policies, ensuring AI serves local needs and public good. Participants will leave with a deeper understanding of a multi-model, multinational AI future and a playbook to drive equitable innovation, empowering them to influence governance and development strategies at IGF 2025 Norway and beyond.

title: IGF 2025 WS #322 Tech kongsi: Building resilient community-led digital infra
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Digital governance frameworks recognizing and supporting community-owned infrastructure initiatives while respecting their independence and autonomy; technical and policy safeguards to protect decentralized infrastructure from state-level censorship and corporate platform dependencies; international internet governance institutions legitimizing community-driven digital resilience efforts without imposing standardization that undermines local contexts and needs
policy_recommendations: Practical methodologies for establishing decentralized digital infrastructure, technical insights on specific tools like Outline VPN configuration, Nextcloud deployment, and Matrix communication server setup, governance frameworks for decision-making and resource allocation, risk mitigation strategies balancing usability and protection against threats, and opportunities to join a network of practitioners in the Asia-Pacific region

title: New Data Governance Models for African NLP Ecosystems
organizers: Technical Community, African Group
key_issues: Licencing and ownership: How can AI training data licenses be adapted to protect cultural sovereignty and ensure equitable benefits for (especially marginalized) language communities? Equity: What concepts in policy mechanisms can prevent extractive practices (beyond prevention of cross-border data flows) in global AI initiatives targeting African languages? Governance: Is there any way that operationalization of National AI strategies (e.g., Kenya, Rwanda, Ghana) can support community-led governance models for language datasets? If so, how and if not why not?
policy_recommendations: Critical Awareness on the power of control of IP: Insights into our work on CC0 licensing; the participants will listen to perspectives from experts on feedback from communities, that is, while enabling open collaboration, this licensing can inadvertently marginalize communities by undermining local control and equitable resource allocation in AI development. Experts will lend their perspectives on African language communities, policymakers, and practitioners on balancing openness with cultural sovereignty, data ownership, and sustainable investment models. Not another roundtable: we will unpack the problems in a relatable way but also discuss practical alternatives such, as community-led licensing, reciprocity agreements, that prioritize equity and ethics.

title: IGF 2025 WS #324 Global South Coalitions Shaping Platform Accountability
organizers: Civil Society, African Group, Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Government, African Group
key_issues: Collaboration between civil society, governments, tech companies, and fact-checkers to combat disinformation and hate speech; improving content moderation and platform governance; strategies for Global South coalitions to engage with tech platforms and policymakers.
policy_recommendations: Strengthening multi-stakeholder collaboration, balancing trust, safety, and freedom of expression in content moderation; enhancing engagement with tech platforms and policymakers despite funding constraints and regulatory challenges.
networking_goals: Cross-regional collaboration, knowledge sharing, coalition-building, and partnerships among civil society, governments, tech companies, and fact-checkers.
agenda: Roundtable discussion on strengthening collaboration to combat disinformation and hate speech, improving content moderation, and exploring cross-regional collaboration on platform governance.
collaboration_outcomes: Formation of National Coalitions on Freedom of Expression and Content Moderation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Colombia, Indonesia, and Kenya; localized content moderation strategies and multi-stakeholder collaboration frameworks.

title: IGF 2025 WS #325 Viksit Bharat – A New Economic Model for LMICs
organizers: Civil Society, Intergovernmental Organization
key_issues: How can Low- and Middle-Income Countries (LMICs) leverage digital public infrastructure (DPI) to drive inclusive economic growth while ensuring equitable access to technology and financial services? What policy frameworks and governance models can help LMICs integrate sustainability and green entrepreneurship into their digital transformation strategies to create long-term economic resilience? How can multi-stakeholder collaboration—across governments, industry, and civil society—accelerate the adoption of digital and sustainable economic policies, ensuring that vulnerable populations are not left behind in the digital economy?
policy_recommendations: Participants will leave with actionable strategies to bridge the digital divide and foster inclusive economic growth, including policy recommendations, best practices, and follow-up collaborations to drive inclusive digital growth in LMICs.

title: Brussels Effect: Platform Regulation at the EU Doorsteps
organizers: Civil Society, Eastern European Group
key_issues: How does the EU shape platform regulation in the EU Candidate States and globally? What are the possible prerequisites for adopting local platform governance legislation in the absence of applicable regional or international instruments? Which enforcement mechanisms can make platforms comply with regulation in smaller markets and be necessary and proportionate?
policy_recommendations: Attendees will learn outside perspectives on the EU regulatory regime for online platforms. Speakers from the EU Candidate States will share their insights on the negotiations with the EU, while DSA Human Rights Alliance representatives will display their advocacy work on making DSA a working instrument elsewhere. Attendees will also be able to shape future recommendations on incorporating outside voices for DSA enforcement inside the EU.
key_takeaways: The EU's DSA sets a regulatory benchmark for platform regulation globally, influencing approaches towards enhanced role diligence. However, there are concerns about its potential misuse by malicious governments to suppress dissent and stifle public debate.

title: IGF 2025 WS #327 Global Majority CSOs Sustainability amid Geopolitical shifts
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Considering the weakening of the international rules-based order and funding reductions for human rights programs, what innovative funding mechanisms and collaborative strategies can be developed to ensure the long-term financial sustainability of digital rights CSOs in the Global Majority? How can cross-border cooperation, particularly South-South collaboration, be strengthened to protect Internet freedoms amidst geopolitical shifts and increasingly authoritarian cyber-sovereignty forces? How can governments, philanthropic organizations, and international bodies address the current challenges to ensure long-term sustainability of Global Majority CSOs working on digital rights?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain valuable insights and explore practical strategies to navigate the complex landscape of Internet and tech governance amidst growing challenges. The workshop will bring together activists, civic technologists, and policy experts, creating a unique opportunity to identify key threats posed by techno-authoritarianism, authoritarian cyber-sovereignty, and geopolitical shifts that disproportionately affect CSOs in the Global Majority. An essential benefit will be the dedicated space for strategizing and planning collective action to address these threats effectively. Participants can expect to establish new connections with regional and international partners, fostering crucial cross-border networks for collaboration and information-sharing. Ultimately, attendees will leave with strategies to enhance their organization’s resilience against volatile geopolitical contexts threatening internet freedom and civic space.

title: IGF 2025 WS #328 Breaking Through Censorship with Built-In Resilience
organizers: Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Private Sector, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: A. How do new censorship circumvention tools impact legal requirements for content moderation, especially concerning platforms operating globally? B. What are the jurisdictional challenges when it comes to ensuring cross-border resilience in global networks? How do we balance resilience with respecting local laws? C. What role should public policy play in proactively fostering the development and deployment of resilient services that can withstand censorship attempts?
policy_recommendations: Workshop participants will learn about existing tools to circumvent censorship that are made for everyday people. Participants from the policy field will learn about the latest developments in network resilience and how shifts in regulation will better suit a resilient and durable information ecosystem. The technical community and private sector might learn about these new models, frameworks and tools to enhance the resilience of their networks and services. This session will serve as a “state of the art” in internet censorship in 2025 from the vantage point of those providing the “core of the internet” services: VPN providers, network measurement, and global DNS services.

title: Greening the Internet: Youth-Led Sustainable Innovations
organizers: Technical Community, African Group, Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group, Technical Community, African Group
speakers: Thomas Olsen Aarheim , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Dina Santana Santos , Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Stepovaya Daria , Civil Society, Eastern European Group
Seun Olatunji , Private Sector, African Group
key_issues: Policies and governance structures to support youth-led sustainable digital innovations, leveraging emerging technologies to reduce environmental footprint, challenges and successes in implementing green technology solutions, and stakeholder collaboration for adoption and impact.
policy_recommendations: Support youth-led sustainable digital innovations with scalable policies, leverage AI, blockchain, and IoT for reducing environmental impact, address challenges in green tech implementation through stakeholder collaboration.
networking_goals: Fostering partnerships, collaboration, knowledge exchange among diverse stakeholders, connecting with like-minded individuals and potential collaborators committed to sustainable internet ecosystem.
agenda: Structured into three key segments: expert insights and case studies (20 minutes), breakout group discussions (20 minutes), and a Q&A and conclusion (20 minutes). Interactive discussions to foster networking opportunities.
collaboration_outcomes: Actionable strategies, case studies, and best practices for implementing sustainable digital practices; fostering connections with potential collaborators in sustainable tech innovation.

title: Work-Based Learning: Enhancing Sustainability & Education
organizers: Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: How can digital Work-Based Learning create innovative and accessible career paths that align with young people's interests, supporting the European Skills Agenda's goal of making vocational education more attractive to youth? How can we ensure the digital readiness of VET educators and training environments to build secure digital work environments through adequate skills training, as emphasized in the European Cybersecurity Strategy? How might partnerships and accessibility initiatives for digital WBL respond to the Digital Education Action Plan's priority of improving digital skills and competences across all European regions, including remote areas?
policy_recommendations: Accessibility strategies - learning how digital WBL can expand quality training regardless of geographic location, including solutions for remote areas. Public-Private Partnership models - insights into how partnerships can address "patchy" implementation of digital WBL and ensure equitable access across different regions. Sustainability knowledge - understanding how digital technologies can enhance environmental and economic sustainability by reducing physical resource requirements. Youth engagement approaches - understanding how digital WBL can support youth interests and align with the European Skills Agenda.
target_audience: VET policymakers and administrators, Digital Innovation Hub representatives, industry partners involved in work-based learning, Educational technology developers, vocational educators and trainers, researchers in digital education and work-based learning

collaboration_outcomes: Developing strategies for platform accountability, fostering partnerships between governments, civil society, and international bodies, and creating follow-up actions for implementing diversity and inclusion in platform regulations.

Best practices from governments, civil society, and grassroots initiatives working to create equitable AI policies. Actionable recommendations for strengthening AI governance in their own regions or organizations.

title: IGF 2025 WS #353 Road to COP30: debating digital technology & climate change
organizers: Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Government, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)

Considering multistakeholder experiences, how can IGFs inform and influence the UNFCCC COPs, bringing both communities closer together?
policy_recommendations: This session aims to bring together the community that works with digital technologies for development and the community that works with climate change and sustainability, shedding light on the nexus between both fields that are seldom in close dialogue. Participants and attendees are expected to gain better understanding on the relationship between technology, innovation and climate change, exploring the potential opportunities of using ICT for climate change monitoring, adaptation and mitigation, with a view to the environmental impacts of such technologies. In addition, in the context of COP 30, attendees are invited to reflect on how technology can support the call for action against climate change and provide inputs that will contribute to the discussions of said meeting. Last but not least, the session will also raise awareness within the IGF community, expanding opportunities of dialogue and engagement in such pressing discussion.

title: IGF 2025 WS #36 Algorithmic transparency, use and protection of data by gove
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)

This concern is compounded by the inherent opacity of algorithms, which require technical expertise to understand and monitor, as well as the need to justify their use, operation and results in law and on the basis of human rights standards. Automated systems have been recognized for reproducing structural biases and inequalities that disproportionately affect historically vulnerable groups.
policy_recommendations: It is therefore imperative to know how these systems operate and what their role is in governmental decision-making.

How can multistakeholder collaborations—including governments, civil society, and technology providers—foster research, knowledge-sharing, and policy innovation to build digital resilience and trust in AI-driven election processes?

title: IGF 2025 WS #362 Incorporating human rights in AI Risk Management

title: IGF 2025 WS #364 Civil Society in AI Policymaking: Global South Perspective

What strategies can enhance meaningful public consultation in AI governance to ensure transparency, inclusivity, and protection of human rights? C. How can civil society overcome structural barriers to effectively participate in AI policymaking and advocate for rights-based governance?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain a comprehensive understanding of AI governance in the Global South, focusing on the challenges and opportunities. Through expert discussions, they will explore structural barriers limiting civil society's role in AI policymaking and discover strategies to overcome these challenges. The session will examine best practices for inclusive, transparent, and rights-based AI policies, emphasizing meaningful public consultation. By analyzing regional AI governance frameworks and international standards like the Report of the UN Multi-Stakeholder High-Level Advisory Body on Artificial Intelligence, UN’s Seizing the Opportunities of Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy AI and UNESCO’s AI Governance Readiness Assessment, participants will gain a comparative perspective on policy approaches. Additionally, attendees will uncover actionable steps to strengthen civil society’s involvement in AI policymaking, building advocacy networks, and fostering cross-regional collaboration. The session will empower participants to engage effectively in AI governance, advocate for ethical policies, and promote human, rights and accountability in AI systems.

key_issues: Existing policy gaps in platform content governance, strategies for addressing these gaps by stakeholders, preventing misuse of regulatory frameworks to restrict freedoms in polarized contexts
policy_recommendations: Collaborative discussion among stakeholders, development of shared understanding for collective solutions, exploration of South-South cooperation opportunities, introduction of toolboxes and approaches from Global South cases

title: IGF 2025 WS #367 Global South Leadership & Innovation Against Disinformation
organizers: Civil Society, Intergovernmental Organization, Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, African Group, Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group

How can international collaborations address the infrastructural and linguistic challenges faced by the Global South in combating mis/disinformation?

Diverse perspectives on how cultural, linguistic, and infrastructural challenges are shaping solutions to mis/disinformation. 3. Practical insights into integrating Global South experiences into global digital governance frameworks. 4. Tools and best practices for fostering community resilience against mis/disinformation.

title: Decoding AI Indexes: Bridging Divides & Ensuring Inclusive AI

Comparison of global AI indexes and national standings
Methodology and indicators used in AI indexes
Gaps in AI development between Global North and South

title: Empowering Young Voices for Africa’s Path to Digital Inclusi
organizers: Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: How African governments and international stakeholders frame policies that enable universal access to digital infrastructure and minimize affordability challenges for young people? What steps should be taken towards increasing youth participation in Internet governance and digital rights policymaking across Africa? What are some of the strategies for scaling up digital literacy programs so that they can provide young Africans with skills required to participate in the digital space, combat disinformation, and innovate?
policy_recommendations: Addressing the infrastructure, affordability, and policy gaps that stand in the way to Internet inclusivity. Digital Literacy for All – Enabling young people to navigate the digital realm and deal with online disinformation. Youth-Led Internet Governance – Empowering young leaders to actively participate in policy formulation and discussions. Tech Innovation for Social Impact – Highlighting the work of Afrian youth changemakers in the context of digital entrepreneurship. Building an Inclusive Digital Future – Promoting the protection of access, privacy, and other human rights in the digital era.

title: Cyber quest: What’s missing in securing the most critical?
organizers: Civil Society, Eastern European Group
speakers: Fei Su , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Maria Paz Canales , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Christopher Sampson , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
E Guang Eugene Tan , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Policy Question(s): How can the UN framework, cyber norms be implemented to prevent cyber threats against CI, minimize consequences, and reduce political escalation risks? In a globally connected digital landscape with a complex supply chain, what responsibilities do tech companies, CI operators, researchers, and civil society have in CI protection? How do these roles shift in times of blurred lines between peace and conflict, and how can the Geneva Manual support them? In a polarized world, can stakeholders secure CI without political capture, or are we heading toward fragmentation? How can we ensure true stakeholder inclusion in cybersecurity policymaking at all levels?
policy_recommendations: Participants will engage in a knowledge-exchange experience focused on critical infrastructure protection and the implementation of agreed cyber norms. Through an interactive cyber quest, attendees will have the opportunity to share their perspectives on the roles and responsibilities of various actors in securing critical infrastructure and responding to cyber incidents. They will discuss these issues from the perspectives of both government and non-government actors. The session will bring together leaders from diverse stakeholder groups to exchange views in a highly interactive simulation exercise, fostering collaboration and mutual learning.
target_audience: Participants in this session will engage in a knowledge-exchange experience focused on critical infrastructure protection and the implementation of agreed cyber norms.
stakeholders_involved: Leaders from diverse stakeholder groups, including government, civil society, tech companies, CI operators, researchers, and civil society.
impact_expectation: By participating in this dynamic exercise, attendees will gain a deeper understanding of the practical steps that each stakeholder group is required to undertake to protect critical infrastructure and how to strengthen collaboration.

title: Change Starts with You(th): A Pathway to Our Digital Future
organizers: Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group, Technical Community, African Group, Civil Society, Eastern European Group
key_issues: Integration of the 2100 Learning Agenda with National and Regional Initiatives (NRIs), policies supporting youth digital entrepreneurship, cross-regional youth-led collaborations, roles of governments, industry, and international organizations in fostering youth-led innovations.
policy_recommendations: Promote sustainable and responsible innovation in youth-driven digital ecosystems, support youth overcoming structural barriers to digital entrepreneurship, enhance digital trust and resilience through multistakeholder partnerships, create enabling environments for youth-led innovations contributing to sustainable development.

title: IGF 2025 WS #374 Open Government Data for Sustainable Development
organizers: Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Frameworks and supporting policies to enable governments opening up their data, policies to facilitate open and free use of OGD by stakeholders including cross-border utilisation, policies to reap benefits from OGD adoption and use for innovation, social good, and sustainable development
policy_recommendations: Participants will explore benefits and challenges of implementing OGD policies, gain knowledge of good practices, learn 'brilliant basics' to get it right, discuss potential risks and pitfalls, and contribute insights into developing a framework for implementing and supporting OGD for various problems

title: Opportunities and policies for AI democratization
organizers: Civil Society, Eastern European Group; Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)

Lea Gimpel , Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)

policy_recommendations: Participants will gain an understanding of public AI policies aimed at democratizing AI, how these policies combine measures related to computing power, data, and model development, and the governance mechanisms that help democratize AI. title: IGF 2025 WS #376 Elevating children’s voices in AI design

title: IGF 2025 WS #378 Un-fragmenting Collaboration for AI Development in Africa
organizers: Technical Community, African Group
key_issues: Stakeholders shaping AI development in Africa, existing models for collaboration, barriers to collaboration, strategies for enhancing trust and partnership.

This session will also create a space for sharing diverse perspectives on the digital economy, fostering intercultural dialogue and collaboration. These interactions will enhance understanding and teamwork within the digital space. title: Innovation, Digital Commons & Privacy: Navigating Trade-offs
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group

Pranesh Prakash , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group

policy_recommendations: The workshop will provide concrete examples of initiatives that have successfully navigated tensions between data protection, access to knowledge, and innovation, offering models that participants can adapt. policy_recommendations: Practical methodologies for designing inclusive interventions; diverse perspectives on balancing security concerns with freedom of expression; assessment frameworks adaptable to different regional contexts; insights into successful capacity-building approaches that improve digital literacy.

title: IGF 2025 WS #402 Heritage Site Interactivity
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
speakers: Allen Hyde , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Robert Adams , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Shadi Alathamneh , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Junshan Liu , Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Maria Jose VIÑALS , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: 1. How can virtual experiences of heritage sites be accessed through online platforms without compromising site safety and security or infringing upon sacred sites or intangible heritage? 2. How can reality captures showcased online and on-site community-based tourism fortify local expertise and build entrepreneurialism? 3. How can digital monitoring systems in heritage sites help mitigate risks related to climate change?
policy_recommendations: This workshop will explore applications and considerations for documentation and analysis techniques at other threatened World Heritage sites, especially those under mounting pressures from climate change and overtourism. This focus on protecting cultural heritage underscores the importance of safeguarding sites for sustainable development and integrated growth. The team will present methods for the promotion of cultural heritage that can contribute to economic growth and social cohesion.

Kilnam Chon , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group

stakeholders_involved: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), African Group, United States, China, Europe

title: Multistakeholder Solutions for Building Digital Trust
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Challenges to strengthening multistakeholder engagement in the Global Majority, ensuring balanced and meaningful participation from various stakeholder groups under authoritarian contexts, possibilities offered by international human rights frameworks for rights-centric and truly multistakeholder approaches to technology governance in the Global Majority, and how international multistakeholder standards can strengthen the participation of the Global Majority in key internet governance processes.
policy_recommendations: Exploring adaptations of multistake, international multistakeholder standards such as the NETmundial principles for Global Majority contexts and discussing ways to strengthen Global Majority participation across regional and global internet governance processes.

title: American Denial: Digital Exclusion for Vulnerable Groups
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: Structural and policy barriers preventing marginalized communities from accessing digital government services, the impact of unstable housing and unreliable connectivity on digital exclusion, redesigning digital government initiatives for accessibility and participation, roles of governments, private actors, and technical community in addressing digital exclusion.
policy_recommendations: Concrete recommendations for governments and private actors to enhance accessibility, participation, and data security; advocacy strategies to bridge gaps in digital inclusion; governance models prioritizing equity, digital rights, and inclusive infrastructure.

title: IGF 2025 WS #408 The weaponization of the Internet and the future of openness
organizers: Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: A. How can Internet blocking be prevented from becoming a tool for censorship or suppression of dissent, particularly in regimes with weak democratic safeguards? B. How can technical standards be leveraged to preserve user autonomy while addressing legitimate concerns around illegal content? C. Given divergent national laws, how can technical and legal cooperation reduce Internet fragmentation while respecting local contexts?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain a clear understanding of how Internet blocking and filtering work at a technical level, including the specific methods employed and their potential for unintended consequences. Furthermore, they will gain insight into the motivations behind blocking and filtering, encompassing the diverse range of actors involved and the legal and political contexts in which these actions occur. In addition to this, they will acquire a deep understanding of the human rights implications of Internet blocking, particularly its impact on freedom of expression, access to information, and the right to privacy. Moreover, the session will provide participants with the opportunity to engage in direct dialogue with experts and stakeholders from diverse backgrounds, fostering collaboration and identifying common ground. Finally, the session will explore and analyze the risks of blocking orders originating from a top-down perspective, assessing the potential for abuse and the need for safeguards.

title: Digital Inclusion of Indigenous Communities in APAC
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: 1. Do rural development programs incorporate digital development for indigenous communities? 2. How can local governments and civil society collaborate with international organizations to advance SDGs (1, 4, 8, 9, 10) by ensuring equitable internet access and meaningful connectivity for indigenous communities? 3. What does connectivity mean for for-profit ISPs in rural areas, and how can policies and partnerships address unfavorable cost-to-benefit ratios to serve marginalized and indigenous communities? 4. How can digital literacy and skills initiatives promote socio-economic growth while preserving cultural diversity and fostering online multilingualism in low-resource settings?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain insights into issues and challenges faced by indigenous communities, socio-economic effects of digital seclusion, how meaningful connectivity can drive sustainable development, the importance of digital access and literacy for cultural identity, and relevant cases of digital development efforts in APAC.

title: IGF 2025 WS #41 Unifying Digital Efforts: Strengthening Multistakeholder Par
organizers: Intergovernmental Organization, African Group; Intergovernmental Organization, African Group; Intergovernmental Organization, African Group; Technical Community, African Group; Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernment, Organization; Technical Community, African Group; Technical Community, African Group
key_issues: How can multistakeholder partnerships enhance digital cooperation to bridge connectivity gaps and promote inclusive digital growth? What role can youth play in shaping digital policies and fostering cross-border cooperation for a more inclusive digital ecosystem? What are the key challenges and opportunities in building sustainable digital partnerships between governments, private sector, and civil society?
policy_recommendations: Insights into successful digital cooperation models and best practices. Diverse perspectives from policymakers, industry leaders, and youth advocates. Actionable strategies for bridging digital divides and fostering collaboration. Youth-centered approaches to innovation, policy, and digital inclusion.
networking_goals: Networking opportunities to build global and regional partnerships
agenda: Roundtable format with a 60-minute duration fostering dynamic, inclusive dialogue among diverse stakeholders. Encourages equal participation, open interaction, allowing for a free flow of ideas, collaboration, and problem-solving.
collaboration_outcomes: Attendees will gain insights into scalable strategies for digital cooperation, leaving with actionable takeaways to build more inclusive and resilient digital ecosystems.

title: Digital Literacy for All: Equitable Access via No-Code Tools
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: How can internet governance frameworks better integrate digital literacy as a core component of equitable access? What role do multi-stakeholder partnerships play in designing inclusive tools and policies that empower non-technical users? How can we ensure that the development and deployment of digital technologies align with the principles of The Tech We Want—transparency, accessibility, and fairness?
policy_recommendations: Participants will leave the session with a clear understanding of how no-code tools like the Open Data Editor work, including a live demonstration of its features and how it can enhance digital literacy in non-technical communities. They will get access to a roadmap for building a community of practice around digital literacy, including templates for organizing local workshops and training sessions. Attendees will benefit from a governance checklist for inclusive technology, outlining key principles such as accessibility, transparency, and sustainability, which participants can apply to their own projects or policies. They will learn about case studies and success stories from the Open Knowledge Foundation’s The Tech We Want initiative, showcasing how inclusive tools and governance frameworks have been successfully implemented in diverse contexts.

title: Truth Under Siege: Tools to Counter Digital Censorship
organizers: Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group

policy_recommendations: Establish legal protections for journalists and sources, support public funding for secure communication tools, incorporate digital literacy education into national policies

title: Global Action for Local AI Innovation: The Role of Open-Sour
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: How can open-source AI projects democratise AI innovation and ensure equitable access to AI-driven solutions in developing countries? What are the key trade-offs for policymakers, developers, and civil society when developing or using open-source AI for sustainable development? What policies and regulatory frameworks are needed to address emergent challenges?
policy_recommendations: What capacities, resources, and institutions are required in order to support and scale emergent best practices to ensure that open-source AI development supports individual and community rights? What will participants gain from attending this session? Participants will gain a more nuanced understanding of the trade-offs inherent in open-source AI development and use for advancing the SDGs in the Global South. It will also help participants understand how global actions and frameworks shape possibilities for local innovation. Participants will get concrete examples of best practices to address emerging challenges around open-source AI. This will help them identify actionable insights and advocate open AI practices within their contexts. This includes strategies for effective data governance, open-source adoption and maintenance, support for community innovation and participation and policy recommendations to guide governments and organisations in creating inclusive and sustainable technological ecosystems. Participants will also hear a variety of viewpoints from experts in academia, industry, and civil society, as well as from different geographies. This will help understand how various stakeholders approach the balance between open and closed AI and how this debate differs across local contexts.

title: Enabling collective redress online for communities at risk
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: How can access to collective redress be operationalized by the communities at risk inside and outside the EU? What are the main obstacles to accessing effective remedies for at-risk communities against platforms' unjustified restrictions? What are the eligibility requirements for CSOs to defend the collective interest of communities at risk? How has enforcing Articles 20 and 86 of the DSA worked so far, and what needs strengthening? Can this new mechanism under the DSA also empower communities at risk outside the EU? How can public regulators, such as Coimisiún na Meán in Ireland, help at-risk communities ensure online safety?
policy_recommendations: The participants will gain a mutual understanding of persistent issues that HRDs face when being silenced or discriminated against by online platforms, for instance, by content policies and their arbitrary enforcement, either by automated content moderation or content recommender systems. By raising these issues, the moderated dialogue will raise awareness among HRDs living in exile, who may defend themselves against this arbitrariness with the support of specialized civil society organizations representing their interest. Second, the community of invited stakeholders will discuss and agree on the main points for the future joint strategy on leveraging new DSA measures for collective redress in the EU. Even if the DSA applies only in the EU jurisdiction, such measures' outcomes may positively shape global redress mechanisms. Finally, the workshop will facilitate joint conversations with relevant stakeholders, including the EU External Service, the European Commission, the Appeals Centre Europe, and national Digital Service Coordinators.

title: Patients with Tech will replace clinicians

policy_recommendations: Policy implications of digital health innovations, challenges in cross-border data flows for law enforcement access to digital evidence, and the role of data and AI in addressing sustainability issues such as climate change, biodiversity, conservation, and water scarcity.

policy_recommendations: Participants will gain practical insights, research-based knowledge, and collaborative opportunities to enhance their efforts in countering misinformation. Through discussions with experts from civil society, government, and the private sector, they will explore the effectiveness, challenges, and scalability of different interventions, including media literacy programs, fact-checking initiatives, and digital tools for misinformation detection. Can banning kids from social media until they reach a certain age be a possible solution or does this bring about other risks for children that may rely on the Internet given their circumstances? Understanding the digital rights of children is critical. We intend to dissect approaches for delivery of interventions and examine the need for customized content for the intended stakeholders. Finally, we shall examine the issue of funding comprehensive safety programmes at a national/regional level and again examine how responsibilities may be linke

How can data governance practices enhance content integrity, media resilience, and inclusive information ecosystems?
policy_recommendations: Participants will learn about how different jurisdictions govern data in AI systems and the implications for sustainable innovation in which the benefits accrue to a wide array of stakeholders. They will gain a deeper understanding of data governance strategies that promote quality and inclusive information ecosystems. It will present research on AI and copyright and AI governance frameworks from Brazil, Europe, Japan, Indonesia, South, Africa, the UK and the US on practical frameworks that prevent power consolidation, as well as examples of inclusive data governance initiatives that support innovative and sustainable AI. Attendees will also acquire actionable ideas for building AI systems that reflect diverse voices, ensuring public interest outcomes in the digital landscape.

How can policymakers, technologists, and advocates collaborate to ensure AI governance is intersectional, balancing innovation with ethical, gender-responsive, and sustainable approaches?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain a critical understanding of how AI governance can integrate principles of sustainability and gender justice, ensuring policies proactively address environmental and social risks. They will leave with: Insight into AI’s environmental and gendered impacts, including how existing governance frameworks may reinforce biases and inequalities. Diverse perspectives from policymakers, AI ethicists, and activists on regulatory gaps and best practices for intersectional AI governance. Actionable strategies to advocate for policies that embed sustainability and gender equity in AI decision-making. A deeper awareness of the long-term consequences of AI governance, helping them critically assess emerging policies to prevent future harms. This session will equip attendees with the knowledge and tools to push for AI policies that do not just mitigate risks, but actively build a more just and sustainable future.

title: IGF 2025 WS #43 Lessons in Bridging the Digital Divide in Times of Crisis
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, African Group

What role can multistakeholder advocacy—civil society, private sector, and policymakers—play in promoting the recognition under international law that deliberately disrupting or preventing people's access to the internet violates human rights?
policy_recommendations: Policy recommendations on regional and global level to strengthen protections for digital access in conflict zones.
networking_goals: Networking opportunities with cross-sector experts and organizations working on similar contexts in geographically distant locations.
agenda: A 90-minute session provides the necessary time for in-depth discussion and interactive engagement, including regional case studies, advocacy lessons, and technical solutions. The additional time ensures that online and onsite participants have space to contribute meaningfully. This duration will allow real-time interaction between remote and in-person attendees without compromising depth or inclusivity.
collaboration_outcomes: Technical knowledge of solutions used in recent crisis settings to reconnect people. Common advocacy strategies to hold stakeholders accountable for restoring telecom access.

policy_recommendations: The session will create a space for exchange between experts and the audience, allowing participants to gain practical knowledge applicable to their daily lives. Strategies for a more balanced use of digital technologies will be discussed, along with recommendations to reduce both individual and collective risks, fostering healthier digital habits.

They will acquire participation skills and learn how to effectively engage in high-level climate discussions, such as COP processes, and amplify marginalized voices in these spaces. By attending, participants will help build concrete steps and recommendations for advancing open climate governance, including how to leverage open data and open knowledge initiatives.

policy_recommendations: Presentation of the Co-governance Guide, discussion on mutually agreed solutions for managing AI technology in workplaces, and exploration of initiatives to enhance AI literacy and ensure responsible development and use of AI systems.

title: Hacking the Future: Rebuilding the Open Internet
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: The session will explore the tension between the original vision of a free and open internet and the current reality marked by the consolidation of power in the hands of 'Big Tech.' It will analyze how the evolution of the internet from a space of citizen empowerment to a geopolitical battleground poses significant challenges to democracy. The discussion will cover the influence of Big Tech in shaping society, from mass surveillance to manipulation of public opinion, algorithmic amplification of content, and commercialization of attention. It will also address the erosion of the free and open internet, once a bastion of free speech and access to information, and the strategies employed by Big Tech companies to create 'walled gardens' that limit competition.
policy_recommendations: The session seeks to encourage participants to critically reflect on the role of large technology companies in society and politics, their challenges to democracy, and the idea of an open and free Internet. Ideas will be offered to strengthen the democratic governance of the Internet and promote open innovation. The session will inspire participants to engage in community action and policy advocacy and even develop new ideas that contribute to reconstructing the concept of a free and open Internet from their areas of action.
