key_issues: What is disinformation and why is it a problem? How strong and clear a baseline do existing international instruments provide for the governance of disinformation? Concerning new governance initiatives, what sort of consultation and decision-making process is best suited to the governance of disinformation, and can the IGF assume a role in the process?
policy_recommendations: The workshop will provide an overview of the controversy surrounding disinformation. The workshop intends to clarify the state of knowledge about disinformation and its effects. The workshop will discuss current regulatory approaches including their impact. It will provide an overview of the different models of cooperative governance that are currently being devised. Some of these are stakeholder-led efforts, such as the Facebook Oversight Board, the Christ Church Call, the DISARM Framework, and the various proposals for new international press councils. Others are intergovernmental ‘minilateral’ or regional initiatives, such as the implementation work of the European Union’s Digital Services Act including the former Code of Practice on Disinformation. Others are intergovernmental initiatives such as UNESCO’s Guidelines for Regulating Digital Platforms. The participants will get a sense of the complexity and culture-dependency of disinformation but also a better understanding of the significant challenges of building international consensus and designing effective institutions.

title: IGF 2023 WS #21 Internet's Environmental Footprint: towards sustainability
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, African Group, Civil Society, African Group
speakers: Yawri Carr , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Lily Edinam Botsyoe , Technical Community, African Group
Innocent Adriko , Civil Society, African Group
Ihita Gangavarapu , Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group
Monojit Das , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
Gabriel Karsan , Civil Society, African Group
Annett Onchana , Civil Society, African Group
themes: Digital Technologies to Achieve Sustainable Development Goals
key_issues: The implications of the growing energy consumption of the internet for greenhouse gas emissions, climate change, and global energy demand; potential long-term ecological and social consequences of the environmental impacts associated with the internet; and how to minimize the environmental impact of submarine cable installation and internet satellite deployment.
policy_recommendations: Enhance participants' knowledge of the environmental impact of the internet and related digital technologies; educate about strategies to mitigate this impact; explore techniques for making the internet more sustainable; promote clean energy and climate action via internet use; emphasize equitable access to the benefits of the internet for environmental sustainability and climate change.

title: Digital Divide and Inclusion: Metaverse for All
organizers: Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
themes: Skills Building for Basic and Advanced Technologies (Meaningful Access)
key_issues: A. How can the metaverse regulate and secure inclusiveness and accessibility? B. How to raise awareness of a metaverse “born accessible”. C. How to engage a diverse civil society and industry towards a joint collaboration for a Metaverse for All.
policy_recommendations: Participants will learn about existing activities that are being carried out in ITU Focus Group on metaverse in general, and accessibility and digital inclusion in particular. Participants will be engaged in issues related to human rights, people with disabilities, social digital inclusion, gender and diversity. Participants will learn about existing UN mandates underlying the need to create a metaverse for all inhabitants, where basic communication issues are considered in the design phase, looking at Design for All as the inspiring methodology.

title: IGF 2023 WS #211 African Women inclusion in Global Cybersecurity Discourses
organizers: Civil Society, African Group, Intergovernmental Organization, African Group
speakers: Margaret Nyambura Ndung'u , Civil Society, African Group
Towela Nyirenda-Jere , Intergovernmental Organization, African Group
Aicha Jeridi , Civil Society, African Group
Shifa Sorene Assefa , Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernment, Organization
Balbine MANGA , Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: Why are women not engaging adequately in Cybersecurity discourses? What can we learn from those who are actively engaging? What training and development opportunities are available to women working in cybersecurity? How can we better support and mentor women on safety, risk and vulnerabilities in the Cyberspace? How can we promote networking and mentoring programs to support women entering or advancing in the cybersecurity field? What form should this mentorship take? How can we ensure equity for women in or aspiring to be in cybersecurity and ensure their inclusion in policy discussions and decisions related to cybersecurity?
policy_recommendations: Equip participants with practical insights, actionable recommendations and expand their network in the cybersecurity field. Promote diversity and inclusion in cybersecurity through: 1. Sharing of knowledge and experiences and suggestions of how to include more women to actively and productively engage safely in the digital space 2. Discussions on how to protect children online with emphasis on multistakeholder approaches. 3. An understanding of what women stand to gain through actively participating in the national, regional and global cybersecurity discussions 4. Learning what organisations such as the Network of African Women in Cybersecurity (NAWC) are doing and the benefits of joining/supporting such initiatives
networking_goals: Promote diversity and inclusion in cybersecurity through knowledge sharing, networking and mentoring programs to support women entering or advancing in the cybersecurity field
agenda: Explore, learn and engage with other women and experts in cybersecurity. Discussions on how to protect children online with emphasis on multistakeholder approaches. Understanding what women stand to gain through actively participating in cybersecurity discussions. Learning about initiatives such as the Network of African Women in Cybersecurity (NAWC) and the benefits of joining/supporting such initiatives
collaboration_outcomes: Participants will gain practical insights, actionable recommendations and expand their network in the cybersecurity field. Promote diversity and inclusion in cybersecurity through knowledge sharing, networking and mentoring programs to support women entering or advancing in the cybersecurity field

title: IGF 2023 WS #212 Marginalized perspectives on the impact of tech on education
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC); Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC); Private Sector, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC); Civil Society, African Group; Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group; Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
speakers: Kseniia Gnitko , Technical Community, Eastern European Group
Theorose Elikplim Dzineku , Civil Society, African Group
Ihita Gangavarapu , Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group
de Araújo Santos Najla Helen Graff , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Bobi Adam , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Legal interventions for equitable access to technology in education, strategies for diversity and inclusion in digital content, and policy frameworks for educator training in technology integration.
policy_recommendations: Output of the session will be shared with governments, international and non-governmental organizations; report summarizing discussions, case analyses, and recommendations will be available for researchers, policymakers, and practitioners.
networking_goals: Enhance collaboration and networking among stakeholders, including policymakers, educators, researchers, and community representatives; stimulate engagement of youth leaders; promote collective action toward more inclusive and equitable use of technology in education.
agenda: Discussion on marginalized perspectives on technology's impact in education, exploration of positive advances and challenges, case analyses, and recommendations; invitation for participants to review work and discuss proposals.
collaboration_outcomes: Output shared with governments and organizations; report available for reference; potential for collective action and enhanced collaboration among stakeholders.

title: IGF 2023 WS #214 Marginalized countries: Technology for or versus Democracy?
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Technical Community, African Group, Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization, Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: How technology impacts democracies, especially in marginalized countries; Platforms, especially AIs, are being used as instruments of control in favor or against democracy; How can online hate speech impact the democracy process?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain understanding of the work done by youth-led initiatives, and access to a report that summarizes the discussions, case analyses, and recommendations presented during the session; which will serve as a reference for researchers, policy makers, and practitioners involved in the field of Technology and Democracy. It is expected to stimulate the engagement of youth leaders, policymakers and platforms. At the  end we will invite participants to review our work and discuss our proposals, while the output of this session will be shared with governments, international and non-governmental organizations.

title: IGF 2023 WS #216 Cybercrime, Regulation and Accountability: Cases & Crisis
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Private Sector, Asia-Pacific Group, Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, African Group, Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Private Sector, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: The session will address how platforms can be effectively regulated and held accountable in cases of cybercrime to ensure online user safety, identify gaps in societal measures, emerging legislation, and current regulatory frameworks regarding platforms' role in combating cybercrime, and explore innovative approaches to improve platform regulation and accountability in the face of emerging cybercrime challenges.
policy_recommendations: The session aims to raise awareness about the importance of platform regulation and accountability in cybercrime cases, highlight challenges and best practices, make concrete recommendations to improve policies and regulations related to cybercrime with emphasis on platform accountability, explore innovative solutions, and stimulate engagement of youth leaders, policymakers, and platforms to result in concrete actions to strengthen regulation and accountability. The output will be shared with governments, international and non-governmental organizations.

title: IGF 2023 WS #217 Large Language Models on the Web: Anticipating the challenge
organizers: Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
speakers: Santana Vagner , Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Yuki Arase , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
Rafael Evangelista, Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Emily Bender , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Dominique Hazaël-Massieux , Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: The workshop will introduce a technical and governance debate about LLM focusing on the Web. Although there are other spaces for discussion on AI governance, this session focuses on raising concerns about the complexity of ethics and governance when incorporating LLMs into the Web ecosystem. Through an interdisciplinary and diverse approach (speakers are from different backgrounds, stakeholder groups, regions, and include a person with a disability), the panel will provide the necessary technical knowledge of how LLMs have the potential to change the Web and some possible governance consequences, such as: the challenge of privacy and consent in data collection, fundamental changes in how users search for information, potential impacts to the digital and physical economy and how to manage content production using AI. The workshop will stimulate the audience to critically think about and question LLMs' emerging governance concerns, especially in the Web context.
stakeholders_involved: Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group

title: IGF 2023 WS #218 Nip it in the bud
organizers: Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: What kinds of citizen enlightenment campaigns have been conducted to raise awareness on cybersecurity? What laws and policies exist to not just punish, but prevent cybercrime? What approaches have worked in different countries and how can they be replicated where it is needed?
policy_recommendations: Expected Outcomes This is a conversation that we hope to discuss at the regional level (WAYIGF & AfIGF), as a key outcome will be to get more people interested in being cybersecurity professionals, instead of cybercriminals. We expect to improve the collaboration between the western countries to see what initiatives, policies, and programs have succeeded in fighting cybercrime early on.

title: IGF 2023 WS #220 Cybersecurity of Civilian Nuclear Infrastructure
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group; Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: A. What are the risks and potential consequences of cyber operations targeting civilian nuclear infrastructure? B. To what extent do existing international law and non-binding norms protect civilian nuclear systems and how can such legal and normative protections be strengthened? C. What policies and cybersecurity best practices, including multistakeholder efforts, are needed to implement legal and normative protections of civilian nuclear technologies online?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain an understanding of the risks and potential consequences of cyber operations targeting civilian nuclear infrastructure, as well as the legal and practical challenges of protecting relevant systems. In particular, they will be exposed to concrete examples of such operations – from malware and ‘denial of service’ attacks to information operations – and their actual impact on individuals and other actors. Participants will also learn about the extent to which existing international legal and norm, the importance of upholding applicable protections, and ways in which they can be strengthened, including through multistakeholder coalitions. An interactive discussion of policy measures and cybersecurity best practices to implement existing rules and norms will allow participants to express their views and influence those policies and practices moving forward.

title: IGF 2023 WS #221 The Amazon Rainforest: greentech answer to the global chaos
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Government, Asia-Pacific Group, Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, African Group, Technical Community, African Group
themes: Digital Technologies to Achieve Sustainable Development Goals
Existing and New Technologies as Climate Solutions
key_issues: How can the internet collaborate to develop Amazon and help to empower the South American population? Why do we have to be cautious with Amazon maintenance? Will people around the globe be benefited by the development of amazon region or is it just market and media speculation? What will participants gain from attending this session? It’ll understand the real importance of the Amazon Rainforest for the world, not just being stuck in international information produced, sometimes founded on a political or ideological side. It’ll obtain specific information to assess the global action against South America and it’ll be able to think and develop new ideas to evaluate and maybe change actions of government participant’s country objecting to help the development of South America for the correct use of Amazon. Furthermore, it’ll be able to understand the importance of technology and the internet in this changing scenery, the great transformation in quality of life worldwide and the empowerment of people from undeveloped countries. At the final, the participants will understand that it is impossible to talk about the future without thinking about South America and the Amazon Rainforest.

title: IGF 2023 WS #222 DataDAO: Pioneering Fairness in Data Economies
organizers: Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group, Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, African Group, Technical Community, Eastern European Group
speakers: Andrew Peek , Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Charles Mok , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
Paola Galvez , Government, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: How can Data DAOs be integrated into existing legal and regulatory frameworks to foster a more equitable and democratic Internet ecosystem? What responsibilities should organizations have in ensuring data subjects' rights, including access, portability, and erasure, are respected and upheld? What collaborations between different stakeholders are necessary to achieve a fair data economy, and how can policymakers facilitate these partnerships? How can public awareness around data rights and privacy be improved to empower individuals in the digital age? What ethical considerations should be taken into account when designing and implementing Data DAOs to ensure inclusivity and fairness?
policy_recommendations: Through open and engaging discussions, participants are expected to deepen their understanding on how data is used today and how the values of their own data can be exploited by data-driven enterprises. With real-world examples discussed in the workshop, they will have the knowledge to re-evaluate their engagement in the data economy and be able to make better choices when engaging with data-driven enterprises. By the end of the session, attendees will have learned about the concept of the DataDAO model and the challenges and opportunities in integrating a DataDAO in existing legal and regulatory frameworks. They will have also gained valuable insights into the transformative potential of the DataDAO model on data governance and how it can promote fairness in the data economy.

title: IGF 2023 WS #223 Engaging commerce, innovation and children's privacy online
organizers: Private Sector, Asia-Pacific Group; Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Online privacy risks and related dangers faced by children in the Global South, measures or best practices to limit or prevent these risks, challenges in implementation of measures, balancing children’s online privacy with innovation and private sector's economic interests
policy_recommendations: Apply the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child online with equal force and urgency, develop and enforce measures to protect children from online privacy risks, ensure measures are developed for and enforced in developing countries

title: IGF 2023 WS #224 Opportunities of Cross-Border Data Flow-DFFT for Development
organizers: Government, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Private Sector, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
speakers: Hon. Neema Lugangira , Government, African Group
Jean-Jacques Sahel , Private Sector, Asia-Pacific Group
Jean Philbert Nsengimana , Private Sector, African Group
Kathleen McGowan , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Tojima Hitoshi (Mr.), Chief Digital Officer, Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA)
Gordon Kalema (Mr.) , Director General, Ministry of ICT and Innovations, Rwanda (in lieu of Hon. Lugangira, Neema )
key_issues: How can we ensure free flow of trusted data without compromising privacy and national security? What would be the governance frameworks necessary for that? How could different stakeholders involve in the development of best practices to enable free flow of trusted data? 2. How could development partners, private sectors, and civil societies/academia support developing countries to create conducive mechanisms to take advantage of cross-border data flow? 3. Should the concept and mechanism of free flow of trusted data beyond national boundary be incorporate into the discussion of DPI? If so, how best could the multi-stakeholder communities support that?
policy_recommendations: Participants of the workshop will gain insights into current global debates over challenges and opportunities, as well as operationalizing free flow of secured data beyond national border from subject matter experts and practioners from Asia-Pacific, Africa, and Global regions. The workshop participants will also have an opportunity to join and provide inputs into the discussions about how could government, private sectors, civil societies, and development partners could support developing countries to maximize the opportunities brought about by the free flow of secured data beyond national border. Moreover, the participants could also receive expert perspectives of whether the concept of the DFFT should or could be incorporated into the current global discussion of expanding Digital Public Goods and Digital Public Infrastructure, and if so how the different stakeholders could support the initiative.

title: Risks and opportunities of a new UN cybercrime treaty
organizers: Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
speakers: Briony Daley Whitworth , Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Claudio Peguero , Government, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Ian Tennant , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Timea Suto , Private Sector, Eastern European Group
Michael Gilles, Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Discussion on key risks and opportunities of the new UN cybercrime convention, state-of-play, how non-governmental stakeholders can maximise impact, and how stakeholders can better co-operate to showcase real-life examples, good practices, and lessons learned.
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain an appreciation of the opportunities and risks inherent in the new UN cybercrime convention and be equipped to better advocate for their views to influence the public and diplomatic debate on the new cybercrime instrument.
stakeholders_involved: UN member states, Ad Hoc Committee (AHC), Government, Civil Society, Private Sector
impact_expectation: A new UN cybercrime convention could build upon and expand existing instruments, enabling greater cooperation in combatting cybercrime, and provide an alternative path for countries not yet signed up to existing instruments.

title: IGF 2023 WS #228 Researcher access to platform data in the majority world
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, African Group, Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
speakers: Tom Barraclough , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Francisco Brito Cruz , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Alison Gillwald , Civil Society, African Group
Nicolo Zingales , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Aishwarya Giridhar , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
Jhalak Mrignayani Kakkar , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
themes: Big Data Architecture, Usage and Governance
key_issues: 1) What mechanisms exist now or might be developed to enable access to data for researchers based in the majority world? What challenges do researchers in the majority world currently face? (Ie types of data, format, infrastructure, and mechanisms) 2) What is the appropriate role of the government in managing researcher access and use of data? 3) Are there any legal frameworks under development for facilitating researcher access in the global majority world, and how should regulators in the minority world foster input of majority world participants in the way these are designed (especially in transnational contexts)?
policy_recommendations: The ACT is supporting majority world researchers to continue their existing work on researcher access mechanisms. This session will share the results of that research. It will also provide an overview of the Action Coalition on Meaningful Transparency, discussing emerging regulatory developments around researcher access to data, and researcher access to data in the majority world.

title: IGF 2023 WS #229 Balancing Child Online Protection and Internet Integrity
organizers: Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group, Technical Community, Eastern European Group, Technical Community, African Group, Intergovernmental Organization, African Group, Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
speakers: Aysha Labiba Labiba , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
Hon. Neema Lugangira , Government, African Group
Fanny Rotino , Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization
Saba Tiku Beyene , Intergovernmental Organization, African Group
key_issues: How may child protection measures lead to fragmentation of end-user experience worldwide? How should these policies be designed to avoid splitting the Internet? Can child protection measures strengthen the Internet, making it safer and empowering children?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain a comprehensive understanding of the policy measures that can be implemented to protect children online while maintaining an open and resilient Internet. They will learn about the different approaches that can be taken to balance the need for online safety, including regulatory frameworks, privacy laws, and content moderation policies. The participants can learn about the latest technical and innovative solutions that can enhance child online protection. They will gain insights into the educational measures that can be taken to raise awareness among children and parents about risks and best practices for online safety. They will learn more about the role of digital and media literacy in promoting online safety and the importance of parental supervision and guidance. Finally, preserving the globally connected Internet will be stressed as a criterion to be included in the policy-making process for child online protection around the world.

title: IGF 2023 WS #231 Realizing the right to social security in a digital world
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
speakers: Kiira Brian , Civil Society, African Group
Bonareri Onyancha Damaris , Civil Society, African Group
Curcic Danilo , Civil Society, Eastern European Group
de Brigard Juan , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Richmond Bishop Imogen , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
themes: Digital Technologies and Rights to Health
key_issues: How does digitization and the introduction of automation impact on the right social security, equality and data protection? How have courts and quasi-judicial bodies tackled human rights issues arising from the introduction of digital systems? What considerations do policy-makers need to take into account when introducing automated systems for the delivery of public services? How could they strike a better balance between increasing efficiency of public systems and meeting the needs of most marginalized groups and individuals?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain a better understanding of the challenges brought about by the introduction of automation and digitization across public sectors, with an emphasis on the impacts on welfare systems and the rights to social security and equality. They will also learn about strategies and tools that have been successful in ensuring that the introduction of these systems is in line with human rights obligations states have under international treaties and conventions. The roundtable will invite participants from other sectors, such as representatives of states and intergovernmental organizations, to dialogue with the speakers and share perspectives that can strengthen policy and practice around the digitalization of public services.

title: Small is Beautiful: A Digital Economy for People and Planet
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization
themes: Digital Technologies to Achieve Sustainable Development Goals
key_issues: How can we rethink AI models to move from universalist frames of big data-based digital intelligence to contextualized intelligence based on small data ? How does this affect the future of data governance and ideas of collective data sovereignty? How do we ensure that the materiality of data and AI infrastructures don’t stress planetary boundaries? Can we redesign the Internet for a just and climate-sensitive digital transition? How do we move from bottomless consumerism to ethical consumption and regenerative appropriation in the digitally-mediated marketplace? What would it mean to encode 'small is beautiful' ethics into e-commerce business models?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain exposure to critical perspectives highlighting the climate risks latent within the current organization and logic of the digital economy, in particular one that is attuned to the larger structural inequities and extractivist dynamics that the status quo also perpetuates. Moreover, participants will also hear significant proposals around policy ideas and guiding principles to orient a transition towards sustainable and just alternatives. They will have the opportunity to fruitfully contribute to the discussion on working towards a transformed digital future, and we hope the event will serve as a site for the catalysation of new partnerships, alliances and strategic initiatives that move in this direction.

title: IGF 2023 WS #233 AI as a tool and weapon in cybersecurity
organizers: Private Sector, Asia-Pacific Group, Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
regional_focus: Asia-Pacific Group, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
themes: New Technologies and Risks to Online Security
key_issues: How can the multistakeholder community effectively assess the multifaceted risks and opportunities posed by the rapid proliferation of AI for cybersecurity purposes, while considering the broader geopolitical and international contexts? Considering the next wave of emerging technologies – metaverse, ubiquity of IoT devices, quantum computing, etc. – what will be some of the biggest cybersecurity challenges and opportunities? How can lessons learned from the software security space – Software Bill of Materials (SBOM), etc., - provide insights for an AI framework that fosters a vibrant AI development ecosystem while ensuring AI systems are safe, effective, and fair?
policy_recommendations: Promote ethical and responsible development, deployment, and use of cybersecurity AI systems to foster trust and confidence in the technology and ensure that AI is used in ways that are consistent with democratic values and principles. Attendees will gain a better understanding of what is needed to effectively and ethically use these tools for improved cybersecurity. Attend, also better understand successful efforts in the software security space and how those apply to AI policy.

title: Overcoming the Global Digital Divide? The South-Based RIRs
organizers: Civil Society, African Group, Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
speakers: Carolina Aguerre , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Nii Narku Quaynor , Technical Community, African Group
Anriette Esterhuysen , Civil Society, African Group
Akinori MAEMURA , Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group
Debora Christine , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: The role of South-based regional multistakeholder Internet governance bodies in narrowing the global digital divide, empowering low-income countries and marginalized groups, promoting inclusive participation, and lessons from South-based RIRs' approach to Internet governance.
policy_recommendations: Generate new conversations through South-South multistakeholder exchanges about redressing digital divides with inclusion through AFRINIC, APNIC and LACNIC; generate novel evidence, insights, and lessons about combatting the digital divide in global Internet governance.
key_takeaways: The session will raise awareness about South-based RIRs, generate new conversations through South-South multistakeholder exchanges about redressing digital divides with inclusion, and generate novel evidence, insights, and lessons about combatting the digital divide in global Internet governance.

title: Leveraging AI to Support Gender Inclusivity
organizers: Private Sector, Asia-Pacific Group, Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
speakers: Christian von Essen , Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Jenna Manhau Fung , Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group
Neema Iyer , Private Sector, African Group
Luciana Benotti , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Lucia Russo , Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernment, Organization
key_issues: How will AI be trained to recognize and desexualize content, and what safeguards might be put in place to ensure that algorithms are not biased or discriminatory? What measures are needed to protect freedom of speech and prevent censorship? How will search engines ensure that the desexualization of content does not inadvertently perpetuate harmful gender stereotypes or reinforce existing power imbalances?
policy_recommendations: Participants can expect to learn about the latest advancements in the field of AI and machine learning, including how AI bias is being identified and mitigated, as presented by industry, academia, and international organization experts. They will also learn about mitigation measures for AI and machine learning techniques that will help prevent bias in search results. International norms and standards and academic research on inclusive AI will be discussed. We will discuss the importance of transparency in search algorithms and how the use of AI and machine learning can help to increase transparency and provide more reliable results.
target_audience: Participants can expect to learn about the latest advancements in the field of AI and machine learning, as presented by industry, academia, and international organization experts.
stakeholders_involved: Private Sector, Technical Community, Civil Society, Intergovernmental Organization
impact_expectation: To address AI biases, generative AI systems can be trained to identify and correct them. This can be achieved by diversifying the training data, incorporating ethical principles, continuously updating and refining the algorithm, and providing transparency.

title: Digital transformation and sovereignty towards autarchy
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: A. How is the state trying to establish political control over the Internet? B. How the state controls national critical information infrastructures? C. Where are we going: digital interdependence or fragmentation?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain knowledge and understanding of new means of Internet regulation in the non-democratic regimes leading towards digital autarchies and fragmentation of the Internet. The workshop will issue warning message against these irrelevant and inefficient regulation measures in order to prevent using negative regulatory practices on national level.

title: IGF 2023 WS #237 Online Linguistic Gender Stereotypes
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: How can such online linguistic gender stereotypes affect users' perceptions of their self-worth and value? Thus, what implications does this have on the current gender digital divide? How can these online linguistic gender stereotypes result in negative experiences for youths, both online and in the real world? How can end users, especially the youth, stop and challenge these linguistic gender stereotypes online from a bottom-up or grassroots approach? What measures can be taken to improve the youth’s awareness of online linguistic gender stereotypes and bridge the digital divide, especially among young girls?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain new knowledge on how linguistic gender stereotypes can affect their perceived self-worth; the impacts of these stereotypes could even affect their future of work and could further increase the gender digital divide. Next, participants will learn how to identify gender-stereotypical language and this can better efforts in cultivating an inclusive Internet. Additionally, they will learn best practices that they can utilize to create an inclusive Internet through the power of language. Upon completing the workshop, participants will also be able to compare their experiences with gender-stereotypical language online and contrast the similarities and differences present in different cultures; this will help build a more global perspective and identify common key areas that need to be addressed to build an inclusive Internet for all.

title: IGF 2023 WS #239 How to build trust in user-centric digital public services
organizers: Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: What makes digital public services trustworthy for users? What are challenges and concerns regarding the trustworthiness of services and what is the role of data governance? How can we create a new “framework for trust” in digital public services? What are principles for user-centric digital public services and mechanisms to ensure these principles are applied? How can users and civil society organisations be empowered and citizens' feedback taken into account? What are good practices of user-centric digital public services and what lessons can be learned?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain a better understanding of user-centric digital public services and what role data governance can play to enhance trust in these services. Participants will learn from the experiences and insights of experts and practitioners from different countries who have been involved in developing trustworthy digital public services. Participants can identify key challenges and opportunities of different approaches for implementing trustworthy and user-centric digital public services.

title: AI and the Future of Work: Bridging Global Digital Divides
organizers: Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: A. How can policymakers ensure that AI technologies advance gender equality in the digital economy? B. title: IGF 2023 WS #257 Content moderation challenges and opportunities in APAC
organizers: Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group; Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
speakers: Kyung Sin Park , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group

key_issues: The rise of harmful content online such as hate speech, mis/disinformation, violent and extremist content, has led an increasing number of governments in the Asia-Pacific region to take excessive measures by making intermediaries to be responsible for such content and even imposing harsh criminal liabilities, which create additional pressures on the ability to express and access opinions and content online. Such laws bestow undue power into the hands of the governments to over-regulate and, in some cases, censor certain contents when the definition of the illegality of contents can be loose and vague – which leaves a huge room for arbitrary decision and abuse. Laws that force a quick turnaround time for removals also create a significant problem when the governments try to become the arbiter of the truth and control the online conversations of people, because these rules create negative incentives for Internet companies to take down content upon government request without sufficient review of human rights and legal impact, for fear of heavy sanctions. Furthermore, the laws allowing access to identify of posting authors without warrant or otherwise free of any procedure
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain insights on what responsible content moderation and user data access would look like for the future of the Internet and how the civil society, big techs and governments can engage with each other to protect the Internet and its democratizing potential, drawing from the experience with the three jurisdictions presenting new challenges such as Indonesia, Korea, and Viet Nam mainly. With a focus on APAC, this will foster a deep understanding of the regulatory landscapes and challenge the participants and audience to think about content responsibility, free expression, and anonymity in 2023 and beyond - and how to work towards a more rights-friendly communication environment in the region.

Considering Internet fragmentation from a democratic perspective may assist the Internet community in tackling this increasingly unavoidable issue, as democratic states view the Internet as a potential threat to democracy. Retracing the history of the Internet and diverse examples of states that were the first to embark on the path of fragmentation, it will explore the links between non-democratic and democratic forms of government and digital sovereignty. The forms of acceptable and unacceptable Fragmentation in the world will be identified in light of the evolving nature of Internet Fragment, SDGs 10. Reduced Inequalities 10.2 10.3 10.6 16. Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions 16.10 16.3 16.7 16.a 16.b 17. Partnerships for the Goals 17.16 17.17 Description: Internet fragmentation is still in its early stages of political problematisation, despite being regularly discussed over the past 20 years among Internet enthusiasts. Meanwhile, states started playing a crucial role in shaping the Internet based on their strategic interests. Internet Fragmentation now emerges as a risk of what has been identified as the "return of the State" to Internet Governance, not only limited to authoritarian States. The perspective of defending national sovereignty and increasing control over Internet-related issues within their borders has also been a relevant discourse in states with consolidated democratic systems. This shift poses a question, to what extent such legislative actions and geographical blocks justified under the guise of defending democracy may actually lead to fragmentation with consequent harms or benefits to democratic principles? speakers: Rafael Zanatta , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Luciano Mazza de Andrade , Government, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Joy Wathagi Ndungu , Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: A. How Global South actors are participating in the consultations of the Global Digital Compact? B. What are their demands for the data protection and artificial intelligence agendas? C. What can be done by each sector to improve these discussions and effectively apply the agenda of the Global Digital Compact?
policy_recommendations: Publication of a policy brief presenting research on the participation of Global South actors in the Global Digital Compact, combined with proposals from workshop participants on possible steps in this global cooperation agenda. Clarification of the role of each actor to ensure common principles and objectives of the Global South are considered and worked within the UN agenda.

title: IGF 2023 WS #288 A Global Human Rights Approach to Responsible AI Governance
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
speakers: Marlena Wisniak , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Juan Carlos Lara, Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Tara Denham , Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Naimi Shahla , Private Sector, Intergovernmental Organization
Pratek Sibal , Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernment, Organization
Rumman Chowdhury , Civil Society, Intergovernmental Organization
Oluseyi Oyebisi , Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: How can the international human rights framework be leveraged to ensure responsible AI governance in a rapidly changing context? What are the global implications for human rights in the absence of effective frameworks and responsible AI governance? How can we foster meaningful engagement by all relevant stakeholders including civil society, private companies, technical experts and governments, particularly from the global south (majority world), to tackle responsible AI governance?
policy_recommendations: Timely snapshot of the most relevant ongoing regulatory processes linked with responsible AI governance, including perspectives on those processes from a diverse group of experts representing different stakeholder groups and geographies. Knowledge of the relevance of the international human rights framework and its significance for responsible AI governance. Deeper understanding of the relationship between national, regional and global efforts on responsible AI governance and how they may complement or conflict with each other. Insights into some of the ongoing efforts undertaken by companies in human rights due diligence of AI products.

title: Enhancing Youth Participation in Decision-making in IG
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
speakers: Veronica Piccolo , Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Anja Gengo , Intergovernmental Organization, Eastern European Group
Phyo Thiri Lwin , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
Marko Paloski , Technical Community, Eastern European Group
Rodrigo Alexandre , Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: Strategies to engage youth stakeholders from all countries, including developing and developed nations, to ensure their meaningful participation in internet governance discussions. Designing inclusive regional and global programs to address youth challenges and opportunities. Fostering cooperation among stakeholders for inclusive access and youth involvement in policy development.
policy_recommendations: Develop youth fellowships, social media dissemination, and networking strategies to engage young people in IGF discussions. Encourage youth involvement in leadership positions and the Multistake, Advisory Group (MAG).
networking_goals: Knowledge sharing, collaboration on youth engagement strategies, and building partnerships among stakeholders to support youth participation in internet governance.
agenda: Session will provide participants with practical approaches such as youth fellowships, social media dissemination, and networking to engage more young people in IGF discussions. Attendees will learn strategies to involve and encourage young individuals in leadership positions and the MAG. Through networking opportunities and inspiring discussions, participants will leave empowered and inspired to make a meaningful impact in internet governance discussions and decision-making processes.
collaboration_outcomes: Potential collaboration outcomes include developing joint strategies for youth engagement, creating shared resources for youth participation, and establishing follow-up mechanisms to ensure sustained involvement of youth in internet governance processes.

title: AI Advances Expand Potential for Gender Equity
organizers: Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization, Government, Asia-Pacific Group
themes: Skills Building for Basic and Advanced Technologies (Meaningful Access)
key_issues: How do policymakers ensure that AI is based on unbiased and fully intersectional data? How can policymakers support skill building for a digital labor force? What does skill building mean in a digital society? How do we determine what digital skills are required and what do these skills look like? What are some policies that will help to minimize bias within data?
policy_recommendations: Participants will better understand the vast implications of AI advances on the gender digital divide. As immersive technology continues to push toward the forefront of technological developments, it is increasingly important to understand its impact on already marginalized and often vulnerable groups. Technological advancements have the unique ability to close this gap by providing new opportunities but may also pose significant risks to progress in the form of data and algorithmic biases. Participants will have greater knowledge of this topic and will be informed about the next steps that governments, policymakers, and business may take to ensure that the digital transition results in positive change for women worldwide.

title: IGF 2023 WS #291 Inclusive Access for Women & Differently-Abled Youths
organizers: Technical Community, African Group; Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC); Private Sector, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
speakers: ENERST MAFUTA KATOKA , Private Sector, African Group
Thokozile Precious Miya , Intergovernmental Organization, African Group
Marta Musidłowska , Civil Society, Eastern European Group
Naijla Hellen , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: 1. What measures can be taken to ensure that women and differently-abled youths have equal access to digital infrastructure such as the Internet, computers, and smartphones? 2. Are there any policies in place to ensure that women and differently-abled youths have equal access to digital skills training and employment opportunities in the technology sector? 3. How can we ensure that digital literacy programs are inclusive and accessible to women and differently-abled youths, particularly those from low-income backgrounds?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain an understanding of the work done by youth-led initiatives, and access to a report that summarises the discussions, case analyses, and recommendations presented during the session; which will serve as a reference for researchers, policymakers, and practitioners involved in the field of Infrastructure alternative. Overall, it is expected to stimulate the engagement of youth leaders, policymakers, and platforms. In the end, we will invite participants to review our work and discuss our proposals, while the output of this session will be shared with governments, international and non-governmental organizations.

title: IGF 2023 WS #292 Revitalizing Universal Service Funds to Promote Inclusion
organizers: Civil Society, African Group, Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
speakers: Nathalia Foditsch , Private Sector, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Risper Arose , Civil Society, African Group
Soledad Luca de Tena , Technical Community, African Group
Teddy Woodhouse , Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Konstantinos Komaitis , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Ben Matranga , Private Sector, African Group
Anoop Nagendra , Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: How to transform and unlock universal service funds through a multistakeholder model? Should universal service funds support community networks and complementary access models? How can universal service funds be part of a blended finance and impact investment model for digital inclusion and connectivity?
policy_recommendations: The session will provide recommendations for revitalizing universal service funds. These recommendations will be summarized in a report that will inform a follow-up event, to take place in November in the form of a webinar.

title: IGF 2023 WS #293 Global Digital Compact in Africa: Challenges and Solutions
organizers: Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: How can affordable internet access be expanded to underserved areas of Africa? What measures are needed to harmonize digital infrastructure in Africa? How can data protection and privacy laws be developed and enforced in Africa? How can digital literacy be improved across Africa? How can critical digital infrastructure be protected in Africa? How can regulatory frameworks be developed for cross-border digital trade in Africa? How can digital technologies be leveraged to promote financial inclusion in Africa? How can digital rights and African freedom of expression be safeguarded?
policy_recommendations: 1. Elicited recommendations for improved GDC and Cooperation based on the submission of the speakers at the workshop 2. Increased cooperation and competition (competition) to sustain an effective and deliberate economic growth and development. 3. Strengthened cooperation among corporate bodies, learning institutions, research organizations, media organizations, governments, and nonprofits. 4. Elicited Solutions from experts discussing the Global Digital Compact and Cooperation within the African Community Context. 5. Improved the African community solutions via discussion bringing organic solutions which are pragmatic for African scenarios 6. Brought improved African context into Global Digital Compact through organic recommendations from African Speakers.

title: Addressing Machine Bias to Foster Sustainable Development
organizers: Technical Community, African Group, Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, African Group
themes: Digital Technologies to Achieve Sustainable Development Goals
key_issues: Ensuring transparency and accountability in algorithmic decision-making systems to address and mitigate machine bias; best practices for collecting, curating, and utilizing diverse and representative datasets; enhancing public awareness, understanding, and participation in algorithmic decision-making processes.
policy_recommendations: Implement policy frameworks or guidelines promoting fairness and equitable outcomes; adopt representative training data and algorithmic transparency; conduct rigorous evaluations, auditing, and ongoing monitoring of machine bias; foster collaboration among diverse stakeholders to share insights and best practices; produce a report capturing the workshop dialogue for accessibility.

title: Digital Inclusion Through a Multilingual Internet
organizers: Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group
speakers: Inne Anne-Rachel , Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization
Edmon Chung , Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Dawit Bekele , Technical Community, African Group
Alan Davidson , Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Akinori MAEMURA , Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group
Theresa Swinehart , Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Ram Mohan , Technical community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Barriers to using the Internet in one's own language, technical and policy coordination to overcome these barriers, and how Internet multilingualism supports digital inclusion goals.
policy_recommendations: Promote languages not yet realized on the Internet, work towards the International Decade of Indigenous Languages 2022 – 2032, and explore collaboration opportunities for multilingualism and digital inclusion.

title: IGF 2023 WS #299 Community-driven Responsible AI: A New Social Contract
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization, Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Intergovernment, Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: A. How should countries, communities, cities and companies collaborate to guide the beneficial development of AI and ensure that no one is left behind? B. What are the strengths of community-led AI governance, and what might its limits be? C. What multistakeholder, deliberative or open-source technologies and practices could be applied to AI governance by countries, communities, cities and companies?
policy_recommendations: Chatham House, OSGEY and Google will tap into the IGF’s diverse audience to overcome Western-centric biases and limitations, which tend to dominate the space at the expense of under-represented communities. The session development will also be informed by Chatham House’s AI Taskforce, bringing together voices from six continents and reflecting their local constituencies in their approach. The moderator will also seek to challenge the participants’ assumptions and biases to capture the widest range of perspectives and unearth under-explored and innovative approaches to foster responsible AI. Supported by deliberative technology, the session will provide an opportunity for knowledge sharing, with participants able to better understand how different communities approach and frame the responsible development of AI. The discussions will ultimately enable participants to identify common ground, build bridges across sectors, and catalyse subsequent reflections and initiatives to foster technologies that empower all.

title: Reshaping the Data Economy: the Power of Youth Voices
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Intergovernmental Organization, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: A. What issues related to the data economy are youth across the globe most concerned about? B. How are youth engaging through social media to effectively advocate for their perspectives on the data economy, and what examples of good practices to engage youth exist and could be implemented by different types of stakeholders? C. What incentives are needed to raise awareness among the "adult community" (policymakers, governments, private companies, etc.) on the importance of youth’s voices and to enhance their participation in policies and the design of data-driven technologies?
policy_recommendations: Participants will be invited to join the discussion and share their own best practices on how to design effective participatory approaches to data policies and technologies, and the valuable perspectives that youth can bring to the table for the future of the data economy. Learnings and good practices on how to effectively engage youth in policies and technologies around data will be shared across sectors and stakeholders, and so participants will be able to diversify their perspectives and potentially work towards a youth-inclusive data economy.

title: IGF 2023 WS #301 Navigating Conflicts and Overlaps in Internet Governance
organizers: Technical Community, African Group, Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Technical Community, African Group, Private Sector, Eastern European Group, Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: How can conflicts and overlaps between Internet Governance initiatives be effectively addressed to promote collaboration and cooperation among stakeholders? What strategies and best practices can be employed to harmonize conflicting initiatives and ensure effective resource allocation in order to optimize efficiency and avoid duplication of efforts among Internet Governance initiatives? How can stakeholder representation be improved to ensure inclusivity and fairness in decision-making processes related to Internet Governance initiatives, and how can differing viewpoints be heard and considered to achieve consensus in decision-making?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain from attending this session by better understanding the problems brought on by coordination issues, technical overlaps, jurisdictional issues, resource allocation, and stakeholder representation in Internet Governance initiatives. They will learn about practical approaches and the role of trust-building, accountability, and legitimacy in fostering effective cooperation and consensus-building between stakeholders from different regions, sectors, and perspectives. Participants will have the opportunity to exchange experiences and best practices with diverse stakeholders, as well as learn from the protocols followed by organizations operating the Internet ecosystem. Participants will have the chance to build relationships with like-minded people and organizations actively involved in Internet Governance, network with them, and explore opportunities for collaboration outside of the session. Participants will be better prepared to make informed decisions in their respective roles within the Internet Governance ecosystem by gaining insightful knowledge and connections, which will help to create more effective, collaborative, harmonious, and inclusive processes.

title: IGF 2023 WS #302 Bridging The Gender Digital Divide: Cultural Nuances

What are the cultural differences that must be taken into consideration when tackling the gender digital divide? C. What can we as Internet end users do to bridge this gender digital divide from a bottom-up approach? D. What measures can be implemented to ensure young girls are not left behind and are ready for the workforce? E. What role can youth initiatives play in tackling the gender digital divide?

title: IGF 2023 WS #303 Management in AI futurism: controversies, risks and benefits
organizers: Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Government, Asia-Pacific Group, Private Sector, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Technical Community, Eastern European Group, Civil Society, African Group
speakers: Luiz Felipe Belisário Macedo , Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Osei Manu Kagyah , Civil Society, African Group
Chepkemoi Cynthia , Private Sector, African Group
Eduardo Leal , Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Giovani Meneguel , Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
themes: Chat GPT, Generative AI, and Machine Learning
Future & Sustainable Work in the World of Generative AI
key_issues: A. How can we develop the development & deployment of AI systems and what guidelines should be in place to address issues such as bias, transparency, fairness and accountability? B. How we can ensure that users and stakeholders have access to understandable and interpretable explanations of AI-driven decisions? C. What policies should be in place to assign liability and accountability in cases where AI systems cause harm or make erroneous decisions, and who should be held accountable?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain understanding of the work done by youth-led initiatives, and access to a report that summarizes the discussions, case analyses, and recommendations presented during the session; which will serve as a reference for researchers, policy makers, and practitioners involved in the field of AI. The session is expected to raise awareness about the importance of platform accountability in AI cases, highlighting the challenges and best practices in this context. Making concrete recommendations to improve policies, and exploring innovative solutions are also objectives. It is expected to stimulate the engagement of youth leaders, policymakers and platforms. At the end we will invite participants to review our work and discuss our proposals, while the output of this session will be shared with governments, international and non-governmental organizations.

title: IGF 2023 WS #304 Deliberate data governance in education for learner autonomy
organizers: Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Private Sector, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
themes: Data Localization, Data Residency, and Data Sovereignty
key_issues: What are the design implications for developing a trusted education data space where learners' social mobility can be improved through education on a global scale? How are education data governance policies envisioning advancing algorithmic systems and the growing data collection in education as a result? How are children’s fundamental rights and freedoms upheld through policy and governance with regards to education data collection and processing through algorithm, AI-based systems throughout the world? What minimum appropriate standards can be envisioned to form part of education data governance and governance of advancing algorithmic systems deployed for education?
policy_recommendations: This session provides several aspects to inform the design of governing education technology. First, V. Hillman will propose a global framework for security standards: GESS, which promotes trust and confidence, access to digital networks, and global regulatory harmonization. Second, Irene Esther Mutuzo, chair of standardization efforts at the IEEE study group on interoperable learning records, discusses implementations of self-sovereign identity with use cases in Africa’s adult learners. The concepts of openness and trust are discussed to better empower learners through examples by Dixon Siu on open data and Fujitsu's distributed personal data store, Keiko Tanaka on open recognitions, and V. Hillman on applications of open science in European project. Overall, the session provides a unique opportunity to bring together the voices from various continents, provide concrete examples of issues and solutions, and provide a direction for harmonizing policies in education data that affect the autonomy of learners around the globe.

title: IGF 2023 WS #306 From local to global: Regulating platforms for human rights
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Intergovernmental Organization, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, African Group, Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
themes: Cyber Diplomacy and Peace on the Internet
Digital Commons as a Public Good
key_issues: Discussion on regulatory approaches in Brazil, Indonesia, and Nigeria; potential of multistakeholder initiatives for coherence in human rights protection; interaction between UNESCO Guidelines and EU DSA with other regulatory processes.
policy_recommendations: Awareness of tools like B-Tech UNGP Compass, DTSP Best Practices Framework, UNESCO Guidelines, GPD platform regulation assessment tool, and GPD/GNI Guide on CSO company engagement.
stakeholders_involved: Civil Society, Intergovernmental Organizations, Private Sector, African Group, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Asia-Pacific Group, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
impact_expectation: Enhanced understanding of platform regulation, international cooperation, and tools for rights-respecting digital governance.

title: Data Governance in Broadband Satellite Services
organizers: Civil Society, Intergovernmental Organization, Technical Community, Intergovernmental Organization, Civil Society, Eastern European Group, Civil Society, Eastern European Group
key_issues: How are national and international laws applied in the governance of LEO satellites and multi-orbital solutions in the context of data flows, privacy, personal data protection, and cybersecurity? What are potential benefits and challenges of satellite-dependent Internet access in achieving the SDGs? How can we ensure this technology is implemented sustainably, respects privacy and personal data protection, and addresses cybersecurity concerns? How can Internet access be considered a fundamental human right and be made accessible to all, including marginalized communities and developing countries? What regulatory frameworks and policies are needed to ensure equitable and inclusive access to satellite-dependent Internet services?
policy_recommendations: Attendees will gain a deeper understanding of the potential benefits and threats associated with this new technology, particularly in regards to transboundary data flows. They will also learn about the existing international legal framework designed to ensure the peaceful exploration and use of space, and how it applies to the regulation of commercial communication satellites. Privacy and cybersecurity concerns related to Low Earth Orbit satellite technology will be addressed with reference to these norms. Furthermore, participants will gain insights into the potential of LEO satellite technology to complement existing infrastructure and further global connectivity, while addressing concerns related to sustainability, privacy, and cybersecurity. We will in particular look at data flows enabled with this new infrastructure component, looking at regional approaches to privacy, personal data and national security concerns. Overall, attendees will leave the session with a better understanding of the opportunities and challenges presented by satellite-dependent internet access, and the necessary measures required to govern its use and implementation.
stakeholders_involved: Civil Society, Intergovernmental Organization, Technical Community, Eastern European Group, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)

title: Public-Private Data Partnerships in the Global South
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, African Group, Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: 1. What are the ways in which private sector is contributing to the data revolution? 2. What are the key policy and practice challenges companies, governments and other stakeholders face in attempting to build partnerships around data sharing for the purpose of monitoring/achieving the SDGs? 3. What are the ways of overcoming these challenges – including policy, economic and technical levers that can be used? 4. How do we align incentives of data collectors/holders, data users, data brokers/facilitators? What do different actors need to do?
policy_recommendations: Through the initial seeding discussion by the speakers and the extensive round-table participation, the participants will a) gain an understanding of the challenges faced when private sector, governments and civil society attempt to form data partnerships; b) the context in which some partnerships may work while others fail; c) an opportunity to diagnose possible improvements to case studies presented by themselves; d) an understanding of the incentives of the various actors; d) economic incentives that may impact behaviours of data owners, data users; e)an opportunity to reflect on the policy changes that will facilitate data sharing while preserving privacy.

title: IGF 2023 WS #309 Right to be heard: promoting children’s voices in the IGF
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: The session discusses obstacles to integrating children into digital governance spaces, perspectives for inclusion, and strategies to increase children's participation in digital governance debates.
policy_recommendations: The session proposes ways to amplify the voices of the most vulnerable in the Internet governance system, both regionally and globally.

organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group; Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group; Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG); Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)

policy_recommendations: Collaboratively develop and propose a set of policy recommendations for local policymakers and multistakeholder communities to address the data divide and data access issues

title: IGF 2023 WS #310 Stop! Child Sexual Abuse- comparing international approaches
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
speakers: Julie Inman Grant , Government, Asia-Pacific Group
Subramanian Uma , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
Antonio Labrador Jimenez , Government, Intergovernmental Organization
Katsuhiko Takeda , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: What do we know about the scale and nature of child sexual abuse online? What is the impact of national and international laws and regulatory frameworks to tackle this issue? Who’s responsibility is it to "own" the response to this issue? How can we better align regulatory efforts internationally to ensure we get "good" effective regulation?
policy_recommendations: Participants would gain an understanding about the scale and nature of child sexual abuse material online. This includes estimates on the amount of images in circulation, the number of offenders that pose a sexual threat to children, information about how the internet industry is currently responding to the threat, the types of tools they are using to respond to the threat, including explanations about the value of image hashing, URL blocking, keywords and what the technical threats are to the deployment of the services are in the future. The panel will explore the differing approaches to regulation internationally. Including international models of best practice, like the Internet Watch Foundation, Australian e-safety commissioner, representatives from the European Union, India and Japan on how these approaches vary from models of self-regulation to explore how regulation might look in the future and how these approaches may differ or complement each other.

title: Global Digital Value Chain: Africa’s Status and Way Forward
organizers: Private Sector, African Group
themes: Skills Building for Basic and Advanced Technologies (Meaningful Access)
key_issues: Considering that Africa is rated as a continent with the least contribution to the GDVC as evident through the dilemma experienced in the advent of the COVID-19: a. How inclusive is the GDVC and as a concerned stakeholder, what are the initiatives or actions required to take to amend the abnormal trend? b. Identify soft areas through which Africa could penetrate the GDVC and the benefits the continent would derive? 2 Africa being home to major raw materials of production is yet with little or no contribution to the GDVC, what could have gone wrong, what are the remedies?
policy_recommendations: The session would also equip participants with information on the required skills and requisite knowledge to obtain so as to strategically reposition African economies among the committee of producing economies that are more self-sufficient through industrialization. It would also delegate responsibilities (through its recommendations) to various stakeholder groups so as to propel them into action.

title: IGF 2023 WS #312 Ensuring Equitable Internet Access: A Fundamental Right
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group

policy_recommendations: Convey the crucial importance of equitable Internet access as a basic right, particularly in light of escalating accessibility issues worldwide.

title: IGF 2023 WS #313 Generative AI systems facing UNESCO AI Ethics Recommendation
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Intergovernmental Organization, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Intergovernmental Organization, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: How can we articulate the private and the public governance of the foundation models? How can we organize a global debate on that technology in order to avoid counterproductive competition between regional approaches? Do we need a moratorium?
policy_recommendations: The contribution of speakers from different regions of the world and from different disciplines will allow the participants to have a first approach of the different ways in which the States and the private actors of the world of generative AI consider the risks linked to this technology and envisage their governance, including in their concrete developments. Furthermore, the speakers will give a first analysis of the different legal and ethical aspects (notably: privacy, multiculturality, intellectual property, harmful content, …). The meaning and the application of the ethical principles of the UNESCO Recommendation will be highlighted.

title: IGF 2023 WS #314 Sending Party Pays and the Future of the Internet
organizers: Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG); Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG); Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
speakers: Alissa Starzak , Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Kyung Sin Park , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
Adrian Wan , Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group
Artur Coimbra de Oliveira , Government, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Rachael Stelly , Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Discussion on network investment approaches by regulators, current levels of investment to manage Internet traffic, options to address increased Internet traffic demand, implications of sending-party-pays model on net neutrality and market actors.
policy_recommendations: Broaden discussion on proposed network usage fees to include history of Internet traffic delivery, infrastructure changes, and current traffic management realities. Explore implications of sending-party-pays model on net neutrality and market dynamics.
networking_goals: Knowledge sharing on interconnection policy, collaboration on addressing Internet fragmentation challenges, partnerships between stakeholders to ensure competitive markets and access.
