title: IGF 2023 WS #509 Human Rights in financing for digital development
organizers: Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
speakers: Cathrine Bloch Veiberg , Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Line Gamrath Rasmussen , Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Isabel Ebert , Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization
themes: Technology in International Human Rights Law
key_issues: A. What is the role of DFIs when it comes to identifying and addressing human rights risks of their tech related projects and activities? B. What are the challenges faced by finance actors in providing development finance for digital projects? C. Which tools and other resources can be used to manage adverse impacts on rightsholders?
policy_recommendations: Outcome report as well as further sharing and disseminating existing resources.

title: IGF 2023 WS #510 Can we effectively enact human rights in the digital space?
organizers: Technical Community, African Group; Civil Society, African Group; Technical Community, African Group; Civil Society, African Group
speakers: Morales Angulo Cristina de los Angeles
regional_focus: African Group; Asia-Pacific Group; Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
themes: Digital Technologies and Rights to Health
key_issues: The session discusses the challenges of enacting human rights in the digital space, including the need for culturalization of regional and national contexts, conceptual and paradigmatic changes in human rights considering digital rights, the state of digital human rights and legal regulations, and the involvement of the multistakeholder model for participation and diversity in legal, political, economic, cultural, and social aspects. It also addresses the complexity of physical reality and digital space, the vagueness of government laws governing digital space, and the importance of a multistakeholder approach over state-centric models.
policy_recommendations: The session emphasizes the need for a normative vision and the establishment of a multistakeholder approach, shifting from state-centric models towards non-state actors and different stakeholders. It highlights the importance of ensuring the digital ecosystem guarantees fundamental rights and the necessity of aligning with the UN Human Rights Council's affirmation that the same rights people have offline must also be protected online.

title: Gender & technology: standing on the edge of a new frontier
organizers: Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization
key_issues: How to mainstream gender perspectives in national digital policies and remove the multidimensional and discriminatory barriers faced by women and girls; How to apply a human rights-based approach to tech design, development and deployment and why is this recommendation essential for achieving gender equality?; How to increase public and private sector commitments and investments in evidence-based initiatives aimed at bridging the gender digital divide?
policy_recommendations: Demonstrate technology and innovation can provide solutions to achieve gender equality the empowerment of all women and girls (deliver on SDG5); Highlight the critical role multi stakeholder partnerships in implementing CSW6, recommendations and thus in advancing gender equality in the digital world, in collaboration with feminists movements.

title: Challenges of Digital Colonialism in the Global South
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: Data colonialism, social and economic challenges of digital activities, impact on inclusion and diversity, alternatives for resistance and mitigation
policy_recommendations: Encourage digital sovereignty of groups and nations, promote datafication awareness, ensure inclusion of all people in democratic processes of development, debate and regulation of technologies
description: The session will analyze the effects of digital colonialism in the Global South. To this end, the discussion will gather insights from specialists of sub-representative groups, including black and quilombola communities from Brazil, Namibia, and Nigeria. Reflections are to be mad
preparatory_focus: To explore how colonial landmarks continue to be shaped especially in the Global South, assessing their ethical, social and economic challenges through a hybrid session with expository presentation and round table discussion

title: IGF 2023 WS #513 Governing the interoperability of Digital ID systems
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
themes: Technology in International Human Rights Law
key_issues: A. How can national and international governance frameworks ensure that there is adequate protection for human rights in the use of interoperable digital ID ecosystems? B. How do critical technical and legal design choices impact human rights and fundamental freedoms and how can they be redressed? C. What role can and do different stakeholders, including multinational corporations, international development agencies, and civil society groups play in impacting interoperable digital ID systems?
policy_recommendations: The workshop will provide valuable insight into specific systems, as well as examples of specific advocacy strategies that have proven useful in making ID systems more transparent and achieving accountability.

title: Empowering Youth to Make Sustainable Tech Choices
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
themes: Existing and New Technologies as Climate Risks
key_issues: How can the current mainstream education enhance learning at the intersection of technology and sustainability? How can conscious behaviour result from a shift from anthropocentrism to planetary future- led thinking? How can new research work in areas of technology, sustainability, well being and heath be used to inform curriculums and learning at the school level? How can young people come together to think and share what it means to grow, learn, explore, and live life online? How can schools, communities and neighbourhoods create space where the young can openly talk about digital experiences?
policy_recommendations: Participants will have the power to make better technology decisions and contribute to building the sustainable digital future we all dream of. The workshop will help unpack the following: 1. Where does your smartphone really come from? The complex global journey of the smartphone 2. Track your smartphone's journey on the world map, and uncover out the global distribution of mining, manufacturing and use. 3. Calculate your phone-economics- Time, attention, accessories, energy and mineral-use. 4. Designed to die: What happens when you dispose a phone? Why are smartphones so hard to repair? 5. Planetary futures: How can we make better decisions around the smartphone which work for us, and for the planet? How can we become better, conscientious tech consumers?

title: Beyond North: Effects of weakening encryption policies
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: The effects of a country/region's Internet policies on other locations; the impact of anti-encryption policies on the Internet ecosystem and human rights; the risk of internet fragmentation and its effects on freedom of expression and privacy; the unintended global effects of legislation targeting encryption in the Global North.
policy_recommendations: Provide a new perspective on addressing legislation that weakens encryption; equip attendees with tools to understand the global impacts of policies designed for the Global North; empower the audience to critically assess policies considering their unintended consequences.

title: IGF 2023 WS #518 The Technology Ecosystem Enabling Future Broadband Networks
organizers: Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Private Sector, Asia-Pacific Group
speakers: Michael Kende , Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Louis Boswell , Private Sector, Asia-Pacific Group
Ellen Blackler , Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: A. What are the facilitative policies to ensure we are incentivizing investment in networks of the future? B. What are the existing gaps that might be holding back network investments and exacerbating digital divides? C. Are there barriers that could arise and prevent stakeholders from making sufficient investments in network innovations?
policy_recommendations: Participants will learn about the ways broadband networks are configured today and the incentives it creates for ongoing investment and innovation that are important drivers for meaningful connectivity. They will have an opportunity to engage on questions about the policy environment necessary to facilitate future investment and ensure that networks are optimized to meet the needs of users.

title: Neither chaos nor control: content governance during crisis
organizers: Intergovernmental Organization
key_issues: The session explores the role of automated content governance during crises, the applicability of international standards on AI and freedom of expression, and the need for tailored approaches to safeguard free speech in crisis situations. It also examines the implications of different regional, language, and situation-specific contexts on content governance.
policy_recommendations: The session aims to explore what different stakeholders can do to ensure human rights-friendly content governance during crises, including the potential for crisis-specific policies around proactively providing authoritative information and the role of platforms in labeling independent quality media.

title: IGF 2023 WS #520 Disinformation and Political Advertising
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization
key_issues: Online disinformation poses a threat to civic discourse and electoral processes, especially when political messages are targeted at specific audiences, or when disinformation mixes with user generated content and is possibly amplified by platforms’ recommender systems. In particular, political advertising is increasingly shaping public opinion and influencing electoral outcomes. Even if political advertising is a well-known model in political marketing and propaganda, its significance has been amplified by the massive spread of false information online and, especially disinformation on social media, which has been aggravated by foreign interferences. The recent case of “disinformation for hire” has underlined the use of covert strategies for disseminating false content, and, more generally, the role of political influencers in addressing topics of public interest.
policy_recommendations: A number of measures have been adopted to address online disinformation in political advertising, including campaign rules that limit micro-targeting, which primarily have been adopted in the European policy framework such than the proposal on political advertising. In addition, measures to address the consequences of political advertising have led to adopting codes of conduct for political candidates, restrictions applied by platforms (either voluntarily or pursuant to national law), co-regulatory measures such as the European Strengthen

title: IGF 2023 WS #521 Multistakeholder platform regulation and the Global South
organizers: Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization, Private Sector, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: How Global South countries can contribute to the debate over platform regulation? How can the multistakeholder model contribute and bring solutions to the local debates of platform regulations? Which are the main challenges to be tackled by these countries? How Global South contributions on platform regulation can foster the achievement of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Goals and provide inputs for ongoing Internet Governance processes, such as the GDC and WSIS+20 review?
policy_recommendations: Participants are expected to recognize the importance of a multistakeholder demand-driven approach to develop platform regulation frameworks in the Global South. It is also expected that they further their knowledge about the need for tailoring broadly accepted models, so that the Global South contributions are not exclusively considered from the point of view of its users, but also from the broad multistakeholder community involved with the development of the Internet in those countries. Finally, the session aims to link the raised contributions to a broader agenda encompassing the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development Goals and ongoing process, such as GDC and WSIS+20.

title: Protecting the open internet to foster civic resilience
organizers: Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: A. How does the open internet support civic resilience during a crisis? B. What are the legal and policy levers (or barriers) to ensuring access to digital infrastructure? C. How does internet fragmentation impact digital infrastructure availability during a crisis?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain insight into the technical challenges of internet fragmentation, how fragmentation can compound a crisis, and how policy can be leveraged to protect the open internet. The session will feature perspectives from the private sector, civil society, and academia all engaged in efforts to protect the global internet.

title: Fostering a governance approach for a Latin-American digital
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: What are the necessary human rights standards and safeguards and avoid setbacks in legislation guaranteeing privacy, data protection, and even sovereignty of countries, in the implementation of international instruments to combat cybercrime? How to promote governance in digital security agendas in the region and at the country level? How to include perspectives from the global South, in relation to local contexts and needs, in international regulation, and designed from the needs of global potentials?
policy_recommendations: Participants will receive two updated documents of analysis with recommendations and suggestions prepared by the AlSur Consortium based on the latest development in local and global regulation.

title: IGF 2023 WS #524 How to defrag the Internet infrastructure?
organizers: Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
speakers: Nathalia Sautchuk Patricio , Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Antonio Marcos Moreiras , Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Merike Kaeo , Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Olatunde Awobuluyi , Technical Community, African Group
key_issues: Discussion around three policy questions: 1) How to prepare the Internet's ecosystem for structural changes without causing fragmentation? 2) Can critical changes be implemented without causing the splinternet? 3) How are national/international laws applied in Autonomous Systems regarding technical fragmentation?
policy_recommendations: Raise awareness, encourage collaboration among multistakeholders, and promote adoption of new standards, protocols, and security measures.
target_audience: Participants and attendees interested in Internet infrastructure and fragmentation issues
stakeholders_involved: Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Western European and Others Group (WEOG), African Group
impact_expectation: Increase concern about Internet fragmentation and engage more people in adopting new standards, protocols, and security measures.

title: IT Master Plan for Local Government
organizers: Government, Asia-Pacific Group
themes: Digital, Media, and Information Literacy Skills
key_issues: Cyberspace collaboration, balancing law enforcement and privacy, ethical AI use for environmental monitoring.
policy_recommendations: Developing digital services master plans, ensuring equal internet access, ethical AI frameworks.
networking_goals: Networking with professionals in digital services development within local governments.
agenda: Session on digital services master plans, challenges and opportunities, best practices, Q&A with speakers.
collaboration_outcomes: Potential collaboration on digital services development, sharing experiences from Thailand and Vietnam.

title: Dark Algorithm, from personal bubbles to continental ones
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Technical Community, Eastern European Group, Private Sector, Asia-Pacific Group
themes: New Technologies and Risks to Online Security
key_issues: Analysis of social network algorithms and their regulation, developments of internet bubbles, social effects and risks faced by younger users, current legislative situation and possible developments.
policy_recommendations: Discussion on state participation in companies producing multimedia content, laws and international bodies that could offer solutions, incentives for private companies to eliminate dark patterns.

title: IGF 2023 WS #528 How can we utilize the internet effectively & comfortably ?
organizers: Private Sector, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Combatting rising international traffic, reducing energy (CO2) needed for internet operations, addressing telecommunications challenges and digital divide.
policy_recommendations: Sharing information on setbacks, triumphs, and potential of new technology to develop more effective and convenient networks, promoting DX (Digital Transformation) and improving people's lives in normal and emergency situations.

title: IGF 2023 WS #529 Defending Critical Infrastructure from Cyber Attacks
organizers: Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group; Private Sector, Asia-Pacific Group; Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
speakers: Hidekazu HARA , Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group
Farooq Hafiz , Private Sector, Asia-Pacific Group
Namra Naseer , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: How can developing countries with limited resources protect their essential infrastructure against cyber attacks? How can loopholes of existing cybersecurity frameworks be improved for better protection? How can existing loopholes in cybersecurity laws be eradicated to prevent the legal system from exploitation in cybercrimes? What should be the role of multiple stakeholders on a national level for protection from cyber attacks in developed, developing & least developing countries? How does definition and work of internet governance cover scope of cybersecurity? How can public-private partnerships be leveraged to enhance cybersecurity capabilities for critical infrastructure protection?
stakeholders_involved: Government, Private Sector, Civil Society, Technical Community

title: Beyond regulation: the challenges of platform policy
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: How have social media platforms policies affected the development of an online public debate that respects the human rights principles of equity and non-violence? How can a multi-stakeholder framework for combating online inequalities be built? And how can responsibilities be balanced within this instance? What is the role of states, civil society and platforms in building a public debate with integrity?
policy_recommendations: The discussion summary will be made available to participants after the session.

title: IGF 2023 WS #532 AI and its ramifications for intellectual property rights
organizers: Civil Society, Eastern European Group, Civil Society, Intergovernmental Organization, Technical Community, African Group, Private Sector, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, African Group
themes: Future & Sustainable Work in the World of Generative AI
key_issues: How should current laws be applied to AI (Does copyright infringement apply to AI creations)? How should the products of generative AI be treated? What is a “derivative work” under intellectual property laws? How can governments ensure the protection of digital rights and foster innovation while promoting sustainable digital commons and ethical considerations in the face of emerging technologies?
policy_recommendations: This workshop will establish a digital framework which ensures that the future of AI development has oversight using human centric regulations that have fundamental freedoms at their core.
networking_goals: Participants will benefit from a multidisciplinary perspective on the nature of AI technology and gain valuable experience working alongside individuals from diverse backgrounds who will provide them with an important viewpoint on how it increasingly affects our society. These participants may encounter contrasting viewpoints on various issues, leading to the generation of distinct solution proposals. During this session participants will have the opportunity to share their empirical knowledge and after productive networking use this experience to deepen their understanding of adverse effects of emerging technologies.
agenda: Participants will learn about concrete policy recommendations from experienced policy-makers, while simultaneously being in discussion with government representatives. Using such a platform, which is based on knowledge-sharing and multidisciplinary approach, this workshop will establish a digital framework which ensures that the future of AI development has oversight using human centric regulations that have fundamental freedoms at their core.
collaboration_outcomes: Governments lack a concrete agreement on how to effectively regulate AI tools and emerging technologies. However, the recent G7 summit addressed some of these concerns.

title: Digital self-determination in collective data governance
organizers: Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: A. How do existing omnibus data governance regulations fail to empower communities when applied in practice? How can coalitions of civil society, academia and government adopt policies to serve the self-determined needs of data subjects? B. What resources, policies, and regulations are effective in mitigating the asymmetry challenges associated with data governance and building trust? C. What are the potential opportunities and challenges of integrating the principles of DSD into data governance models to tackle data asymmetries, promote responsible and ethical practices, and how can these challenges and opportunities be effectively addressed?
policy_recommendations: Supporting regulatory environments that promote individual and collective autonomy, and most importantly DSD. Developing contextual knowledge of different data governance models. Equipped with new insights to facilitate the development of more responsible data governance practices that promote transparency, accountability and fairness in the digital world.

title: IGF 2023 WS #534 End-to-End Encryption: The good, the bad, and the ugly
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG); Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
speakers: Julie Inman Grant , Government, Asia-Pacific Group
Vittorio Bertola , Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Keily Blair , Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Ian Stevenson , Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Benefits and consequences of deploying end-to-end encryption on messaging apps with child users; balancing privacy rights and child protection in encrypted environments; setting conditions for protecting encryption while ensuring user safety
policy_recommendations: To explain differences between standard and end-to-end encryption; highlight benefits of strong encryption; explain concerns about E2EE implementation and its impact on child protection; discuss steps to preserve privacy and safety in encrypted environments

title: War crimes and gross human rights violations: e-evidence
organizers: Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: How can international legal frameworks be utilised to facilitate cross-border cooperation and secure electronic evidence for addressing war crimes and gross human rights violations, and what are the challenges? How can admissibility and chain of custody requirements be respected in relation to collection and use of electronic evidence and OSINT, and what conditions and safeguards for the protection of human rights should be in place in accountability processes? How can public-private partnerships be effectively leveraged to enhance the collection, preservation, and sharing of electronic evidence for prosecuting war crimes and human rights abuses?
policy_recommendations: Participants will have the opportunity to delve into specific case studies where electronic evidence and OSINT played a pivotal role in documenting and exposing war crimes and human rights abuses. These case studies will highlight successful strategies, methodologies, and lessons learned, providing attendees with practical insights. The workshop will emphasize the importance of international and multistakeholder collaboration in utilizing electronic, evidence and OSINT effectively. Participants will explore existing frameworks, partnerships, and mechanisms to enhance cooperation among countries, organizations and other stakeholders, paving the way for a more unified and coordinated approach towards accountability. The session will tackle critical policy questions related to collection, admissibility, processing and cross-border exchange of electronic evidence and OSINT, fostering dialogue and debate among different stakeholders and disciplines. By examining policy implications and exploring potential solutions, participants will contribute to shaping effective policies and frameworks in addressing war crimes and human rights violations.

title: IGF 2023 WS #536 Cyberpsychology-Tackling Human Behaviours Behind Online Harm
organizers: Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: How can cyber psychology be adopted and applied in cybersecurity and online safety education and awareness programmes? How do researchers from across the world collaborate to share knowledge and insights on emerging behavioural vulnerabilities? How does cyber psychology become a mainstream discipline in the digital era?
policy_recommendations: The Workshop will feature presentations that seek to give participants an understanding of psychological and social factors driving behavioural online vulnerabilities and the possible remedies through psychological interventions. The presentations and discussions will also aim to gain and give understanding on the effects on online harms on user psychological and social wellbeing. Presentations will also outline roles of different stakeholders such as academia, researchers, psychologists and sociologists in tackling behavioural factors driving online harms. They will also give guidance on ways cyber psychological can inform online safety interventions and awareness campaigns.

title: IGF 2023 WS #537 Engaging Technical Operators Throughout the Internet Stack
organizers: Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: A. As policies are formulated to govern the ways in which AI can be implemented in network administration, how important is it to have technical AI experts at the table? B. As we engage in discussions about cyberattacks and the role of the Internet operator in mitigating them, should network cybersecurity technicians be centered in those conversations? C. While we discuss plans for broadband capacity-building projects in developing nations, how important is it to have ISP technicians with implementation-level expertise as part of those discussions?
policy_recommendations: This session will engage its participants to help create a series of outreach recommendations, which they can then use to facilitate individual outreach activities as we seek to bring more stakeholders to important Internet policy-related discussions. Participants will walk away with a much better understanding of what goes into building the Internet's infrastructure. From there, they will map areas of conversation already part of the IGF dialogue and help to frame scenarios that incentivize those with additional technical perspectives to join the discussion. Once those insights emerge, the actual outcome documents produced will serve as a guide for individual outreach campaigns. The final outcome document will provide detailed notes on the types of technical operators we seek to reach, why we believe they should be interested in Internet governance conversations, and how they can engage in the IGF process. These resources should make future engagement campaigns easier to implement.

title: IGF 2023 WS #538 Navigating Online Gender-Based Violence: The Mentoring Gap
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
speakers: Saba Tiku Beyene , Intergovernmental Organization, African Group
Lia Hernández , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Aji Fama Jobe , Technical Community, African Group
Marko Paloski , Technical Community, Eastern European Group
Luke Rong Guang Teoh , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: How does mentoring help shape an individual’s journey in advocacy, e.g. online gender-based violence? What is the potential for youth as mentors or emerging leaders, in topics like online gender-based violence? How can we sustain youth engagement and encourage youth into career pathways connected to fighting against online gender-based violence through trust?
policy_recommendations: Explore the value of work-related mentorships, as well as the important potential of youth as mentors or emerging leaders. The session will also discuss best practices for mentoring, and future strategies for sustainable mentoring relationships.

title: IGF 2023 WS #539 Small digital business challenges in a shifting landscape
organizers: Private Sector, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
speakers: Lawrence Olawale-Roberts , Private Sector, African Group
Jaqueline Pigatto , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Mark Datysgeld , Private Sector, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: A. How have small digital businesses been affected by the “digital and e-commerce turning point” precipitated by the COVID-19 pandemic? B. What are the challenges that have been affecting small digital businesses in the past few years, particularly in relation to finding a market? C. Which strategies have been employed by this global community that could be adopted to consolidate better business practices that generate positive results?
policy_recommendations: The outcomes of this session will be compiled with other data so

title: Equi-Tech-ity: Close the gap with digital health literacy
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Government, Asia-Pacific Group, Private Sector, African Group, Technical Community, African Group, Civil Society, Eastern European Group, Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
themes: Skills Building for Basic and Advanced Technologies (Meaningful Access)
key_issues: A. How can comprehensive frameworks and assessment tools be developed to capture and assess different dimensions of digital health literacy, ensuring holistic understanding of individuals' abilities in navigating digital health information and services? B. What strategies towards health equity can be adopted to ensure digital health literacy programs effectively address unique needs and challenges faced by marginalized communities, promote inclusivity and equitable access to digital health resources? C. How can partnerships between key stakeholders including healthcare providers, educational institutions, technology companies, and governments be leveraged to enhance digital health literacy skills, foster collaboration and knowledge sharing to advance health equity?
policy_recommendations: Participants could contribute to shaping policy recommendations, guidelines, and frameworks, alongside engaging in knowledge-sharing and potential collaborations with both onsite and online participants from diverse backgrounds, all for ensuring digital health for everyone.

title: IGF 2023 WS #540 Disinformation Forest: How social media shapes the Amazon
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: A) What are the dimensions that hate speeches assume on digital platforms in the Legal Amazon in the Latin American context of political polarization? B) What are the transparency gaps on the platforms, who are the agents that finance the misinformation ecosystem regarding environmental themes and what interests do they serve? C) What are the impacts of this process on the people who live in the Amazon, especially traditional peoples and communities, and what are their respective impacts on democracy? D) What methodologies can be used by stakeholders to unravel the pathways of disinformation and financed distribution of online information?
policy_recommendations: 1) Awareness about the threats of financed disinformation networks that have direct impact in policy making for the environment, especially considering the protection of humanity's biggest rainforest 2) The knowledge of a robust methodology for researching financial flows of information in a context of lack standardized transparency platform rules, collaborating with the audience in order to collect best practices and innovative research strategies; 3) Strengthen the knowledge about the environmental impacts of disinformation in the Amazonian context, bringing panelists who are Amazonians to share their own experiences and realities; 4) Connect multistakeholders who can build knowledge-sharing networks that approach the theme of environmental and digital protection; SDGs 13. Climate Action 16. Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions 17. Partnerships for the Goals

title: IGF 2023 WS #541 Unlocking Rural African - Diaspora Cooperation
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, African Group, Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, African Group, Civil Society, African Group
speakers: Danielle Smith , Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Taiwo Peter Akinremi , Civil Society, African Group
Jane Asantewaa Appiah-Okyere , Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Wisdom Kwasi Donkor , Civil Society, African Group
Kwaku Antwi , Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: Policy reforms to facilitate rural African communities and the African diaspora to unite virtually for SDGs, policy barriers for remote volunteer work to support affordable community Internet access, policy measures to leverage affordable Internet and energy access with diaspora engagement for SDGs.
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain new knowledge through dialogue, collaboration and knowledge sharing on Africa-led innovation in affordable community Internet shared service models and technologies. Participants will learn of new technologies for affordable Internet access to achieve UN SDGs. Communication amongst African and African Diaspora stakeholders and other multistakeholders about strategies to filling digital policy gaps for rural and disadvantaged urban impoverished communities. Participants will learn about a new tool, the Internet Backpack and its use as a shared community Internet, with Internet Backpack Operators acting essentially as one-person rural ISPs - backstopped by the Diaspora and others living beyond their rural and peri-urban African communities - will be introduced.
launch_purpose: Introduce a new tool for affordable community Internet access in rural and peri-urban African communities through diaspora engagement.
target_audience: African rural and peri-urban communities, African diaspora, multistakeholders involved in digital policy gaps.
stakeholders_involved: Speakers from Civil Society, African Group, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Private Sector, and participants from various stakeholder groups.
impact_expectation: Advance progress towards achieving gender equality, education, health, and other SDGs through affordable Internet and energy access in rural African areas with diaspora engagement.

title: IGF 2023 WS #544 What is the role of algorithms on indigenous preservation?
organizers: Private Sector, African Group, Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Private Sector, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
speakers: de Araújo Santos Najla Helen Graff
themes: Online Hate Speech and Rights of Vulnerable People
key_issues: A. How can internet governance frameworks be enhanced to ensure adequate representation and participation of indigenous and traditional peoples, considering their unique cultural perspectives and rights? B. What measures can be implemented to address the issue of cultural appropriation and misrepresentation of indigenous and traditional cultures in online spaces, and how can internet governance play a role in promoting respectful and accurate representation? C. What policies and strategies can be developed to bridge the digital divide and ensure equitable access to digital infrastructure and opportunities for indigenous and traditional communities, thus promoting their inclusion in the digital realm?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain understanding of the work done by youth-led initiatives, and access to a report, available on the Natural Resources Law and Sustainable Development Research Group website ( https://sites.google.com/ccom.unb.br/ndsr-gern ), that summarizes the discussions, case analyses, and recommendations presented during the session; which will serve as a reference for researchers, policy makers, and practitioners involved in the field of algorithms and indigenous people. The session is expected to raise awareness about the importance of technology accountability for preservation of indigenous and traditional peoples, highlighting the treaties, challenges and best practices. Making concrete recommendations to improve policies, and exploring innovative solutions are also objectives. It is expected to stimulate the engagement of youth leaders, policymakers and platforms. At the end we will invite participants to review our work and discuss our proposals, while the output of this session will be shared with governments, international and non-governmental organizations.

title: Boosting journalism with a market-driven approach
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: How do current regulatory frameworks worldwide create an obligation for algorithm-based services to boost journalism vs. dis-/misinformation? What will participants gain from attending this session? — ISO standard and the news publishing industry: how it is meant to be used by newsrooms and what everyone else (tech companies, programmatic advertising, funders, fact checkers, etc.) is expected to do with it. — How the JTI standard is designed to feed algorithms. — Policy frameworks in which the JTI standard is mentioned (Digital Services Act's Code of Conduct of the European Commission, the European Media Freedom Act, etc.) — Use cases of tech companies making use of the JTI standard: NewsGuard with the JTI Emergency Protocol launched in May 2023 in Ukraine; Microsoft's tech tools for journalism as part of their recently launched Journalism Hub; Internews' Ads For News and GroupM's Back to News initiatives.
policy_recommendations: Expected Outcomes Following this session, it is expected that: - policymakers engage with our advocacy team to understand how the JTI standard should be used in their country; - a working group with the private sector be created to start enabling this market-driven approach; - publications and media impact is generated.
launch_purpose: To promote transparency of news outlets, guarantees of editorial independence and the professionalism of fundamental editorial processes through an ISO-type standard.
target_audience: Policymakers, private sector, newsrooms, tech companies, programmatic advertising, funders, fact checkers
stakeholders_involved: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Intergovernmental Organization, NewsGuard, Microsoft, Internews, GroupM

Panelists will elaborate on children’s perception of their 'data self' and the many types of children’s privacy online. Participants will also be given a flavor of the varying national and international conventions concerning the rights of children regarding their data. As our speakers come from a range of stakeholder groups, they’ll provide the attendees with a detailed idea on how a multistakeholder, intergenerational, child-centred, child-rights based approach to data governance related policies and regulations can be created.
target_audience: Participants will first 'un-learn' the current trend of the universal (often, adult) treatment of all users, which fails to respect children’s 'evolving capacity', lumping them into over-broad categories (under-13s, under-18s).
stakeholders_involved: Government, Private Sector, Civil Society, Technical Community
impact_expectation: The main difference between general data protection and children's data protection is that children's data needs our special attention. Massive amounts of children’s data are being collected every second as we speak, hence, children’s data needs our special attention.

title: IGF 2023 WS #63 Intergenerational Dialogue on Digital Harms & Online Safety
organizers: Government, Asia-Pacific Group; Private Sector, African Group; Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group; Technical Community, African Group; Civil Society, Eastern European Group
speakers: Matthew Watson , Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Man Hei Connie Siu , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
Edmon Chung , Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group
Emma Day , Civil, Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Anastasiia Agarkova , Civil Society, Eastern European Group
key_issues: What specific digital harms and intersectional factors threaten young people face online? How does adultist perception-driven policies impact young people’s potential participation in (or purposeful abstinence from) the Internet? How can youth views be incorporated in policies made by stakeholders such as Donors, NGOs, and corporations to effectively tackle digital harms globally and locally, and to facilitate intergenerational justice in the digital arena for young people?
policy_recommendations: Participants will gain an insight into the youth’s lived experiences of digital harms. Their knowledge on and awareness of the different types of digital harms and the tools available to combat those will be enhanced. They will develop a better grasp on the contemporary generational gap in the policy arena concerning digital harms and online safety. They will gain a better understanding of how age-influenced social and power relations impact young people’s online lives. They will be appraised of the fact that there can be no meaningful policy for the youth without the youth. They will have a clearer idea on how the youth can be given a more proactive role in policymaking on online safety and how different stakeholders can collaborate with the youth to facilitate safer environments for youth online.

title: IGF 2023 WS #64 Decolonise Digital Rights: For a Globally Inclusive Future
organizers: Government, Asia-Pacific Group, Private Sector, African Group, Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Technical Community, African Group, Civil Society, Eastern European Group

title: IGF 2023 WS #66 Community leadership and their impact at local Communities
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group; Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group; Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC); Government, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC); Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: A. What policies can be implemented to support community leaders in promoting digital inclusion and access at local communities, especially in underserved areas? B. How can community leaders be better represented and have their voices heard in decision-making processes related to Internet governance at the local level? C. What policies can be implemented to address the challenges faced by community leaders in accessing funding and other resources to support their initiatives related to Internet governance?
policy_recommendations: To examine the role of community leadership in promoting digital inclusion and access at local communities. To identify the challenges faced by community leaders in promoting digital inclusion and access at local communities. To propose strategies for strengthening community leadership in promoting digital inclusion and access at local communities. Exploring the current power struggle in community leaders and context of national, regional and international. Creating a better understanding of new leadership challenges and their interest SDGs 11.2 11.7

title: Manga Culture & Internet Governance-The Fight Against Piracy
organizers: Private Sector, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Discussion on the protection of authors and their works internationally, especially Manga artists, in an era of rapid information copying; application of domestic and global legal frameworks to online circulation of copied works; and structuring Internet governance to encourage cultural advancement.
policy_recommendations: Need for international cooperation between various parties involved in Internet governance to eradicate piracy; understanding how the Internet community can assist in the dissemination of Manga works.

stakeholders_involved: Japanese publishers, lawyers, copyright holders, ISPs, CDNs, hosting providers
impact_expectation: To raise awareness about the impact of piracy on Manga artists and the importance of international cooperation in combating online piracy.

title: IGF 2023 WS #70 Rebuilding digital mutual trust between big powers
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
speakers: Wolfgang Kleinwaechter , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Jovan Kurbalija , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Yves POULLET , Intergovernmental Organization, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: The current landscape of global digital technology competition is severely disrupted by the emergence of digital mutual trust issues, such as the technology conflict between the US and China, the US ban on TikTok, and cross-border data flow conflicts between the US and Europe. These issues pose a threat to the security and stability of global cyberspace and have the potential to impact the existing international order. In the digital era, digital mutual trust is crucial for building a new international order, and the lack of trust between major powers is a significant source of conflict.
policy_recommendations: Provide participants with an in-depth understanding of the current status of digital mutual trust between big powers in the world. It also explores the upcoming challenges and opportunities concerning lack of digital mutual trust between them. The ultimate objective is to establish a shared vision for rebuilding digital mutual trust among big countries, which can be achieved by identifying common values and principles that serve as a foundation for trust-building efforts. This workshop also seeks to explore various mechanisms that can be utilized to foster digital mutual trust among big powers in the realm of data governance.

title: IGF 2023 WS #72 Defence against the DarkWeb Arts: Youth Perspective
organizers: Civil Society, Eastern European Group, Technical Community, Eastern European Group, Private Sector, Eastern European Group
speakers: Betelehem Samuel , Technical Community, African Group
Izaan Khan , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Pedro de Perdigão Lana , Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
ABRAHAM SELBY , Technical Community, African Group
Man Hei Connie Siu , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
themes: New Technologies and Risks to Online Security
key_issues: The forbidden fruit is always the sweetest: will a total ban help in the fight against the darknet, or should we focus on educational and explanatory activities? How should we regulate Darkweb? What role can emerging technologies play in the fight against the DrakWeb? Not so dark: what are the benefits of Darknet for ordinary users and are there any of them? What will participants gain from attending this session? Workshop aims to provide different opinions on DarkWeb issue and also have a debate about it that can lead to finding a common solution to the problem. It is also set to make listeners understand what hides behind a scary name ‘dark’, how this part of the web appeared and how it can be regulated. Discussion should also provide useful insights about DarkWeb and how it affects our society in many unusual ways: from cyber- and usual crimes to journalists investigations. Also, as this is a youth perspective event, workshop will present new fresh views on the topic and introduce young professionals.

agenda: Discussion on the current status of AI governance, exploration of a collective vision for global AI governance, identification of common values and principles, evaluation of communication channels between governments and stakeholders, and strategies for implementing global AI governance interconnection.
collaboration_outcomes: Opportunity to discuss strategies for implementing the interconnection of global AI governance mechanisms, promoting transparency and accountability in AI development and deployment, and fostering collaboration among stakeholders.

agenda: Examine policy gaps on labor laws for digital work, identify key barriers to digital access, share case studies of successful initiatives, discuss best practices for empowering youth for meaningful work

title: IGF 2023 WS #77 Exploring ethical governance of AI, empowering a better life
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Private Sector, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
themes: Chat GPT, Generative AI, and Machine Learning
key_issues: 1. Build a scientific and effective AI ethical governance system: What kind of governance measures are effective and do not unduly constrain the development and use of AI? How to ensure that the developed technical logic, industry standards, laws and norms can be implemented? 2. Improve the ethical awareness of stakeholder groups: What are the existing risk categories and potential challenges in AI ethics? How to establish an effective ethical risk assessment mechanism? How to strengthen the scientific dissemination and ethics popularization of AI and improve the level of public awareness?
policy_recommendations: Participants will learn about the latest development in AI technology, recognize the risks brought by AI technology to human society, and the latest international discussions and future trends in AI ethics and safety governance. For governments, they can fully understand the different theoretical and practical progress of AI ethics and safety governance in various countries, and provide a rich basis for improving its domestic laws and regulations related to AI ethics. For enterprises, they can understand how to improve their AI ethics and compliance system when developing or applying AI products and promote the sustainable development of their AI technology.

It will help to raise awareness of, and build the evidence base for, positive changes and effective interventions on an international scale.

collaboration_outcomes: Calls to action for IGF community to advance accessibility, potential for cross-sector collaboration, follow-up actions to implement policy recommendations

title: IGF 2022 WS #13 Evaluation of ICT impact on rural areas development
organizers: Government, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: The workshop examines the impact of information technology as an enabler infrastructure in sustainable development, focusing on rural areas. It explores whether connecting villages to the Internet leads to favorable social, economic, and environmental outcomes. The discussion includes the experience of national-wide planning for connecting rural and least developed areas to the internet, challenges, and problems in this project. It also covers the results of a national-level project surveying the impact of connecting villages to the Internet, with a focus on least developed areas and the negative and positive impacts of ICT provision in rural areas.
policy_recommendations: The workshop discusses the need for policies that support the development of connections for all people, especially in rural areas, and how to improve the positive impact of ICTs in rural areas. It also addresses the types of services that should be provided together with the connection and access for people with special needs. The policy recommendations include increasing investment in rural infrastructure, correcting trade restrictions through e-commerce solutions, and developing ICT infrastructure to support economic development and human well-being with affordable and equitable access for all.

title: Digital Wellbeing of Youth: Selfgenerated sexualised content
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Discussion focused on governmental strategies, national policies, and legislation regarding young people's online behavior, alignment with General Comment No. 25, internet governance approaches across political systems and cultures, youth involvement in designing solutions, and platform provider support. Also addressed online gender-based violence, victim support, digital literacy, and legislative harmonization for non-consensual intimate image abuse.
policy_recommendations: Advocating for transposing UN Committee on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC) General Comment 25 into national legislation, tailoring recommendations to individual countries during GC25 dialogues, strengthening peer support networks for victims of online gender-based violence, improving digital literacy through education, and harmonizing legislation to protect victims of non-consensual intimate image abuse.

policy_recommendations: The session aimed to stimulate discussion on policy questions related to interoperability as a tool for open digital markets, with potential sub-questions on implementation challenges, regulatory frameworks, and market dynamics. The exact content was to be developed by panellists and moderator, with possible workshop-merge proposals from the MAG.

title: IGF 2022 WS #189 Internet Access & Digital inclusion in developing countries
organizers: Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: The session will discuss the role of the internet in inclusivity efforts, progress made in bringing digital opportunities to underserved communities, challenges facing these efforts, and solutions to the identified challenges. It will also explore how the internet can help overcome challenges in underserved communities and the experiences of digital inclusion experts working in these areas.
policy_recommendations: The session aims to provide lessons to improve the contribution of the internet to digital inclusion in underserved communities, share experiences that will help participants understand the challenges and solutions, and contribute to the development of the Global Digital Compact.

policy_recommendations: Ensure that the benefits of connectivity are widely shared, protect human rights in a digital world, increase internet access in developing countries and for marginalized communities.

title: IGF 2022 WS #200 Ecological water transport, medicine and training online

policy_recommendations: Proposals include establishing remote medical clinics using satellite internet, drones, and solar power; launching ecological water transport for renewable energy; and online training programs for engineers from countries with emigration to Europe. These initiatives align with UN's 12 commitments and SDGs to improve access to healthcare, education, and sustainable transport.
initiative_or_product_name: Remote medical clinics, ecological water transport, online training for engineers
launch_purpose: To address healthcare access, education, and sustainable transport in hard-to-reach areas through innovative solutions like remote medical clinics, ecological water transport, and online training programs.

stakeholders_involved: Civil Society, Intergovernmental Organization, Private Sector, United Nations, UN Office for Partnerships

title: Sustainable and human-centric blockchain
organizers: Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Eastern European Group, Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: Environmental sustainability: Can a proof-of-stake blockchain foster trustworthy and an environmentally sustainable use of DLTs rather than the proof-of-work based one? Decentralisation of Power: Proof-of-Stake has the potential to re-centralize the decentralised nature of blockchain by depending on an individual’s/entities’ stake towards the technology. Can a human-centric blockchain ensure that every individual has power on the blockchain without staking their cryptocurrencies? Reimagining governance: In permissionless networks, cryptocurrencies reward those who maintain the network. On the other hand, in permissioned networks, those who maintain the network have different incentives, e.g., they have formed a consortium to run a business or deliver a service. This means that there are many possibilities that can be explored without making money the central point of everything to ensure that people are treated fairly on the blockchain. What are these possibilities; and can the governments regulate and control this specific technical issue?
policy_recommendations: Connection with previous Messages: Katowice IGF 2021 Messages -Faced with the realities of anthropogenic climate change, it is clear that the environmental impact of technology needs to be further investigated and adequately addressed -Acknowledge and encourage the contribution of youth: Young people play a key role in the achievement of sustainability and environmental conservation, and their actions need to be supported by providing necessary infrastructure and connectivity 2021 IGF Youth summit key messages: -Ethics for DLT. The ethical aspects of the phenomenon of the increasingly widespread tokenization of everything, including even people, just for the sake of profit should be taken into account. The development of DLT ethical code could help to address many issues in this area.

impact_expectation: SDGs 1, 8, 9, 10, 16 are addressed by exploring the potential of blockchain to reduce inequities by favouring credit access and decent jobs, to improve efficiency and security of supply chains, as well as to build strong and reliable infrastructure for public services. SDG 13 is addressed by stimulating

title: AI: Need for fundamental regulation for the Global South
organizers: Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization, Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: AI systems governance is a complex discussion and developing nations must invest in basic conceptual and normative frameworks that are inclusive and safeguard the interests of the marginalised population. Risk identification with AI systems and serving the needs of a modern heterogenous society demands basic regulatory practices in place. A basic regulatory framework serves the fundamentals of society and safeguards and upholds the rights of its citizens. AI systems must serve the needs of and empower local communities. While AI governance provides the framework conditions to do so in a responsible way, digital public goods such as open AI models and open local AI training data serve as the technological foundations.
policy_recommendations: The proposal is rooted in progressive development cooperation via the use of AI and shall provide actionable steps for policy adoption and creation of favourable regulatory frameworks that keeps a check that AI does not exacerbate inequality.

title: IGF 2022 WS #207 Accountable Data Sharing to achieve SDGs
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Why and how to build, achieve and sustain trustworthy and accountable data, information and knowledge sharing ecosystems in this Digital Age, to help address local, regional, national and global societal challenges while aiming to achieve the 17 Sustainable Development Goals? From the risk perspectives: How to avoid these digital, cyber or cyber-physical deployments and use thereof become a foe? How to avoid it increasing mistrust, or creating other detrimental effects? Connection with previous Messages: This Workshop is aimed to support all 17 SDGs and its respective targets, and it many – intertwined – cluster of SDGs and targets. Obviously, SDG 17 linked to SDG 16 are the baseline enablers for this Workshop about trust and accountability, where all 17 provide for global, collective inspiration, ambition and focus.
policy_recommendations: To what extent can digital ecosystems and related governance tools help? What are the benefits? And what are the downsides? In this Workshop, we will dive into these topics, touching the ‘why’ but mostly focusing on the ‘how’. To share or not to share, is the trust question. For instance, why and how do we trust experience, knowledge, information and other data, offline and/or online? Where and how can digital technology, organisational, policy and other governance capabilities lend a helping hand, while aiming to build, achieve a sustain trusted data sharing in this Digital Age, to achieve SDGs? With the help of experts in this domain from different sectors and continents, and with different perspectives, this Workshop is managed, moderated and loaded, to spur the discussion with the audience, and focus on an

title: Metaverse or Dataverse: Which “Verse” Should We Trust?
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Eastern European Group, Technical Community, African Group, Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: Who would be liable for cybercrimes committed inside the Metaverse, such as the fraudulent actions concerning cryptocurrencies? Who would be the right holder of the creative products created inside the Metaverse, including intellectual property? How and by whom must the cases of hate speech and sexual harassment inside the Metaverse be regulated?
policy_recommendations: The session contributes to SDG Targets 8.3, 9.1, 16.1, and 16b by addressing the need for fair and resilient regulatory infrastructure for the Metaverse, building development-oriented policies, and combating hate speech and sexual harassment.

title: Privacy in Practice: Ensuring Data Protection in Workplaces
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Intergovernmental Organization, Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: How can employers be more incentivised to implement the requirements coming from data protection legislation in the workplace? How can a balance be created between security, usability and privacy in the workplace? What regulatory approaches could be effective in upholding privacy rights of employees and offering adequate remedies in case of rights violation?
policy_recommendations: The session aims to build further on the IGF 2021 message about adding labour dimensions to digital policies and regulations to protect workers' rights. It links with SDG Targets 8.8 and 16.10, promoting a safe and secure working environment where the right to privacy is respected and creating awareness of privacy rights and remedies available when this right is breached.

title: Blurred lines between fact & fiction: Disinformation online
organizers: Intergovernmental Organization, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Intergovernmental Organization, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
regional_focus: Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: Does online disinformation undermine our democratic values and principles and how? How do policymakers and the industry tackle the problem? Is the media literacy education landscape equally well established in all the countries? If not, what is the baseline of actions that a country should take to create digitally literate societies?
policy_recommendations: Adequate enabling environments (e.g. policies, legislation, institutions) need to be put in place at the national, regional and global levels to foster just, safe, resilient and sustainable digital societies and economies. Artificial Intelligence (AI) needs to be developed and deployed in manners that allow it to be as inclusive as possible, non-discriminatory, auditable and rooted into democratic principles, the rule of law and human rights. Policies implemented by Internet platforms to deal with harmful online content need to be transparent, acknowledge the limits of automated content moderation, and ensure a proper balance with the right to freedom of expression. Regarding online education and learning, many countries are faced with a lack of devices, weak infrastructure and low levels of digital literacy and digital skills. Increased support and international collaboration and partnerships to tackle these issues are key. Individual actors at local and regional levels should also take responsibility in finding solutions together. Multiple different actions are needed to fight against illiteracy, in particular in the Global South. There is insufficient common language between stakeholders, inadequate participation and lack of critical assessment of whether engagement is meaningful. There is a need to improve coherent use of terminology which can impact the effectiveness of Internet policy debates. For example, having better translation between languages, but also exchange within and between regions.

title: Responsive regulation: regulation at speed of technological
organizers: Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Government, Intergovernmental Organization
key_issues: How can we make use of digital and emerging technologies to promote innovations that are inclusive, resilient and sustainable? How do we make regulatory framework as an enabler without compromising with protection of citizens and environment? How can we make sure that digital and advanced emerging technologies are not developed and used for harmful purposes? What values and principles should guide the development and use of technologies to enable this?
policy_recommendations: Regulations for digital era need to act as enablers of innovation and promote new industries that offer more inclusive and sustainable products and solutions for the society while increasing the share of digital economy in country’s economic growth and output. This is specifically important for KSA as it is on a journey to diversify its economy away from an oil based economy and position itself as a leading digital government around the world. Advanced and emerging technologies must not further social and economic divides and therefore regulations need to play a critical role in leveling the playing field including restriction of practices that makes it difficult for new market entrants to offer their products and services, hoarding of data within few large organizations and their unethical usage.

title: IGF 2022 WS #224 Ethical and legal boundaries for OSINT practices
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: What risks do OSINT practices pose to human rights? What are or should be the criteria for determining the regulatory limitations for OSINT or cyber patrolling practices? Should those limitations be the same for both public and private sector practices?
policy_recommendations: The panel aims to raise awareness of the potential risks that OSINT practices pose to human rights. When employed by government forces, OSINT diminishes the expectation of privacy and limits people’s ability to express freely online. This ultimately restricts the exercise of the right to freedom of expression and access to information as recognized by international human rights laws and standards. The panel will contribute to the discussion on the appropriate regulatory solutions to this issue, aiming to improve the information ecosystem and the protection of human rights online.

title: IGF 2022 WS #225 Reinvigorating the Debate: The Role of Law in IG
organizers: Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)

Shona Moreau , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Émilie Weidl , Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: What should be the role of law in Internet Governance? What are the challenges of judicial institutions and legal frameworks in addressing human rights on and off the internet? How to achieve consensus in a multistakeholder context while ensuring that a diversity of voices are heard? Balancing between freedom of expression and the limitation of harmful online content. The potential development of a legally binding agreement on technology and human rights.
policy_recommendations: Participants will walk away with a better appreciation of the limits of legal systems in supporting human rights and SDGs through internet governance. The workshop will continue the debate on the potential development of a legally binding agreement on technology and human rights and invite stakeholders to present their points of view in a non-combative forum.

policy_recommendations: Enhance global dialogue and cooperation, promote transformation of the global Internet governance system, foster a peaceful, secure, open and cooperative cyberspace, and establish a multilateral, democratic and transparent global Internet governance system.
stakeholders_involved: Technical Community, Government, International Community
impact_expectation: Address global challenges in personal information leakage and online fraud, support sustainable development goals, and improve internet governance through global partnerships.

impact_expectation: Promote digital fairness, reduce inequalities through better policies and legislation against dark patterns, and ensure responsible use of AI algorithms.

policy_recommendations: Reach a full alignment status between all parties when it comes to the importance and impacts of having RM and BCM in the government sector; facilitate rich discussions between the panel and the audience; plan for follow-up sessions to talk about every topic in detail; audience will take some publications related to RM and BCM; panel will be happy if they receive any feedback from the audience either by a survey or live during the session

title: Data Flows Regulations and Surging Internet Fragmentation
organizers: Civil Society, Eastern European Group
key_issues: Acute problems of data economy development in the modern world. Reasons and pursuits of government requirements for transnational IT companies towards data localization and creation of data centers. Transparency issues with methods and purposes of personal data collection, storage, and processing carried out by transnational IT companies. Prospects of designing unified global regulations on data flow and data storage: a utopic dream of a consensual solution vis-à-vis a sensible perspective. Mechanisms mitigating the negative impact of the national regulations on Internet fragmentation.
policy_recommendations: Adequate enabling environments (e.g., policies, legislation, institutions) need to be put in place at the national, regional and global levels to foster inclusive, just, safe, resilient and sustainable digital societies and economies. Stakeholders have a joint responsibility in ensuring that digital transformation processes are diverse, inclusive, democratic and sustainable. Agile regulatory frameworks – at the national, regional and, where possible, global levels – need to be put in place to outline rules, responsibilities and boundaries for how public and private actors behave in the digital space.

title: IGF 2022 WS #234 Pushing for IT Companies’ Moderation Policy Accountability
organizers: Civil Society, Eastern European Group
key_issues: Effectiveness of contemporary content moderation policy in fighting extremism vis-a-vis its side effects featuring digital space fragmentation. Defining the malware and harmful content: clear criteria and straightforward transparent moderation guidelines. Mechanisms of control and observation over the content moderators on the social networks. Alternatives to bans and blocking: promoting inclusion moderation policy towards the disseminators of the non-mainstream views.
policy_recommendations: Policies implemented by Internet platforms to deal with harmful online content need to be transparent, acknowledge the limits of automated content moderation, and ensure a proper balance with the right to freedom of expression. To ensure that human rights are enforced and upheld in the digital space, a careful reflection is needed on how technology serves humanity, as opposed to simply putting in place safeguards around the edges and waiting until harms occur. States’ duty to prevent potential harm of human rights (e.g. through regulation and enforcement) needs to be complemented with (a) effective access to remedy when people are victims of human rights violation, and (b) responsibility on the part of relevant actors in integrating human, rights due diligence and impact assessments throughout the entire life cycle of a technology.

title: Dialogue on the 'Declaration for the Future of the Internet'
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Fostering global cooperation on an open, free and secure internet without creating a digital Cold War; identifying internet policy issues with broad consensus and points of disagreement; exploring alternatives to the Declaration if it's not the right vehicle; bringing non-government stakeholders into dialogues.
policy_recommendations: Developing a coordinated global vision for tackling digital policy problems through initiatives like the IGF, UN Digital Cooperation Agenda, and the Declaration; fostering dialogue among supporters, signatories, neutral analysts, and representatives of non-signatory countries.

title: To Regulate or not to Regulate?
organizers: Government, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
speakers: Jon Stever- Innovation for Policy Foundation (i4policy)
key_issues: The right level of regulation of technology and data to ensure human rights and fundamental freedoms, while leaving space for innovation and economic competitiveness; the role of agile, human-centred and innovative regulatory approaches; the role of international harmonization processes in shaping national technology and digital policy regulations.
policy_recommendations: Stakeholders have a joint responsibility in ensuring that digital transformation processes are diverse, inclusive, democratic and sustainable. Commitment and strong leadership from public institutions need to be complemented with accountability and responsibility on the part of private actors. Agile regulatory frameworks – at the national, regional and, where possible, global levels – need to be put in, place to outline rules, responsibilities and boundaries for how public and private actors behave in the digital space. More awareness should be raised about the interplay between big platforms, competition, and consumer rights, among both consumers and global, regional or national antitrust regulators. Antitrust regulation could incorporate the concept of public interest, addressing the issue of market power and concerns about fundamental rights such as the right to freedom of speech. Tailored approaches like pro-ethical design in regulation should also be considered. Policies implemented by Internet platforms to deal with harmful online content need to be transparent, acknowledge the limits of automated content moderation, and ensure a proper balance with the right to freedom of expression. There is an urgent need to understand why policy solutions already known and proven to be effective are not being more widely implemented. There is a necessity to strengthen the multistakeholder approach, in order to be truly inclusive and to develop effective policies that respond to the needs of citizens, build trust and meet the demands of the rapidly changing.

title: IGF 2022 WS #237 Impact of U.S technology sanctions on SDG targets in Sudan

key_issues: Impact of U.S sanctions on SDGs targets, impact on civil and political rights activists, poverty and social/economic complications, lack of access to digital platforms and education, government surveillance of activists
policy_recommendations: Need for review of sanctions' impact on SDGs, support for digital infrastructure development, protection of civil rights and access to information, addressing the digital divide and ensuring equitable access to technology.

title: IGF 2022 WS #240 Pathways to equitable and safe development of AGI
organizers: Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, African Group, Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group

Joanna Mazur , Civil Society, Eastern European Group
Oarabile Mudongo , Civil Society, African Group
