How can policymakers and platforms combat spam, disinformation, and cybersecurity threats while preserving people’s ability to engage anonymously online?
policy_recommendations: Anonymity and privacy contributes to gender equality by eliminating biases inherent in receiving information where the receiver is aware of the gender designation or presentation of the speaker. Misogyny, transphobia, and other prejudices against differing expressions of gender will not be present (or will be significantly mitigated) if the speaker is able to remain anonymous in their communication. It is essential that girls, women, and other gender minorities be able to anonymously access and share comprehensive and accurate information on sexual health, sexual violence, and other topics that they may be prevented from safely accessing in other ways. Proposals to require online identity verification, retention, and disclosure threaten the human rights of girls, women, and other gender minorities. Preserving the right and ability to browse, communicate, and participate anonymously online will empower and promote the social and political inclusion of all irrespective of age, sex, disability, race, ethnicity, origin, religion, economic or other status.

title: IGF 2022 WS #443 How can we make the Internet safer for girls and women?
organizers: Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Discussion on limits of freedom of expression, definition of online harassment and discrimination, regulatory paternalism in online spaces, and the gender digital divide with focus on online gender-based violence.
policy_recommendations: Introduce new indicators to the Gender Digital Divide Index (GDDI), produce publications on online gender-based violence and the concept of the 'safe internet', and discuss the 'declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace' and online harassment.

title: IGF 2022 WS #444 Open Justice Data for Enhancing Access to Human Rights
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: Obstacles and opportunities for advancing open data-driven policies to enhance access to human rights in Latin America’s justice sector institutions; technological and institutional capabilities of judicial institutions to promote open data policies; steps to foster use of open justice data for evidence-based policies in the justice sector.
policy_recommendations: Exploring connections between open justice data and human rights; focusing on potential impact of open justice data to improve policies such as gender violence, environment, access to public information, and police abuses; linking discussions to relevant SDGs; including a section on findings related to SD, and proposed interventions to deepen the connection between discussions and the 2030 Agenda.

title: Freedom of expression vs the law in the information disorder
organizers: Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: Legislative efforts to combat information disorder, human rights considerations in law interpretation/enforcement, utilizing law to combat information disorder while promoting human rights
policy_recommendations: Realign laws with their intended purposes, ensure equal access to justice, promote non-discriminatory laws for sustainable development

title: IGF 2022 WS #446 Harnessing the Power of Accessible Technology
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: How can universal design principles for accessibility be advanced across the internet to improve the experience of those with disabilities? What can the IGF community do to further action and cross-sector collaboration to realize the potential of the internet to improve the experience of those with disabilities? What priorities and/or changes are needed from an Internet governance policy standpoint to accelerate progress towards a more inclusive internet for persons with disabilities?
networking_goals: Partnerships, collaboration, knowledge exchange
agenda: Round table discussion on universal design principles for accessibility, cross-sector collaboration, and Internet governance policy priorities for an inclusive internet
collaboration_outcomes: Follow-up actions and outputs related to cross-sector collaboration and policy recommendations for an inclusive internet

title: Tackling Deceptive Design and Regaining Consumer Autonomy
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group; Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group; Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: Identifying scenarios where deceptive design manifests, barriers to ethical design adoption, opportunities for policy interventions, and the impact on vulnerable groups.
policy_recommendations: Promoting legislation, policies, and collaborative spaces for companies, governments, and civil society to create product and policy solutions for a fairer, safer web.

title: Context and localization in algorithmic content governance
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
speakers: Javier Pallero , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Babette Ngene , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Toledo Amalia , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: How could social media companies better take into consideration local context when moderating content on their platform? What are some key challenges for adequately, consistently, and fairly considering local context? What risks and opportunities related to content governance could come from novel models of social media platforms (e.g. decentralized platforms) and rule design and enforcement?
stakeholders_involved: Civil Society, Government
impact_expectation: Content moderation and curation that adequately considers the unique social, political and cultural contexts in which content is shared – often within patriarchal environments – is urgently needed. Social media platforms thus have a responsibility to moderate and curate content in a way that promotes marginalized and vulnerable users’ (and broader stakeholders’) enjoyment of human rights, instead of harming them.

title: Creating Safe Spaces online
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Role of DSTs in enabling safety, security and accountability: How does a DST benefit each stakeholder group in achieving better digital security? Can DST's solve the online harassment faced by women? Connection with previous Messages: SDGs 5.b Targets: Our major target audience is women who are excluded because of the harassment that they face only. This session will equip them to create their own safe spaces by themselves.
policy_recommendations: We would like to expand the training worldwide, training trainers who would in place in turn train the common public to foster a culture of security and privacy. We would also like feedback to make this more inclusive.

title: Confidence Building Measures for Africa: Global Perspectives
organizers: Intergovernmental Organization, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Intergovernmental Organization, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Intergovernmental Organization, African Group, Intergovernmental Organization, African Group
key_issues: How can regional organisations like the African Union facilitate the development and implementation of confidence building measures for cyberspace that respond to the region’s specific needs? What might regional CBMs look like in an African context, and how could they contribute to strengthening the international cyber capacity building agenda?
policy_recommendations: Building confidence building measures for cyberspace can contribute to ensuring public access to information and the protection of fundamental freedoms in accordance with national legislation and international agreements, particularly by building capacity to implement the 11 norms of responsible state behaviour in cyberspace. 16- a - Building confidence building measures for cybers, space can strengthen relevant national institutions by building points of contact and facilitate international cooperation for building capacity at all levels. They also prevent violence and conflict through reducing the risks of misperception or miscalculation in cyberspace, which pose a serious threat to international peace. 17.8 - By contributing to the safety and security of citizens online and building resilience, confidence building measures for cyberspace can help create the preconditions for the development of sustainable digital growth and transformation.

title: Reducing Disparate Outcomes with Digital Health Tools
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: 1. Has digital health risen to the challenge of expanding quality care during the pandemic? 2. What is the best way to bridge the digital divide that not only separates rural areas from urban, but the global south and developing nations from the rest of the world in terms of access to digital health? 3. How can policymakers ensure that patients retain strong privacy and security assurances as the provision of some healthcare moves from in-person to online?
policy_recommendations: While clearly beneficial in the context of a pandemic, digital technologies offer great potential outside of social-distancing mandates, as they can provide patients with greater control and personalization in their treatment. These benefits could reduce global health inequities and improve the quality of life, especially for the traditionally underserved. However, these technologies also bring no shortage of challenges. Those most in need of connected healthcare are the ones who are least able to access it. Impediments include lack of smartphone access and internet coverage in rural areas, as well, as regulatory barriers stemming from legacy approaches to healthcare. Greater provision of healthcare over the internet also enhances the opportunity for cyberattacks and can create new privacy risks.

title: Accountability in Building Digital ID Infrastructures
organizers: Civil Society, African Group; Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
speakers: Laura Bingham , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Mercy Sumbi , Private Sector, African Group
Elizabeth Atori , Civil Society, African Group
Thomas Lohninger , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Digital ID systems are being introduced worldwide as solutions to financial and social welfare exclusion, healthcare access, and government service access. However, governments are creating frameworks that link essential services to these IDs, increasing exclusion risks for certain groups. Examples include SDGs 1.3, 1.4, and 1.b related to poverty eradication and financial inclusion.
policy_recommendations: The session discussed obligations of corporate actors in digital identity markets, incentives for alternatives to centralized surveillance, and accountability thresholds for affected groups. It connected with SDGs related to poverty eradication and financial inclusion.

title: Data Privacy and Knowledge Equity
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: How can regulatory frameworks that protect privacy benefit and protect the free exchange of knowledge? What can platforms and policymakers learn from online spaces that operate in the public interest about how to protect privacy and their users? What more needs to be done to protect data privacy? What specific uses of data and types of data create the greatest privacy risks?
policy_recommendations: Stronger data privacy protections will incentivize innovation within the industry that will revolutionize the way many companies make money and will bake privacy into future technology design. Creating new privacy protections will eliminate the disparity where marginalized and low-income populations must agree to allow their personal information to be exploited in order to have access to new technologies. Privacy protections ensure accountable institutions because they ensure people will not be exploited and can hold powerful actors accountable for misusing information about them in harmful ways.

title: Building Inclusive Democratic Technology Norms in Changing I
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Reforming internet governance fora to promote equitable and peaceful societies, ensuring digital technologies are not developed for harmful purposes, defining values and norms for digital policies, responsibilities of governments, businesses, technical community, and civil society for digital inclusion and human rights, connecting global instruments to national contexts, role of local, national, regional, and international stakeholders in digital inclusion.
policy_recommendations: Revitalizing multistakeholder institutions to remain relevant and responsive to stakeholders not traditionally included, developing and implementing global digital policy norms and standards in a locally-relevant and human rights-respecting manner, ensuring inclusive and democratic conversations in internet governance.

title: Universal Service and Access Funds and complementary connect
organizers: Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
speakers: Nathalia Foditsch , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Juan Peirano , Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Jane Roberts Coffin , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
regional_focus: Latin American and Caribbean, Western European and Others
key_issues: How can Universal Service and Access Funds promote inclusion towards universal connectivity? Connection with previous Messages: Economic and Social Inclusion and human rights - this session puts forward a discussion on how USAFs can play a part in an adequate enabling environment at national levels to foster inclusive, just, safe, resilient and sustainable digital societies and economies. Giving complementary connectivity solutions access to USAFs would provide communities with the opportunity to startup local networks and giving them a strong foundation to build a sustainable way to connect to the Internet. Universal Access and Meaningful Connectivity - access to USA, Funds would allow communities to develop connectivity solutions that fulfill their needs and reach areas where traditional operators have failed to connect. This would also help regulators and stakeholders to have a better understanding of their connectivity environment and the community networks ecosystem, which would allow them to better support these solutions.
policy_recommendations: A study developed by the Alliance for Affordable Internet in partnership with the Internet Society shows that billions of dollars in Universal Service and Access Funds (USAF) were not used as intended in several countries in Latin America and the Caribbean. There are many ways these funds could support the growth of Internet infrastructure, and one of them is funding complementary connectivity solutions such as community networks. This session will provide an overview of how USAFs have been used as seen in the study, and discuss why it would be beneficial for complementary connectivity solutions to be able to access them. Expected Outcomes We expect this event to feed in the discussions national governments and regulators are leading on how to make the best use of Universal Service and Access Funds to help close the digital divide.

title: IGF 2022 WS #458 Do Diverging Platform Regulations Risk an Open Internet?
organizers: Female, Switzerland, Female, Indonesia, Female, United Kingdom, Female, United Kingdom, Male, United Kingdom
speakers: Jacqueline Rowe , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Jamila Venturini , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: What forms of online platform regulation are emerging in different parts of the world, and in what ways do they diverge? What risks does policy divergence pose to an open and interoperable Internet, as well as to human rights? How can these risks be mitigated, and what opportunities are there for encouraging harmonisation and consensus?
policy_recommendations: The session builds on the IGF 2021 Message that emphasizes the need for harmonization to ensure the Internet remains a global, unified platform enabling human rights. It promotes understanding of platform regulation elements requiring harmonization and opportunities for consensus. It also links to SDG 9.c and 16.10 by exploring how to maintain an open and interoperable Internet and addressing platform regulations that may restrict human rights.

title: Community-driven Models and Combatting Disinformation
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Community-driven models for combatting disinformation: How can platforms harness the expertise of the communities that participate in them to combat disinformation spread on the platform? Can online public interest spaces with existing community-driven content moderation practices provide guidance and advice to other online platforms on effective methods for countering disinformation? What actions can and should governments and international bodies be taking to incentivize responsible platform action to combat disinformation globally? What dangers does society face if it fails?
policy_recommendations: Develop strategies to ensure that disinformation can be fought at all levels, including by educating people with regard to recognizing and correcting disinformation that they encounter in their daily lives. Eliminate disinformation to promote strong institutions, strengthen trust and increase access to justice by ensuring that the information environment upon which we rely to make decisions is accurate and free of misleading and harmful content.

title: IGF 2022 WS #460 Internet For All: The role of Media in driving Accessibility
organizers: Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: How are internet policies/telecommunication policies affecting access in Nigeria? Who are the major actions influencing this policy? What is the role of the media in driving Accessibility and Inclusion in Nigeria? Connection with previous Messages: SDGs 5. Gender Equality Targets: Access to the internet gives a lot of opportunities. It could reduce poverty by giving access to for instance farmers in remote rural communities information about how to improve their farming and access to customers beyond their immediate community. It will also reduce the digital gap which will enhance equality. Internet enabled continued education during the COVID19 lockdown.
policy_recommendations: Action plan from media professionals on interventions that could drive or increase internet access in Nigeria. Advance the debate on affordably and internet penetration in Nigeria

title: IGF 2022 WS #461 When giants change the rules: WhatsApp case reflections
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
speakers: Burcu Kilic , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Juliana Oms , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Luã Cruz , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRUL,AC)
key_issues: Discussion on the challenges data protection regulators face, the role of users and civil society organizations, and the impact of WhatsApp's policy changes on data protection laws and enforcement.
policy_recommendations: Need for adequate enabling environments and agile regulatory frameworks at national, regional, and global levels. Consideration of pro-ethical design in regulation and the incorporation of public interest in antitrust regulation to address market power and fundamental rights.

title: AI and Human Rights: An African Perspective
organizers: Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: Key regulatory issues on AI and human rights in Africa, issues, challenges and opportunities presented by AI and other emerging technologies in the African context, role of the treaty monitoring bodies
policy_recommendations: The African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (ACHPR) adopted Resolution 473 on the need to undertake a study on human and peoples’ rights and artificial intelligence (AI), robotics and other new and emerging technologies in Africa. It is anticipated that the ACHPR, based on the findings and recommendations of the study, will adopt the relevant human rights instrument that will provide the necessary guidance in ensuring the development and use of AI, robotics and other new and emerging technologies in Africa is compatible with the rights and duties in the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights and other regional and international human rights instruments.

title: Strategic Litigation for Digital Rights in Latin America
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: How should civil society organizations address personal data protection cases for strategic litigation in Latin America? How should strategic litigation be approached in personal data protection cases? How can civil society act in the face of threats to privacy?
policy_recommendations: Any new surveillance systems implemented at local or national levels should comply with basic human rights such as the principle of innocence and the right to assemble on public roads. Furthermore, they should only be implemented after proper consultation, with accountability and legitimacy checks.

title: Sending Party Pays and the Future of the Internet
organizers: Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Implications for net neutrality with the adoption of a sending-party-pays internet model, divergence from longstanding practices in telecommunications markets, potential impact on telecommunications infrastructure investment.
policy_recommendations: Discourage threats to disrupt the underlying infrastructure enabling a free and open Internet, ensure that interconnection policies do not undermine the future of the Internet.
networking_goals: Knowledge exchange on interconnection policies, collaboration on addressing challenges to net neutrality and telecommunications markets.
agenda: Short presentations by speakers to open discussions, 80% of time allocated to open discussions, encouragement of on-site and online participants to present views and solutions, balanced time allocation between online and on-site participants.
collaboration_outcomes: Further discussion on how interconnection policy has worked, reasons for new approaches, and potential impacts on Internet architecture.

title: Measuring Africa’s digital progress towards the SDGs
organizers: Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: Discussion focused on measuring digital progress in Africa towards SDGs, addressing inequality, access to data, and the impact of digitalisation on education, gender equality, and economic growth. Examined how intersectional factors affect digital access and the need for data-driven policies to mitigate pandemic impacts and support SDG achievement.
policy_recommendations: The session emphasized the importance of collecting disaggregated ICT data to inform policy-making, support SDG targets, and address inequalities. It highlighted the need for data-driven strategies to ensure equitable access to digital tools and education, particularly in the context of pandemics and digital substitution.

title: CyberPeace Corps: a movement to crowdsource CyberPeace
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: In the absence of binding regulations or norms, how can digital citizens ensure or increase safety and security in cyberspace globally? Why is the need to establish a global CyberPeace corps imminent right now?
policy_recommendations: The CyberPeace Foundation has established a volunteer-driven CyberPeace Corps consisting of digital citizens, academia, members of civil society, subject-matter experts, and organizations, all of whom volunteer their time, interests, and skills to establish peace in cyberspace.

title: IGF 2022 WS #468 Mixnets and tokens to advance privacy in the Global South
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Policy Question(s): What are Mixnets and how can they foster privacy and digital sovereignty? What could be the potential opportunities for the Global South to adopt a distributed mixnet to advance privacy? Which are the potential obstacles or threats for the Global South to adopt a distributed mixnet to protect privacy? Are incentives to run privacy infrastructure legal for individuals or collectives in the specific countries of the attendees? Connection with previous Messages: SDGs 16. Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions Targets: The proposal is looking to advance strong institutions protecting citizens *SDG16 as well as responsible production of technology, SDG 12, Infrastructure, SDG 9 and economic growth, SDG 8.
policy_recommendations: Expected Outcomes: An understanding of limitations or opportunities for countries in the Global South to advance their technical privacy-enhancing infrastructure. A community of experts that could start exploring mix nets as viable and scalable solutions to rapidly advance privacy in sensible data infrastructures, such as payments and health data. Raise awareness of regulatory obstacles or opportunities to test and deploy novel economic and social incentives for distributed digital infrastructures. Advance digital sovereignty.

title: IGF 2022 WS #469 Due diligence in the tech sector: Southern perspectives
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Intergovernmental Organization, Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
regional_focus: Latin America and the Caribbean, Africa and Asia-Pacific
themes: Environmental and human rights due diligence
key_issues: How can current debates on environmental and human rights due diligence in the tech sector be informed by policies, regulations and practices in the global South? How much are Inter-American standards (from the human rights system and the Escazu Agreement, for example) aligned with the current proposals for EU directives and norms on human rights and corporate sustainability due diligence?
policy_recommendations: The session will contribute to ongoing research and multi-stakeholder discussion towards improving policies and regulation

title: Addressing children’s privacy and edtech apps
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: Concerns about digital education apps and platforms, development of actions and regulation for better data practices in the edtech sector, technical alternatives to student-data-commercializing business models.
policy_recommendations: Debate on solutions and practices that consider the actions of all stakeholders for more sustainable and protective educational virtual practices.
target_audience: Governments, industry, stakeholders, children
stakeholders_involved: Civil Society, Private Sector, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Asia-Pacific Group, Human Rights Watch
impact_expectation: Promote sustainable and protective educational virtual practices while respecting children's rights to privacy and data protection.

title: IGF 2022 WS #472 Gendered Abuse Online through AI and VR
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Discussion on measures taken to control toxic behaviors in the metaverse, human-centric design of metaverse platforms, criminalization of sexual assault in virtual reality, and the impact of embodied digital representations on experiences of sexual violence.
policy_recommendations: Enhancing understanding of the Metaverse, exploring discrepancies between user concerns and platform safety designs, working towards human-centric policy-making for AI and VR, and understanding the distinction between sexual violence targeted at individuals vs avatars.

title: IGF 2022 WS #473 Not Just Connect: Closing Gender digital Divide in Africa
organizers: Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: Discussion on the extent of meaningful connectivity transformation for women and girls in sub-Saharan Africa, policy constraints and actions to close the gender digital divide, and policy contributions for women's digital empowerment.
policy_recommendations: Advancing digital empowerment for women and girls, identifying policy constraints and actions to close the gender digital divide, and using case studies from Uganda, Tanzania, and Ghana.

title: Balancing Digital Sovereignty and the Splinternet
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Eastern European Group, Civil Society, African Group, Civil Society, Eastern European Group
key_issues: Safeguards to prevent Digital Sovereignty from enabling Digital Rights abuses; harnessing diversity and regional/cultural particularities in digital spaces despite fragmentation; involving young people in reducing harmful trends in Internet fragmentation; Universal Access and Meaningful Connectivity; Emerging Regulation on market structure, content, data, and consumer rights; Inclusive Internet Ecosystems and Digital Cooperation; Trust, Security, and Stability.
policy_recommendations: Focus on individual autonomy of Internet users; promote collaborative, equitable, and inclusive Internet governance; build trust through IGF's role in digital cooperation; embrace policy controversies to adapt to the future.
networking_goals: Partnerships, collaboration, knowledge exchange among stakeholders to address digital sovereignty and fragmentation challenges.
agenda: Round table discussion on Digital Sovereignty and Splinternet, exploring policy questions related to Digital Rights, regional/cultural diversity, youth involvement, Universal Access, Emerging Regulation, Inclusive Internet Ecosystems, and Trust, Security, and Stability.
collaboration_outcomes: Potential collaboration outcomes include fostering inclusive Internet governance, building trust through IGF's role, and developing strategies to address digital fragmentation and promote digital rights.

title: Datafication in the South: opportunities and challenges
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: Designing sustainable ICT-based initiatives for digital transformation, addressing data-intensive policies, ensuring data governance, stakeholder involvement in application design, impact of data-driven technologies on rights, digital identity, consent, autonomy, privacy, responsible data-sharing for policy development, protection of digital rights in crisis situations.
policy_recommendations: Debate on solutions and best practices for sustainable and inclusive development in datafication, considering actions of all stakeholders, aligning with IGF 2021 Messages on Economic and Social Inclusion and Human Rights, Universal Access and Meaningful Connectivity.

title: Promoting human centric approaches while deploying AI in CA
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Current state of access of CA countries to knowledge, tools, data and best practices for AI policy and practices development; improving partnership and multistakeholderism to protect human rights and democratic values; extent of multilateral advisory support for legal frameworks; reliable international legal framework for CA countries.
policy_recommendations: Designing and submitting the concept of this Workshop based on knowledge from IGF 2021, aligning civil society role with SDG targets 10.1 to 10.6 to ensure inclusive and human centric approaches in AI development, reduce inequalities, eliminate discriminatory laws, and promote appropriate legislation.
networking_goals: Partnerships, collaboration, knowledge exchange among civil society, technical communities, and governments to promote human centric AI development and ensure human rights protection.
agenda: Discussion on AI policy, human rights, digital governance, and multistakeholder approaches; sharing of experiences from IGF 2021; designing a workshop concept for CA countries.
collaboration_outcomes: Designing and submitting a workshop concept based on IGF 2021 knowledge, aligning with SDG targets to ensure inclusive AI development and reduce inequalities.

title: IGF 2022 WS #48 Balancing Child Online Protection and Rights to the Internet
organizers: Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization, Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Intergovernmental Organization, Asia-Pacific Group, Private Sector, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Discussion focused on balancing child online protection with the right to access the Internet, exploring joint governance mechanisms among state, society, family, and school; addressing how technology companies can avoid over-restriction while protecting children; and improving laws/policies to align with UN Convention on the Rights of the Child principles.
policy_recommendations: Promote multi-dimensional participation in child online governance, ensure stakeholder representation in policy formulation, and emphasize the balance between children's right to access the Internet and online protection.
target_audience: Governments, civil society, private sector, and international organizations involved in child online protection and Internet governance.
stakeholders_involved: Intergovernmental Organizations, Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Groups, Private Sector, Governments, and International Organizations.
impact_expectation: Enhance global cooperation on child online protection, promote the implementation of child rights in the digital environment, and ensure equitable access to the Internet while safeguarding children from online harms.

title: IGF 2022 WS #480 Ensuring Digital Safety for Children with Disability
organizers: Civil Society, African Group, Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: Discussion on policies to protect children with disabilities online, ensuring their safety, and addressing digital inequalities affecting different groups.
policy_recommendations: Advocacy towards safer internet education for children with disabilities and developing targeted policies for their digital safety.

title: IGF 2022 WS #481 Multistakeholder Approaches to Advancing Economic Inclusion
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: How can local business communities, civil society, governments, and the technical community work together to address key barriers that hinder the advancement of economic inclusion online? What approaches, tools, or resources have been/could be instrumental in supporting small- and medium-sized enterprises to build the knowledge and skills necessary to meaningfully participate online?
policy_recommendations: Recommendations for governments, business, and civil society to consider in order to reduce digital divides and ensure equitable access to the internet for all.

title: IGF 2022 WS #482 Internet Shutdowns: Diverse risks, challenges, and needs
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: How can multistakeholder communities in countries that experience internet shutdowns develop multi-pronged strategies to resist shutdowns and push for more resilient networks? What are the reasons governments are using internet shutdowns and interfering with networks in both democracies and autocracies? What are the situations that lead to increases in shutdowns? What are policy proposals and narratives that can push governments to take alternative approaches instead of shutting the internet?
policy_recommendations: The session will pull on quotes and data from the private sector (banking institutions, digital infrastructure providers, small e-businesses) to reflect on the impact of shutdowns on industry innovation and resilience infrastructure. Apart from the obvious economic impact that shutdown, the presentation will also discuss how disrupted internet impacts the ability to provide quality formal and informal education and distribute information, and how shutdowns are used during elections and protests to destabilize democracies and delegitimize governing institutions. We will also draw on the perspectives of health institutions to discuss how internet shutdowns not only prevent effective health delivery, but increased disinformation and rumor during Covid-19 and have widespread and deleterious mental health effects on those who experience them. Finally, internet shutdowns exacerbate digital and physical equalities both within and across countries, especially when it comes to the gendered digital divide.

title: IGF 2022 WS #484 Data Justice: Lessons Learned in Africa, Latin & South America
organizers: Civil Society, African Group, Civil Society, African Group, Civil Society, African Group, Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
speakers: Isaac Amuku , Civil Society, African Group
María Paz Hermosilla , Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Eliana Quiroz , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
regional_focus: Africa, Latin America and South America
key_issues: 1. Is data governance practices and processes being done as provided by the existing policies and laws, looking at power, equity, identity, access, knowledge, and participation? 2. Are the policymakers, developers, and impacted communities aware of their rights and responsibilities to ensure data justice for everyone? 3. What are the existing legal frameworks on data protection and privacy globally and what steps should be taken to ensure there is data justice?
policy_recommendations: Connection with previous Messages: SDGs 9. Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure Targets: SDG 9, Industrial Innovation and Infrastructure aim to build resilient infrastructure, promote sustainable industrialization, and foster innovation. Our session discusses data governance which is a key component of innovation. SDG 10, Reduce inequality, our session discusses data governance, data equity, and data justice that is aimed at promoting equality when it comes to access, usage, and participation of data. SDG 5, Gender Equality, our sessions look at data justice in a way of eliminating all forms of discrimination against women and girls in regards to data. SDG 16, Peace Justice and Strong Institutions, our session on data justice that also looks at social justice is linked to SDG 16 that aims at access to justice for all and build effective, accountable, and inclusive institutions at all levels.

title: Overcome effectiveness challenges in CNs' project
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Technical Community, African Group
key_issues: Engaging policymakers and regulators to support open market participation through licensing regimes and spectrum allocation practices; promoting affordable and meaningful connectivity through community networks; methodological approaches to involve beneficiaries in internet access and digital inclusion processes.
policy_recommendations: Mapping community networks to build participatory training curriculums; reviewing Universal Access Funds requirements to support small cooperatives and community networks; considering regulatory measures and public policies for private sector investment sustainability; aligning with SDGs 8.2, 8.3, and 9.
stakeholders_involved: Civil Society, Technical Community, African Group, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
impact_expectation: Enhancing internet access and digital inclusion in marginalized regions; promoting sustainable community networks; supporting telework and healthcare accessibility; contributing to SDGs 8.2, 8.3, and 9.

title: IGF 2022 WS #486 How to fight disinformation in digital age
organizers: Civil Society, Eastern European Group
key_issues: Discussion focused on solutions to combat disinformation, effectiveness of fact-checking initiatives, strategic communication improvements between governments and civil society, and connections to SDGs 4 and 16. Topics included the role of quality education in combating fake news, the need for digital security education at personal and state levels, international norms of conduct in cyberspace, and the participation of developing countries in global governance.
policy_recommendations: The session emphasized the importance of quality education (SDG 4.4 and 4.7) for combating disinformation through lifelong learning for stakeholders and future decision makers. It highlighted the need for international norms of conduct in cyberspace (SDG 16.1) and the inclusion of small states in global governance (SDG 13.10). Recommendations included developing educational materials for media literacy, fostering collaboration between states, and ensuring inclusive and trustworthy information dissemination.

title: Gender Violence Online: A Global Threat
organizers: Civil Society, Intergovernmental Organization, Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Current regulatory legislation in EU, UK, and US affecting global internet and gaps in gender protections; disinformation in national elections; deepfakes as tools of gender violence; need for accountability criteria for misleading content.
policy_recommendations: Increase awareness of the scale of the problem, increase participation by diverse actors with improved digital literacy, add new voices and pressure for transparent and responsive technology platforms and informed regulators.

title: IGF 2022 WS #49 African Data Protection Landscape
organizers: Government, African Group; Intergovernmental Organization, Eastern European Group
speakers: Mercy King'ori , Civil Society, African Group
Nevana Ruzic , Civil Society, Eastern European Group
key_issues: The role of African DPAs and the challenges they are facing in safeguarding the data protection rights of individuals across the country, continent, and internationally; the enablers and barriers, including legal, institutional and financial hurdles, for enforcement of the data protection laws by African DPAs; how can DPAs best cooperate on enforcing the rights and freedoms of individuals across the continent and internationally?
policy_recommendations: The proposal is linked to a number of SDG targets as the discussion aims to address the effectiveness, transparency, and accountability (target 16.6) of the African DPAs and the role of national supervisory authorities in protecting fundamental freedoms, including privacy and public access to information (target 16.10). Moreover, as DP, as regulators play a key role in digitalization and sustainable developments in Africa, the panel aims also to discuss opportunities for policy coordination and policy coherence at the national, regional, and international levels (targets 17.13 and 17.14) and the role of the DPAs in encouraging effective public, public-private and civil society partnerships (target 17.17).

title: IGF 2022 WS #490 Using human rights due diligence to navigate crises
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
speakers: Laura O'Brien , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Berhan Taye , Civil Society, African Group
Farzaneh Badiei , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
Marlena Wisniak , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Should companies have a responsibility to conduct heightened corporate due diligence in times of crisis? How does international humanitarian law intersect with international human rights law in the context of conflict? What responsibilities are specific to tech companies in times of crisis? How should companies engage with conflicting parties? How can companies and internet governance bodies work with civil society and states to understand state sanctions and shape practices to protect human rights while promoting connectivity?
policy_recommendations: Build upon previous discussions on digital transformation processes being diverse, inclusive, democratic and sustainable. Narrow in on defining 'the concept of meaningful access' and connectivity. Prioritize corporate human rights due diligence that considers unique social, political and cultural contexts, especially in patriarchal environments. Strive to connect all those in least developed countries to the internet as per SDG 9.c.
stakeholders_involved: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), African Group, Asia-Pacific Group, Technology Companies, Internet Governance Bodies, States
impact_expectation: To ensure that digital transformation processes are diverse, inclusive, democratic and sustainable. To define 'the concept of meaningful access' and connectivity. To protect human rights while promoting connectivity and access to ICTs, especially for vulnerable and marginalized communities in times of crisis.

title: The future of Interplanetary networks - A talk with Vint Cerf
organizers: Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Civil Society, Eastern European Group, Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group
speakers: Vinton CERF , Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Veronica Piccolo , Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
Nicolas Fiumarelli , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Mauricia Cindy Abdol Tshilunda , Intergovernmental Organization, Intergovernmental Organization
key_issues: 1. Innovation Potential of the Internet. Is a similar breakthrough in the context of digitalization, which took place when the Internet was created, still possible? 2. Potentiality of Interplanetary networks. What are the opportunities for the world with the Interplanetary networks and which problems that exist today may disappear with the further development of these new systems? In particular, will it solve the meaningful connectivity challenge that we face today for good? And if not Interplanetary networks, how do we ensure meaningful digital connectivity to every denizen of the Earth? 3. Challenges of Interplanetary networks. The most groundbreaking inventions in the history of mankind were born "out of nothing", while today’s innovation builds on top of previous ones and it requires international cooperation. When it comes to interplanetary networks what are the main difficulties to be overcome from a technical, geo-spatial and geo-political point of view?
policy_recommendations: SDGs 4, 8, 9, and 17. Interplanetary networks do not yet exist but they may have the potential to provide Internet access in remote areas provided that a new delay and disruption tolerant protocol is developed and implemented. This requires huge investments in R&D in the ICT industry, staff upskilling, as well as the upscaling of undergraduate education and postgraduate research.
format: U roundtable but with one speaker - Vint Cerf - in the spotlight. The other seats will be occupied by youth leaders and youth audience. There will be an air of informality during the discussion to facilitate honest exchange of thoughts between Vint and youth.
networking_goals: Incorporate more youth in mainstream discussions as they are one of the key stakeholders and the future custodians of the Internet.
agenda: Discussion on the innovation potential of the Internet, potentiality of Interplanetary networks, and challenges of Interplanetary networks. The session will include a roundtable discussion with Vint Cerf and youth leaders and audience.
collaboration_outcomes: The session targets SDGs 4, 8, 9, and 17. It aims to explore how Interplanetary networks can provide Internet access in remote areas through the development of new protocols, requiring investments in R&D, staff upskilling, and education.

title: IGF 2022 WS #493 Is encryption a human right? Voices of human rights actors
organizers: Civil Society, Eastern European Group; Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: International standards: Does encryption require special protections under international human rights law due to its enabling and protective functions for exercise of human rights online, particularly for, but not limited to, the right to freedom of expression and the right to privacy? How should different stakeholders approach encryption in the drafting and shaping of the international cybersecurity agreements? Enabling safety and security: How can the multistakeholder community ensure that the implementation of laws and policies that restrict encryption does not exacerbate the threats and challenges already faced by civil society and human rights actors?
policy_recommendations: Connection with previous Messages: One of the messages in the IGF 2021 Outcomes in the "Trust, security, stability" issue reads as follows: "...cyber norms should include the views of all stakeholders (including victims, first responders, and frontline defenders) and address meaningfully their needs and responsibilities. Processes need to be based on research and analysis which include these communities." This proposal responds to this message by seeking to emphasize the perspectives of the human rights actors on the policies that govern the use of encryption as a tool that is essential in their work. SDGs 16. Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions Targets: All over the world human rights defenders, activists, journalists and other civil society actors work in pursuit of the targets outlined in SDG 1,6. To do so effectively they rely on encryption every step of the way. Encryption enables human rights defenders to communicate safely and build strategies, protects sensitive data and evidence that can help achieve accountability and justice. Encryption empowers journalists and activists to expose wrongdoings and abuse of power while keeping their sources anonymous. More broadly, encryption empowers civil society to stay resilient in times of crisis and conflict. As such, encryption is at the core of the fight for human rights in the digital age, empowering civil society and human rights actors to continue with their important work despite the threats and challenges they face on a daily basis.

title: Cutting Ties: Citizens caught between conflict and tech
organizers: Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Discussion on the impact of digital service restrictions on citizens, rules for tech companies, compliance with laws affecting human rights, and the concept of Digital Apartheid.
policy_recommendations: Agreed consensus on the need for principles and guidelines to dictate restrictions, and the importance of balancing human rights with legal compliance.
networking_goals: Knowledge sharing, collaboration on digital rights issues, and fostering partnerships between civil society and the private sector.
agenda: Interactive roundtable discussion on the policy questions related to digital service restrictions, content moderation, and the impact on citizens' rights.
collaboration_outcomes: Potential follow-up actions include developing guidelines for tech companies and states, and fostering partnerships to address digital rights issues.

title: IGF 2022 WS #495 Strategising for an EcoInternet- A Multistakeholder Dialogue
organizers: Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group, Private Sector, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
key_issues: Policy recommendations to achieve an EcoInternet, key factors and challenges to effective collaboration between government and industry in policymaking and implementation to monitor and reduce the environmental impact caused by booming digitalisation, main reasons of Asia Pacific region lagging behind in 'greening' the Internet or other green initiatives, and how to strategise in order to keep up with other regions e.g. Europe and North America.
policy_recommendations: Facilitate strategic planning and policy making to tackle environmental impact caused by the Internet, promote and advocate for the Internet’s sustainability through global platforms.

title: Designing an AI ethical framework in the Global South
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC); Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC); Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
speakers: Thiago Moraes , Government, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Juan Carlos Lara G. , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Smriti Parsheera , Civil Society, Asia-Pacific Group
Wayne Wei Wang , Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group
Bobina Zulfa , Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: Exploring AI regulatory frameworks in the Global South, alignment with UNESCO's AI Ethics Recommendation, inclusion of marginalized groups, oversight and enforcement mechanisms.
policy_recommendations: Reinforce the importance of diversity and multistakeholderism in AI regulatory processes, align initiatives with UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence.
description: The aim of this proposal is to explore how regulatory frameworks for AI have been shaped in the Global South as well as to what extent they align with UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence. The session will include an expository presentation (panel) followed by a round-table discussion, with speakers presenting AI regulatory initiatives from their countries and engaging in discussions to answer three policy questions.
preparatory_focus: To explore AI regulatory frameworks in the Global South and their alignment with UNESCO's AI Ethics Recommendation, with a focus on inclusion, oversight mechanisms, and multistakeholderism.

title: Free Access to Information - a human right
organizers: Civil Society, African Group; Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG); Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: How can we achieve access to digital goods and information as a universal human right? How to we enable access especially for people and groups who are left-behind in traditional business models? How can we provide local access to decentralised information to address the global challenges and achieve the sustainable development goals (SDGs)?
policy_recommendations: The session follows up on Katowice IGF Messages regarding Universal Access and Meaningful Connectivity - There is an urgent need to understand why policy solutions already known and proven to be effective are not being more widely implemented. - Ensuring that all people everywhere have meaningful and sustainable access to the Internet must be a priority. Access to the open Internet is key for bridging the digital divide, as well as fostering democracy and human rights. - The open Internet can be considered a multistakeholder domain, fostering dialogue. There are three main elements that structure the concept of meaningful access: (a) affordable access (e.g. to connectivity, devices); (b) social environment (skills, education, content, multilingualism); (c) meaningful, permanent, and quality connectivity (including the technical foundation that allows meaningful access to become a reality). - Public access through institutions such as libraries can help deliver on all of the components of access that help drive development – equitable and inclusive connectivity, content and competencies. The COVID-19 pandemic has demonstrated that countries had to prioritise the massive development of connectivity infrastructure to connect the unconnected to an increasingly digital world. SDGs 1.4 4.a 5.b 9.c 16.10 Targets: The proposal addresses all SDG targets related to the access to information and services - SDG 1.4 Equal access to basic services - SDG 4.A Education facilities for effective learning for all - SDG 5.B Use of enabling technologies - SDG 9.C universal and affordable access - SDG 16.10 ensure public access to information The universal and inclusive access to information is the basis for digital inclusion, better health (SDG 3), quality education (SDG 4), empowerment of girls and women (SDG 5), reduced inequalities (SDG 10) and all targets in need of bringing information out to every single human being.

title: IGF 2022 WS #499 A right to digital knowledge: building an agenda
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: The costs of an approach focused only on curing symptoms of dysfunction; taking a positive approach to promoting the creation, sharing and use of knowledge digitally; where priorities should lie; ensuring that initiatives like the fight against harmful content do not inadvertently harm public interest research and education.
policy_recommendations: A comprehensive, positive approach to digital knowledge; defining key principles for promoting digital research and knowledge; addressing barriers to access, skills, and relevant laws; ensuring coordinated approaches across SDGs.

title: IGF 2022 WS #500 Role of Community to Achieve Universal Acceptance
organizers: Civil Society, African Group, Civil Society, Asian-Pacific Group, Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group, Technical Community, Eastern European Group, Technical Community, African Group
speakers: Hadia Elminiawi , Civil Society, African Group
Anil Kumar Jain , Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group
Maria Kolesnikova , Technical Community, Eastern European Group
Ajay Data , Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group
Dessalegn Mequanint Yehuala , Technical Community, African Group
key_issues: The role of stakeholders (businesses, communities, governments) in achieving Universal Acceptance; training and capacity building requirements for UA; mechanisms for sustainable growth of UA.
policy_recommendations: Collaboration between governments, businesses, and communities to implement policies supporting UA; capacity building for domestic institutions; enabling access to internet users through local languages; promoting UA-ready businesses for global market access.
stakeholders_involved: Governments, businesses, communities, technical communities, civil society organizations
impact_expectation: Promote consumer choice, improve competition, support local culture and products, create new business opportunities, enable equal and meaningful internet experience for all users regardless of language.

title: IGF 2022 WS #501 Spyware Industry, human rights, and the Internet ecosystem
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
speakers: David Kaye , Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
André Ramiro , Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
Jeanette Hofman , Technical Community, Eastern European Group
key_issues: The session discussed principles concerning user's rights such as privacy and data protection, freedom of expression and physical integrity that States should consider when evaluating the necessity and proportionality for the use of spywares in law enforcement. It also addressed the regulation of governmental hacking and the spyware industry, including development, importation, and exportation aspects. The role of civil society, academia, the private and public sectors in governing the spyware industry was also explored. The session connected with previous messages from IGF 2021, emphasizing the need for legally binding agreements on technology and human rights, and the impact of cyberweapons on trust, security, and stability of the internet.
policy_recommendations: The session proposed advancing the debate on the protection and enforcement of human rights through possible regulation approaches towards industries that have violated human rights. It suggested considering moratoriums or bans on the spyware industry and promoting legally binding agreements on technology and human rights. The session also highlighted the importance of addressing the use of cyberweapons to maintain trust, security, and stability in the internet ecosystem.

title: Platform regulation: perspectives from the Global South
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: Discussion on the impact of content moderation policies on different regions, regulatory principles for content moderation, challenges in regulating global platforms, and regional approaches to ensure alignment with human rights standards.
policy_recommendations: Advocating for principles such as transparency, global taxonomy of service providers, rights application, proportionality, and harmonization to guide policy approaches towards market competition and consumer protection.
stakeholders_involved: Civil Society, Government, Technical Community, Private Sector
impact_expectation: To advance discussions on platform regulation, ensure alignment with international human rights standards, and promote inclusive decision-making processes.

title: Metaverse: incorporating children’s rights in its design
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: Risks to children's safety, privacy, and rights under UNCRC in augmented realities; implications of metaverse and VR on children's development; governance standards and regulatory frameworks for children-friendly metaverse design.
policy_recommendations: Development of technical and legal frameworks ensuring children's rights in virtual reality; promoting sustainable consumption and production; reducing inequalities through South-global voices; ensuring healthy technologies for vulnerable populations.

title: DNS Abuse: Where are we and where do we want to be?
organizers: Private Sector, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Private Sector, African Group, Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Trends in DNS Abuse, collaboration to decrease abuse rates, emerging issues in DNS Abuse
policy_recommendations: Inclusion of all stakeholders in the development and implementation of cyber norms, processes based on research and analysis including communities, ensuring a safe online experience for all users
format: Birds of a Feather - Auditorium - 30 Min
networking_goals: Collaboration to ensure abuse rates decrease, knowledge exchange on DNS Abuse trends and emerging issues
agenda: Discussion on trends in DNS Abuse, collaboration to decrease abuse rates, exploration of emerging issues in DNS Abuse
collaboration_outcomes: Sharing of information between diverse actors, follow-up on DNS Abuse discussions and work streams

title: Connecting Girls in ICT and Safeguarding online GBV
organizers: Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: Barriers and challenges that hinder online safety of young girls, recommendations and policies on models that can work to ensure digital rights are safeguarded online
policy_recommendations: Discussion will address the barriers and challenges that hinder online safety of young girls, will provide recommendations and policies on models that can work to ensure digital rights are safeguarded online

title: IGF 2022 WS #508 Banning Facial Recognition in Public Security
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: Deconstructing the idea that facial recognition is beneficial for public security, promoting awareness among marginalized groups, and discussing strategies to ban the technology.
policy_recommendations: Promote campaigns to ban facial recognition in public security, aligning with SDGs 11 and 16 to ensure inclusive cities and effective institutions.
stakeholders_involved: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
impact_expectation: To contribute to global efforts in banning AI for mass biometric surveillance and promote human rights and inclusive institutions.

title: IGF 2022 WS #509 Copyright and innovation in a data-intensive world
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC); Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC); Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)

Additionally, the session shall be broadcast via YouTube, to the extent deemed possible, on the official channels of the organizations involved.

title: Financing mechanisms for locally-owned Internet networks
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: Discussion on financial mechanisms to complement public efforts for universal meaningful connectivity, encouraging private investment collaboration with civil society organizations, and ensuring long-term financial sustainability of community networks.
policy_recommendations: Policy suggestions on enabling financial mechanisms, fostering private sector-civil society collaboration, and ensuring sustainable funding for community networks.
subtheme: Connecting All People and Safeguarding Human Rights
format: Birds of a Feather - Auditorium - 90 Min
description: Connecting the next 2.9 billion requires changing old network deployment models, and policy/regulatory and financing frameworks. How will we help your community create change and digital equity? We'll bring you a panel of community network experts and experienced impact investors who are working on a new study that aims to catalyze communities to change local circumstances and increase digital equity and inclusion through adaptable and sustainable community network deployment and creative financing models. See this link for a preview: We'll include data from existing community networks deployments, data on creative ways to finance these non-traditional networks, and hands-on financial modeling to help you and your communities through a financial modeling workshop
preparatory_focus: This session amplifies IGF 2021 messages on Universal access and meaningful connectivity and builds on emerging regulations and inclusive Internet governance ecosystems, aiming to catalyze communities towards digital equity and inclusion through sustainable community network deployment and creative financing models.

title: IGF 2022 WS #512 Are Platform Regulations Leading to Internet Fragmentation?
organizers: Civil Society, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: 1. Does a competition vs. fragmentation tradeoff exist within currently circulating digital platform proposals, given their proliferation across different markets and legal regimes? Is fragmentation avoidable while respecting the sovereignty of nations and regions to create their own regulatory paradigms? 2. How is the trend toward digital platform regulation influenced by regional economic imperatives? 3. How is the average internet user helped or harmed by jurisdictions taking individualized approaches to digital platform regulation?
policy_recommendations: Stricter platform competition rules could broaden access, increase consumer choice, and incentivize platforms to compete on innovative privacy practices and services. At the same time, if proposals are not appropriately tailored, they could inadvertently create privacy or security risks for end-users and/or undermine the ecosystem for innovation. Finding the appropriate balance is crucial to continued progress toward numerous SDGs.

title: IGF 2022 WS #513 The technology-environment nexus: Connectivity Alternatives
organizers: Technical Community, African Group, Technical Community, Asia-Pacific Group, Civil Society, African Group, Technical Community, African Group
key_issues: 1. How can eco-friendly design, policy reform, and sustainable internet usage be improved in the wake of emerging technologies? 2. What strategies exist to implement climate-safe e-waste recycling initiatives in countries? 3. Can e-waste management initiatives enhance connectivity plans in Digital Inclusion Strategies? 4. The E-waste economy fueled by consumerism 3.0, how do we create end-user accountability eco-friendly policies and enforce green technologies and energy transitions?
policy_recommendations: Encourage circular economy and tackle e-waste: Whenever a digital device is bought, significant environmental damage has already occurred. It is thus crucial to strive toward circular business models, keeping the devices and resources in use as long as possible. Enhance device refurbishment, redistribution, and repurposing as an approach to connecting people who are not connected due to device barriers. Build a conceptual framework for e-waste recycling and digital sustainability for cities. Connect the unconnected communities is inherently a matter of sustainability. SDGs 11. Sustainable Cities and Communities 12. Responsible Production and Consumption 13. Climate Action

title: IGF 2022 WS #514 Is it possible to connect communities to broadband Internet?
organizers: Technical Community, African Group; Government, African Group; Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: The session explored five key policy questions related to connecting communities to broadband Internet, including infrastructure investment in rural areas, digital policy blueprints, spectrum allocation practices, the Digital Global Compact, and the Digital Cooperation Report. It also connected these issues to the SDGs, particularly focusing on poverty eradication and digital inclusion.
policy_recommendations: The session did not explicitly agree on specific policy recommendations, but it highlighted the need for stakeholders to address the challenges in infrastructure investment, digital policy development, spectrum management, and the implementation of the Digital Global Compact and Digital Cooperation Report.
talk_topics: Infrastructure and Investment: Are UN member states/stakeholders committed to investing in infrastructure in rural areas?
Digital Policy: Do the UN Member States each have a Digital Policy Blueprint?
Spectrum Allocation/Management: Spectrum cost as a roadblock for community Internet Service providers
Digital Global Compact: Does this compact make sense to the stakeholders?
Digital Cooperation Report: Have the UN member states done a bare minimum for the report?
key_takeaways: The session emphasized the importance of connecting rural and underserved communities to broadband Internet as a key driver for socio-economic development and poverty eradication. It highlighted the need for collaborative efforts among stakeholders to address infrastructure investment, digital policy, spectrum management, and the implementation of global digital initiatives like the Digital Global Compact and Digital Cooperation Report.

title: IGF 2022 WS #515 Adjustments for the Deployment of Resilient Infrastructures?
organizers: Civil Society, African Group, Private Sector, African Group, Government, African Group

Political leadership: Encouragement to effectively play its major role so that other stakeholders take their responsibility and contribute in an inclusive manner to digital acceleration in and after the Covid-19 era; Advance the participation and involvement of our African countries; and ensure that our governments and regulators, as well as other stakeholder actors, regularly and increasingly intervene and contribute in these governance spaces to ensure that African interests and viewpoints, in each of the stakeholders of its sub-ecosystem, on digital issues, are known and taken into account; Reform and establishment of an adequate framework in line with the international law regime to clearly regulate the Internet and digital space in Africa and Cameroon; Implement digital policies for the unconnected and for the disconnected; Collaborative Framework of all actors involved in the issue of digital inclusion to provide access through digital infrastructure to all; SDGs 4.4 4.5 4.6 4.7 4.c 5.1 5.2 9. Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure 9.1 9.2 9.3 9.4 9.5 9.a 9.b 9.c 10.1 10.2 10.3 10.4 10.5 10.6 10.7 10.a 10.b 10.c Targets: Each of these, as well as others, are aided by the protection of the right to access to the Internet; both as a source of information and sharing. In all cases, this access and sharing can be aided by reasonable applications of Internet Governance.
subtheme: Connecting All People and Safeguarding Human Rights
description: The complete topic the IGF Cameroon will cover will treat about about Accelerating the Digital Transformation looking at which Adjustments for the Deployment of Resilient Infrastructures? The African leadership’s style will determine the way in which Africa will be involved in the discussions cur
preparatory_focus: Focus on capacity building, training, or pre-discussion themes related to resilient infrastructure deployment and digital inclusion.

title: IGF 2022 WS #517 New data on fairer access to health using the Internet
organizers: Private Sector, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC), Intergovernmental Organization, African Group, Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG)
key_issues: What are the key areas in which the Internet Governance community can contribute to the furthering of fairer access to health using the Internet? How can health data be leveraged in an ethical manner to generate human-centric solutions that result in greater well-being to people around the world? What are the next steps for fora such as the IGF and its different initiatives to take in order to help promote fairer access to health using the Internet?
policy_recommendations: Encourage and promote effective public, public-private and civil society partnerships, building on the experience and resourcing strategies of partnerships Data, monitoring and accountability.

title: IGF 2022 WS #52 De-platforming as Censorship Means in the Digital Era
organizers: Civil Society, Eastern European Group
key_issues: Discussion on content moderation and de-platforming as censorship means, examining their role in fighting extremism, preventing violence, and addressing digital space fragmentation. Analysis of who is most targeted by de-platforming and digital censorship, definition of harmful content, mechanisms to mitigate moderator bias, and guidelines for balancing freedom of speech with hate speech. Exploration of state effectiveness in regulating social media and digital services.
policy_recommendations: Need for transparent content moderation policies by platforms, balancing freedom of expression with human rights. Reflection on technology's role in serving humanity, not just implementing safeguards. States' duty to prevent human rights harm through regulation and enforcement, along with access to remedies and human rights due diligence in technology development. Prioritizing universal Internet access and sustainable connectivity. Focusing on individual autonomy in digital sovereignty debates. Promoting collaborative and inclusive Internet governance.

title: Digital rights and meaningful access in the African diaspora
organizers: Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC); Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC); Civil Society, African Group; Civil Society, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: Promote public policies to overcome digital divide for social justice in diaspora; measure disparities and compare intersectional efforts of access in Africa and its diaspora with regional peculiarities; promote digital equality for media diversity and freedom of expression
policy_recommendations: Connect and advance approaches to racial justice in internet governance and digital technologies; pursue non-discrimination, diversity and inclusion; ensure affordable and accessible Internet for all, including fighting illiteracy in the Global South

title: Health Data Governance in Africa and Sharing Agency
organizers: Civil Society, African Group
key_issues: How do we include context of African societies in health data collection tools? Who are the multi-stakeholders involved in African health data eco-system? How important is the re-use of health data for sustainable healthcare? What model of health data governance will make Africans feel empowered? How governments and donors facilitate the use of health data for the benefits of society?
policy_recommendations: Awareness of multistakeholder health data governance model approaches. Development of draft policy document on culturally sensitive health data governance frameworks. Form an Eco-system of African health data governance advocates.

title: Youthful approach at data protection in messaging apps

While the EU’s adoption of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) has galvanized governments around the world to consider new approaches to data protection, there is a need to enable collaboration and information sharing for new data protection models, advocacy approaches, debates, and best practices emerging from the Global South. During this session, panelists from these organizations will describe the challenges they faced in the legislative process, implementation, and enforcement of data protection policies as well as the best practices developed specifically for other organizations working in similar contexts. title: IGF 2021 WS #115 Fan the Flames? Regulating Competition in Digital Markets
organizers: Private Sector, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Technical Community, Western European and Others Group (WEOG), Civil Society, Eastern European Group, Technical Community, Latin American and Caribbean Group (GRULAC)
key_issues: Regulation, competition and innovation: How could regulatory and self-regulatory frameworks help foster more competitive Internet-related markets, a larger diversity of business models, and more innovation? Protecting consumer rights: What regulatory approaches are/could be effective in upholding consumer rights, offering adequate remedies for rights violations, and eliminating unfair and deceptive practices from the part of Internet companies?
policy_recommendations: Anti-competitive practices are not a new issue. They have always been there; however, as the Internet-related markets boomed, not only during the COVID-19 pandemic but also before, and large tech companies grasped a huge market, the extent of such monopolistic practices changed and shifted to digital platforms. The change, on the other, necessitated a sophisticated approach to regulating Internet-related markets. Of course, it is on the regulatory bodies to ensure a competitive market structure, and apparently, they have taken this duty quite seriously. For example, the recent Media Bargaining Code in Australia that was aimed to restore market power balance between local news media business and large digital platforms like Google or Facebook is interestingly promoted by another tech giant, Microsoft, in other large economies arguing that it is good for democracy. Such emerging regulations targeting Internet-related markets are not only local or regional; another example of the impacts of similar regulations can be seen in the EU General Data Protection Regulation as an ongoing one, and in the EU Digital Services Act (DSA), the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) and the EU New Competition Tool (NCT) as emerging ones.
